articles.title: The US Arms Bottleneck Is Impacting Its East Asian Allies
articles.body:
In May, Taiwan was offered no less than four different explanations for the delays in receiving a $14 billion arms package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors and NASAMS air defense systems.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao testified to senators that the United States was “doing a pause” on the arms sale to Taiwan “in order to make sure we have the munitions we need for Epic Fury,” the U.S. military operation in Iran. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio then claimed that the sale was under review, not “paused.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said it wasn’t about Iran at all: “our stockpiles are more than suited… both there [in Iran] and around the globe.” Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump said the arms sales were “a very good negotiating chip” with China, suggesting a purely political motivation for the delay.
Beyond the problem of conflicting explanations, none of these statements provided the answer Taipei really wants: a delivery date.
Taiwan is not alone in waiting for promised U.S. weapons. The U.S. government informed Japan that delivery of 400 long-awaited Tomahawk cruise missiles would be delayed two years to meet drawdown demands from the current war in Iran.
The problem is obvious: the U.S. has finite supplies of these missiles, and a growing need. Taiwan and Japan are queuing up, in the same line, behind Ukraine and behind resupplies for the Iran war.
Lockheed Martin exceeded their production record with over 500 interceptors in 2024. But the U.S. military itself shot nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors in the Iran war. In the fiscal budget for next year, the U.S. Army asked for over 2,700 interceptors, a large jump from the 357 it previously funded. Taiwan’s order of 102 interceptors sits somewhere within that request. Japan’s order does too.
The U.S. requirement for 2,700 interceptors merely scratches the surface of the problem. The United States is facing depleted assets of its own while also tasked with supporting vital allies through arms deliveries. If the United States spent 1,500 interceptors in a matter of months on Iran, what will Taiwan require to defend itself? Certainly, more than the 102 systems that currently only exist on paper.
In evaluating the strength of U.S. deterrence, Chinese military and political leaders will consider whether or not they can deplete U.S. and allied stocks more rapidly than they can replenish them. Beijing doesn’t have to guess if the United States can sustain a major war in the Indo-Pacific; the U.S. fiscal budget request, the contracts awarded, and the backlog of arms sales are all public information.
U.S. allies aren’t blind to this. Chen Yi-fan of Tamkang University wrote that even if the deal was opened up for bidding immediately it would take four to five years for a Patriot system to arrive in Taiwan – and that’s the exact timeframe during which American and Taiwan planners believe a crisis could occur.
Meanwhile, the AUKUS initiative was retooled in May due to the realization that the United States would be unable to produce new submarines for Australia. Allies know what that means.
You can’t ramp up factories, suppliers, machine shops, and skilled labor immediately. Even when Congress appropriates budgets, production capacity slotted to come online in 2030 isn’t going to deter Beijing in 2027. Funding the U.S. munitions supply chain is no longer the bottleneck. The challenge is accelerating the construction timeline for new production capacity.
The normal sequence is government demand first, then new capacity being developed. Contracts are awarded before firms invest in facilities, machines, and the people who will do the work. Flipping that model on its head could shorten the time between a shortage and the production to address it by years.
Some private firms are rapidly building capacity and production, before contracts are even awarded. They’re putting their own money where their mouths are and betting on guaranteed future demand. One of the leaders in that race is Hadrian, recently valued at nearly $8 billion in its latest funding round. In March, the private manufacturer opened Factory 4: a 2.2 million square foot machine shop in Cherokee, Alabama making parts for the Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines, the most relevant vessels to a potential war in the western Pacific. Under AUKUS, the United States was supposed to provide Australia with a new Virginia-class submarine before production constraints forced it to settle for in-service subs instead.
Hadrian’s move seeks to directly address one of the largest challenges facing the United States’ Navy and its Indo-Pacific presence. This approach is the one which should be replicated: they invested over $1.5 billion in private capital before receiving a roughly $900 million contract from the Navy.
The same model could expand the capabilities needed by Taiwan and Japan. In December, Lockheed Martin signed an MOU with Hadrian to co-locate a machine shop and inspection facility within Lockheed’s factory that produces the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors. To be clear: this is an arrangement, not a production deal. The company claims their Opus manufacturing system can have new production facilities operational in less than six months and new technicians operating at full productivity in 30 days.
These are not vetted performance metrics, just internal targets. That said, Hadrian has already been producing parts for Anduril’s autonomous weapons since 2023. Anduril says it has decreased delivery times up to 50 percent. Scaling up machine shops is no longer a pipe dream.
Part of the solution will also come from other countries. Japan currently produces PAC-3 interceptors under license at Mitsubishi Heavy Industries at a rate of about 30 interceptors per year, with the potential to double production. In November, Japan successfully exported its first domestically manufactured PAC-3 interceptors to the United States.
Production is bottlenecked by the Boeing seeker; the new seeker production lines won’t be running until 2027. However, Japan and the United States are negotiating joint production of the PAC-3 MSE. Japan could expand production of its own seekers, avoiding the bottleneck for itself but also for every other Patriot user in the area.
Taiwan cannot manufacture Patriots under license, but it can ramp up manufacturing for drones, naval mines, and shore-based missiles. These conversations might not make headlines, but they would contribute more to Japan and Taiwan’s defense than one more extended deterrence communique.
How quickly a country can replenish its arms is a key question of deterrence. Taken together, there’s a rough blueprint for quickly addressing production constraints. The United States can encourage the private-sector-first, public-sector-later approach Hadrian took to financing production, but only for already-approved suppliers on both sides of the Pacific.
Private firms taking action is the beginning of a solution, but without global engagement with allies, interceptor batteries will stay empty. Second, Washington should develop a surge production roadmap among allied industries: what U.S., Japanese, Australian, South Korean, and Taiwanese industries can ramp up or repurpose in six, twelve, or eighteen months, starting with seekers, rocket motors, and castings/forgings. National export controls are crucial for this, but I am advocating for selective industrial integration, not open and indiscriminate technology sharing.
Finally, Taiwan and Japan should demand to know, officially and on the record, how long their Patriot and other major arms systems will take to deliver once funded, and the Pentagon should provide those numbers. Taiwan’s 102 interceptors are lumped in with the U.S. Army’s 2,798, along with other allied requests, as well as the re-supply for each missile used over Iran. Japan’s Tomahawks are in that same queue. The United States can make a statement immediately, but what Taipei, Tokyo, and just as importantly, Beijing care about is the delivery at the pier.

articles.title: As US influence wanes, China expands Middle East security role
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
As war with Iran weakens US influence, China expands Middle East security role
The clearest example is the recent “Eagles of Civilisation 2026” military exercises with Egypt. The drills demonstrated capabilities that went beyond symbolic military diplomacy. China deployed J-16 fighter aircraft, a YY-20A aerial tanker, a KJ-500 airborne early-warning aircraft, an electronic warfare aircraft, and other support assets to Egypt.
For the first time, Chinese jet formations flew more than 6,000 kilometres beyond Asia to reach Egypt, with aerial refuelling conducted en route. Prior to this deployment, China had only sent the J-16 to the Russian Far East and Pakistan. As recently as last year, China-Egypt exercises involved smaller J-10C fighter jets and support aircraft.
Since then, Chinese and Egyptian pilots have conducted medium- and close-range air combat drills involving Chinese J-16s and Egyptian Rafales.
While the deployment does not suggest Beijing intends to fight a war in the Middle East, it demonstrates the People's Liberation Army's ability to operate alongside regional militaries and sustain forces far from China, well beyond its immediate neighbourhood.
China has also maintained a military presence in the wider region at sea. Since 2008, it has conducted naval escort operations in the Gulf of Aden and waters off Somalia. As recently as August, its 49th escort task force departed for the region. Officially, the mission is focused on protecting international shipping and conducting anti-piracy operations.
Beijing has also expanded its military engagement through joint exercises. In 2025, it held naval drills with Iran and Russia in the Gulf of Oman. This August, it conducted the fourth Falcon Shield air force training exercise with the United Arab Emirates.
These deployments have increasingly featured more sophisticated platforms, including J-10 fighters, KJ-500 airborne early-warning aircraft and YY-20A aerial tankers.
A growing Chinese footprint
China is also becoming an increasingly significant, albeit indirect, player in Middle Eastern security. This comes as its close partner Pakistan expands its defence ties across the Gulf through the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia, the Mecca Pact involving Turkey and Saudi Arabia, and a recently confirmed defence agreement with Kuwait.
As Islamabad deepens these partnerships, Chinese-made military equipment is likely to play a growing role in regional security architectures. Pakistan relies heavily on Chinese defence technology and has recently deployed HQ-9 air defence systems and JF-17 fighter jets, which it jointly produces with China, to Saudi Arabia.
For Beijing, such developments provide an opportunity to showcase its defence industry without assuming a formal security role in the region.
Instead, Chinese military technology can expand its footprint indirectly through Pakistani deployments, while systems such as the Beidou satellite network, already used across parts of the Arab world, further support the integration of Chinese-made platforms into regional security networks.
Could Beijing assume a larger security role?
Commenting on the prospect of a larger Chinese security role in the Middle East, Theodore Karasik, a fellow on Middle Eastern Affairs at the Jamestown Foundation, told The New Arab that Chinese technology and drones are already deeply embedded across the region, a trend he expects to continue.
Karasik argued that Beijing has benefited from US-Iran tensions while maintaining what he described as a “position of relative comfort”. Through infrastructure projects, commercial investments and growing arms sales, China has steadily expanded its regional footprint. He noted that Beijing's involvement now extends to defence cooperation, including support for Saudi Arabia's ballistic missile programme.
He also argued that America's longstanding strategic focus elsewhere has created opportunities for China to deepen its engagement in the Middle East. Combined with platforms such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), he said, these developments point to an increasingly fragmented global order.
However, Karasik suggested that the future trajectory of China's regional role may depend largely on Washington's response. A renewed US effort to discourage partners from deepening ties with Beijing could constrain China's ambitions, even as American policymakers remain focused on domestic political challenges and war with Iran.
While the Trump administration may seek to increase economic pressure on China, Karasik questioned how effective such measures would be. He added that President Xi Jinping's anticipated visit to the White House could help shape Beijing's approach.
Limits of Beijing's emerging role
Lacking a network of alliances, bases, or permanently deployed forces comparable to those of Washington, China has little security infrastructure in the Middle East beyond its only officially acknowledged overseas military base in Djibouti. Therefore, even if Beijing seeks to keep Gulf waterways open or expand military cooperation, it lacks the capacity to deploy large-scale forces to defend Gulf states against Iran.
Moreover, China maintains similar close ties with multiple regional actors, including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iran and Egypt through Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships (CSPs), and an Innovative Comprehensive Partnership with Israel. Any steps Beijing takes are therefore likely to remain non-confrontational.
Zeeshan Shah, an analyst at FINRA in Washington, told The New Arab that China has adopted a more subtle approach since the US-Iran war began. However, “regardless of official Chinese pronouncements on securing international waterways, or recent military exercises with Egypt”, he argued that Beijing is unlikely to move towards a more muscular form of engagement.
In his view, China primarily sees competition with the United States through an economic lens. While the threat of US sanctions has irritated Beijing, China has historically refrained from enforcing other sanctions against Iran.
Shah also noted that, despite maintaining strong commercial relations with Israel, China has generally refrained from using that relationship to influence Israeli policy. Whether Beijing chooses to leverage those ties more actively in the future, he argued, remains an open question.
The Chinese perspective
China's position during the Iran war has highlighted both the opportunities and contradictions in its emerging regional role. Beijing has presented itself as a stakeholder in de-escalation, particularly as the conflict has threatened Gulf security and the free flow of energy.
On 24 August, Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Kuwait's foreign minister that the Middle East and Gulf had reached a "critical juncture" and called for a return to dialogue, while saying China was ready to strengthen coordination with Kuwait and contribute to regional peace and stability. China has also engaged directly with regional actors and mediators as it seeks to protect its economic interests and prevent the conflict from disrupting trade and energy supplies.
But Beijing's position is complicated by its alleged role in sustaining Iran's military capabilities. US officials and recent reporting have identified Chinese companies and intermediaries as suppliers of military equipment and components to Iran, including a reported deal for hundreds of Chinese-made QW-12 and FN-16 man-portable air-defence missiles during the conflict.
Chinese manufacturing has also been central to Iran's wider drone ecosystem, with Chinese firms and suppliers providing components used in Iranian systems. At the same time, Washington has increasingly targeted China-linked entities over support for Iran's missile, drone and oil sectors.
In other words, Beijing could assume a larger regional role if it chose to do so.
For a clearer understanding of China's intentions and the limits it places on its regional ambitions, The New Arab spoke to Li Chao, Deputy Editor-in-Chief of China Media Group (CMG) Middle East.
In his view, although China's role in Middle Eastern security affairs is expanding, Beijing has no desire to challenge, replicate the American model or become the region's new “policeman”.
Describing the shift as a move away from a relatively narrow focus on economic and diplomatic engagement, Chao said China is pursuing “a broader, more integrated, but still restrained form of security involvement”. Driven by practical interests such as energy, trade, investment and the presence of Chinese personnel in the Middle East, he argued that it has become “increasingly difficult to sustain the old model of deep economic engagement but limited security involvement”.
However, Chao stressed that Beijing is not pursuing military alliances or large-scale permanent deployments. Instead, it is expanding its security presence through low-intensity instruments that form a “mutually reinforcing framework”, which is intended not to replace the United States but to reduce the risks that regional instability poses to Chinese interests.
He argued that China's Middle East strategy is centred on the normalisation of security engagement rather than militarisation. At the same time, Chao acknowledged the limits of this approach, noting that China does not possess an extensive military network comparable to that of the United States.
As a result, Chao said Beijing is likely to follow "a model of limited commitment, selective participation and avoidance of formal alliances". He argued that China's role would only enter a more substantive phase if it began participating in multilateral security mechanisms or institutionalised security cooperation across the region.
Until then, China's expanding security footprint is likely to remain cautious, selective and largely shaped by its economic interests.
Sabena Siddiqui is a foreign affairs journalist, lawyer and geopolitical analyst specialising in modern China, the Belt and Road Initiative, Middle East and South Asia.
Follow her on X: @sabena_siddiqi

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: ‘Shameful’ – Zelenskyy furious after shootout between Kyiv’s spy services
articles.body:
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted Ukraine’s SBU and GUR after a shootout in Kyiv between the two intelligence and security services reportedly left three officers injured. The SBU is Ukraine’s internal security service, like MI5 or the FBI. The GUR, or HUR, is its armed forces counterpart and also carries out military activities and special operations. Reports said the gunfight stemmed from the SBU taking into custody a leader of an anti-Kremlin Russian unit that fights for Ukraine under the watch of the GUR. Ukraine’s president called the situation “absolutely shameful” as he called in prosecutors and investigators, as well as firing a senior SBU officer. “Here in Ukraine, shooting is only permissible at Russian occupiers in defence of Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “Our state will not perceive any other shootout as something that anyone is allowed to do.”
- 
  Russian drones hit central Kyiv on Wednesday in a seventh day of intense strikes on the capital. Explosions were heard again in the early hours of Thursday morning. On Wednesday, 11 people were wounded, and residential and university buildings damaged. Russia also struck power facilities in the southern Odesa region with missiles and drones, authorities said, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes. Two people were killed and eight wounded in strikes on the south-eastern city of Dnipro, the regional governor said, where food warehouses and educational buildings were damaged.
- 
  Norway has seized a Russian cruise ship over unpaid compensation for the illegal annexation of Crimea. In April 2023 a tribunal in The Hague ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.22bn to compensate for its Crimean assets that were seized when Moscow’s forces invaded. Naftogaz is a Ukrainian state oil and gas firm. Russia has refused to pay the compensation. Naftogaz said the seizure was ordered by the Nord-Troms and Senja district court on 31 August. It said the vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was owned by Russia and used for commercial expedition cruises, including to the Norwegian archipelago Svalbard.
- 
  Ukraine has urged the UN’s aviation agency, the ICAO, and its member countries to ban their airlines from Russian airspace, a day after Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned it was “becoming completely unsafe” because of Ukrainian drones. Ukraine wrote to agency seeking “the full prohibition by ICAO member states of civil aircraft operations within the airspace of the Russian Federation”. In response to Ukraine’s warning, the ICAO called on its members to ensure the safety of civilian aircraft. “Long-range weapons systems, unmanned aircraft systems [UAS], global navigation satellite system radio frequency interference, and advanced air defence systems are among the military technologies jeopardising civilian aviation.”
- 
  It could take Ukraine several years to start building Patriot air defence interceptors and doing so is not an immediate solution for Kyiv, Marco Rubio has said. “I mean, these are highly sophisticated weaponry,” the US secretary of state told Fox News. The US was negotiating with Ukraine over licensed production of Patriot missiles, Rubio said. “That may come to fruition, but it really won’t solve the short-term challenge that they’re pointing to,” he said, adding that “the whole world is asking for more air interceptors” but US needs came first. “It’s become the number one defence need on the planet, not just for Ukraine, but on the planet,” including in the Middle East because of the US-Israeli war against Iran.
- 
  Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s air raid alerting system would be revised into two tiers – red for missiles, yellow for drones – allowing for more “predictability and a better understanding of how to react”. He added that curfew hours would be reduced and more above-ground transport options offered to compensate for metro closures. The measures were a response to “Russia’s changing tactics” and “its use of drones to wear down civilian life in our cities and disrupt normal economic activity across our country”, Zelenskyy said.
- 
  Belgium has continued to block EU attempts to use €200bn in frozen Russian assets for Ukraine’s benefit. Opposition from Belgium has forced EU members to instead give Ukraine a €90bn loan off their own backs – but as that fund runs down, four countries have pushed to reopen the debate on the Russian assets. Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said the Belgian government’s position remained “unchanged … Using these assets through a process akin to confiscation carries significant risk.” The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said after ministerial talks in Ireland that fresh funds for Ukraine should ultimately come from Russia. “That is why some of the member states were proposing to go back to the discussion of the frozen assets. And we will continue that discussion.”
- 
  Britain’s sanctions enforcer, the OFSI, has fined Citibank £4.7m (US$6.35m) for failings and errors that led to banned Russians getting access to funds. Most of it happened between February and November 2022, the OFSI said. The CBNA London branch processed 970 payments totalling £19.7m – some for state-owned shipping company PJSC Sovcomflot, as well as Alfa-Bank, PJSC Gazprombank and Credit Bank of Moscow. The agency did not consider there to have been any intent by CBNA London to breach sanctions, and the bank voluntarily disclosed most of the breaches. A Citi spokesperson said it welcomed the conclusion of the case and took sanctions compliance seriously.

articles.title: With an eye on Russia, Finland runs Europe's largest civil defence exercise since WWII
articles.body:
Western officials say Russia is carrying out a campaign of sabotage and disruption across Europe that has involved fires, attacking power stations and sending drones into EU airspace.
In a civil defence shelter cut into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and breathing masks are measuring radiation levels as they take part in an exercise to turn a cave into a place of safety for thousands of people.
Inside, in what is normally a sports hall, hundreds of people are sleeping overnight on camp beds.
More than 2,000 people including volunteers and students are taking part in the biggest civil defence exercise in Europe since the end of World War II.
In the scenario, critical infrastructure in the central Finnish city of Kuopio, including power and water, has been disrupted by cyberattacks and there’s the threat of missile strikes from Finland’s neighbour, Russia.
The goal is for local authorities and ordinary people to rehearse what they would do if they came under attack for real.
But while underground bunkers and shelters may offer some protection from missiles, they are no defence against the campaign of sabotage and disruption that Western officials say Russia is carrying out across Europe.
That has involved starting fires, attacking water facilities and power stations and sending drones on sabotage operations into European Union airspace.
Finland's border with Russia stretches more than 1,300 kilometres from the Baltic Sea up to the Arctic Circle.
In 2024, along with Sweden, Finland joined NATO, following Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Until then, Finns were prepared to defend themselves against Russia largely alone.
Lessons from Ukraine
Finland’s defence, said retired Army Colonel Asko Muhonen, relies not only on the military but on the “mindset” of ordinary Finns who are ready to take responsibility for their country’s security.
Muhonen, who organised the exercise in Kuopio, said that comes partly from the system of conscription which continued in Finland, even after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Not everyone is happy about doing national service but “it’s our duty to serve and protect this country like people have before us. That’s why we have our independence,” said Jyry Pietikainen, 23, a conscript who was taught how to run the Kuopio shelter overnight.
Finland also needs to learn lessons from Ukraine, Muhonen said.
While the biggest shelter in Kuopio can accommodate 7,000 people, Ukrainians sometimes only have a few minutes to run to a subway station or underground parking lot.
That means people need a shelter they can reach easily that offers some form of protection and not necessarily one that can withstand a nuclear attack, he said.
Dmytro Untila, 20, a Ukrainian student at the university in Kuopio, was at home in Odesa when Russian missiles struck his city on 24 February 2022, the first day of the war. He sheltered in the entrance hall of his building because he didn’t have anywhere else to go, he said.
Training for such a situation would have definitely helped in Ukraine, he said, “because nobody knew this could happen.”
The biggest threat to energy infrastructure in the Kuopio region is heavy snowfall, storms and bad weather, said Juha Räsänen, CEO at the Savon Voima electricity company.
But since the invasion of Ukraine and the company’s decision to stop buying Russian biofuel, the number of cyberattacks against the network has significantly increased, Räsänen said.
Last year, engineers also found at least 10 stickers placed on particularly vulnerable parts of the energy network infrastructure. Other energy companies in Finland have also found them and don’t know where they came from, he said.
“If there was an explosion at that point, it could destroy a whole dam,” Räsänen said. Drones have also been spotted over power lines but those responsible have not been identified, he said.
It is not possible to guard against all threats, Räsänen said, which is why it’s important people are prepared to look after themselves without help for at least 72 hours, if the power supply goes out, or if water becomes undrinkable.
The Finnish Security and Intelligence Service said it investigated “a wide range of observations” and found nothing of concern.
Since 2022, people have been more vigilant because of the security situation and therefore have reported things like reflective stickers related to land survey works, it said in a statement. Drone sightings, it said, have “largely been explained by everyday occurrences.”
“Small things are happening all the time,” including Russian jamming of GPS signals, said Vuokko Lahtinen, 32, who was visiting a sauna in Kuopio.
For that reason, “the best defence of Finland is to make it not worth attacking,” she said.
That relies on the country’s military and defence forces but also Finnish people who feel like “we have something we want to fight for,” she said.
In Finland, she said, there is a “general feeling of responsibility,” which has grown out of local community groups and even initiatives such as recycling.
“On a very simple daily level, if you do things that matter, then it has a butterfly-wing effect,” Lahtinen said.
Finland vs the Soviet Union
In its wars with the Soviet Union, Finland lost around 11% of its territory and more than 400,000 people, around 12% of the population, fled their homes from an area that is now in western Russia.
At Kuopio's veterans’ museum, Risto Mönkkönen, 95, showed a piece of paper on which he had written down the dates the city was bombed and who died.
“I cannot forget it,” he said explaining how, as a child, he and his father ran into a shelter just as a bomb hit, killing five of his father’s friends.
Pirkko Naukkarinen, 102, recalled how, aged 16, she worked in a field kitchen by the front lines, sometimes sharing dugouts with soldiers and diving for cover in ditches as the Soviet air force attacked the retreating Finnish army.
Aili Toivanen, 92, said she was forced to leave her home twice over the various wars. Both times, her family was told by Finnish soldiers that they had one hour to pack their belongings.
The first time, she looked back and saw her home burning, set on fire by Finnish soldiers who did not want to leave anything behind, she said.
The second time, she explained, the Soviet air force bombed the family’s departing train and they jumped out, hiding in ditches before they took refuge in Kuopio.
When Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, she said, with tears in her eyes, that she worried she would have to leave her home for a third time.
A country worth fighting for
At the shelter in Kuopio, thousands of people filed in, including schoolchildren and university students.
“Kids would need to know this, because they might have to do something alone. The adults can’t always help,” said Amanda Hill, 11, whose school studied in the shelter for the day.
Sitting on the floor of the shelter with his fellow conscripts, Pietikainen explained why it’s not crazy to practice what happens in a crisis.
“We’re Finns, so we’re kind of pessimistic about life in a way,” but history shows what can happen with Russia, he said.
When it comes to the threats from Moscow, Muhonen said, “don’t believe what they say but observe what they do.”

articles.title: Has Iran modified its rocket systems to fire mines into the Strait of Hormuz?
articles.body:
Has Iran modified its rocket systems to fire mines into the Strait of Hormuz?
Fighting escalated in the Middle East over the weekend after US airstrikes on Sunday targeted Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak. The exchange of fire was instigated by the US in retaliation against Iran’s new capabilities for firing mines from rockets into the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s use of rocket launchers to deploy sea mines into the strategic waterway would be unprecedented, but not implausible. Even so, some analysts remain sceptical.
The motive behind the US strikes on Sunday, which hit Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, appears to have been the prevention of a new threat to shipping in the vital waterway.
Officially, the US military decided to resume its strikes after a month-long hiatus because Iranian forces from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) were preparing to “launch rockets loaded with sea mines into the strait.”
Read moreIran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks as US blockade squeezes Iran oil exports
Rocket launchers as mine launchers
Some maritime security experts say they were taken by surprise by the US’s claim.
“This alleged new capability by the Iranians to deploy mines into the strait is puzzling,” said a specialist in maritime conflicts who preferred to remain anonymous.
Since the conflict with the United States and Israel began, Iranians have typically transported sea mines in small, fast boats and then scattered them across the Strait of Hormuz. This has made the strait extremely dangerous as vessels have had to navigate it not knowing the exact location of the underwater explosives.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Sea mines have also been delivered typically by small submarines or dropped by aircraft flying at very low altitudes.
They can be positioned on the seabed or moored above it – or left just beneath the surface of the water where they detect passing ships before exploding on contact with a vessel.
A not so new novel method?
According to Dirk Siebels, a maritime security specialist at Risk Intelligence, using land-based rocket launchers to shoot sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz “would, as far as I know, be a novel method”.
Harlan Ullman, a former US Naval officer, agreed. In an interview with Al Jazeera, he said it was “unlikely” rocket launchers would be used to fire mines because they would be “highly likely to be damaged upon impact with the water,” he said.
However, reports have been circulating for several months about Iran’s capacity to use missiles to lay sea mines.
Iranian state television broadcast a report on the Fajr-5 Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS) as early as January 2025, referring to it as the newest weapon for mining in the Strait of Hormuz.
Read moreHow ships are risking ‘safe’ passage through the Strait of Hormuz
“Iran has been conducting tests with Fajr-5 multiple rocket launchers for this purpose for some time now,” said Sidharth Kaushal, an expert on the impact of new technologies on naval warfare at the Royal United Services Institute for Defense and Security Studies (RUSI), one of Britain’s leading strategic think tanks.
A quicker way to deploy sea mines
In principle, weapons can be used to deploy mines.
“Missiles carry the explosives and drop them over the target area,” said Mark Hilborne, an expert in aviation and space security at King’s College London.
“The impact can be minimised by equipping the mines with small parachutes, for example.”
If Iran has indeed begun launching mines into the strait using Fajr-5 systems, it would greatly undermine the rhetoric from US President Donald Trump and the Pentagon, who have boasted of having “completely destroyed the Iranian navy”.
For Iranians, “this would be a way to demonstrate their ingenuity and their ability to overcome the destruction of their fleet by the Americans,” explained Shahin Modarres, an Iran specialist at the International Team for the Study of Security (ITSS) in Verona.
And it would give the Iranian regime yet another advantage. “It’s also faster. Using a boat requires loading the mines, assembling the crew, travelling to the site, and dropping the mines. With a rocket launcher, all you have to do is load and fire,” Kaushal said.
Time saved can make all the difference.
“It limits the opportunities the Americans have to detect and prevent a threat,” the RUSI analyst added.
Despite its strategic merits, the rocket system is not a panacea. There are practical reasons why using boats is preferable. First, it’s possible to carry more mines on a boat.
“A naval mine is a fairly large and heavy warhead because it must be powerful enough to damage a ship’s hull. It’s difficult to fit many of them into a single rocket launch, because to travel a long distance, the warhead must be lightweight,” Kaushal explained.
Second, rocket-launched mines are not particularly precise compared to other methods. The rocket system tends to scatter mines once they have been fired, making it difficult even for the Iranians themselves to ascertain their location.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Propaganda or a veritable escalation?
Siebels considers the military tactic “rather reckless”, suggesting that Iran would be shooting itself in the foot because “Iranian cargo ships also need to know exactly where the mines are in order to avoid them.”
Without knowing the whereabouts of these mines, it is impossible to guarantee ships safe passage through the strait, even if they have paid the transit fee Tehran is demanding.
Siebels said he is doubtful that rocket launchers are being used. Despite the drawbacks of naval missions – particularly the risk to crews – these more traditional methods would align more with Iran’s overall strategy in the Strait of Hormuz.
Others share his scepticism.
“It’s war propaganda,” argues Christian Bueger, a specialist in maritime security issues at the University of Copenhagen.
He said he believes that the United States needed to find a new threat to maritime traffic to “justify the strikes” and to reassure shipping companies.
“The United States is seeking to demonstrate that the mine threat is under control,” Bueger said.
Regardless, it cannot be ruled out that laying mines is part of the psychological warfare being waged by these military rivals. With their January 2025 video touting the new capabilities of the Fajr-5, the Iranians sought to demonstrate that they could still wreak havoc in the Strait of Hormuz – whether it is true or not.
“The advantage of mines is that the mere risk of their existence may be enough to discourage ships from passing through the Strait of Hormuz,” Bueger said, adding that the official response by the US to the bombings on Larak Island would be justified because of Tehran’s actions in the strait.
Modarres is less convinced.
“The use of rocket launchers is typical of how Iran employs unconventional methods to thwart enemy plans.”
Confronted by Washington’s declaration of an all-out economic war, he said Iran may want to demonstrate that it is still capable of imposing its military might over the Strait of Hormuz, blindsiding the Americans by wielding a new weapon to disrupt the vital maritime route.
Whatever the reality – whether bluff and psychological warfare or a veritable threat to the strait – this latest development in the intransigent conflict between Iran and the US reveals that, in an era where drones and AI-enhanced warfare dominate, the threat of mines remains highly effective.
This article has been adapted from the original in French by Nicole Trian.

articles.title: “Shielded his comrades with his body”: How Russian propaganda turned a pedophile fugitive into a war hero
articles.body:
On Sept. 2, schools across Russia’s Komi Republic held lessons in courage dedicated to Alexander Vlasenkov, a corporal who was killed fighting in Ukraine. By decree of Vladimir Putin, Vlasenkov was posthumously awarded the title of Hero of Russia. A monument and several memorial plaques have been erected in his home region, and a museum dedicated to him has opened at his former school. On the day of the lessons, schoolchildren watched a film about Vlasenkov and learned about his life. The campaign to glorify the fallen corporal’s “feat” was spearheaded by Alexander Matovnikov, a former member of Putin’s security detail who also happened to advise Vlasenkov to volunteer for the war. However, as The Insider has found, Vlasenkov had been placed on a special Interior Ministry register for pedophilia and went to the front to evade police supervision and escape massive debts.
Expelled from the Interior Ministry university after trying to rape a teenager
Alexander Vlasenkov, a world and Russian junior champion in hand-to-hand combat, took out 500,000 rubles in loans in his own name between 2019 and 2021, and nearly another 400,000 rubles using his grandmother’s passport. By then, he had spent a year evading both debt collectors from RVS LLC and court bailiffs. He even skipped a promotional event in Kaliningrad, fearing he would be detained at the airport during a police check.
Police officers also made regular visits to Vlasenkov due to the fact that he was on a special Interior Ministry register for pedophilia, a legacy of his days as a cadet at the St. Petersburg University of the Interior Ministry, where he tried to rape a 13-year-old boy before being scared off by passersby.
The university authorities quickly swept the scandal under the rug, but Vlasenkov, who was in his second year, was immediately expelled. Mandatory military service in the air defense forces, however, spared him from prison.
After being demobilized in 2019, Vlasenkov found work as a coach in Irkutsk before police officers came to the school and warned its management about their new trainer's sexual proclivities. Vlasenkov was eventually forced to return home to the village of Chim in Russia’s Komi Republic and live with his grandmother, Zoya Ivanovna, who had raised him. That grandmother, incidentally, is well known throughout the area and is fondly called “our craftswoman” for her decades of work making unique dolls.
It wasn't Vlasenkov's first homecoming. In 2015, when he won the Russian junior hand-to-hand combat championship, the entire village turned out to welcome him, and a red carpet was rolled out in front of his school. The second return home was far less triumphant — Vlasenkov took a job as an electrician, and occasionally, at the request of his first coach, Khodzhar Isaev, he gave hand-to-hand combat seminars. He was deeply afraid that the local police officer supervising him might reveal something about his past.
The village of Chim has a population of just 297. It boasts a community center located in a barracks and an orphanage where Vlasenkov’s grandmother worked all her life. Most of the houses are in a dilapidated state, and there is virtually no work.
In early 2022, desperate to climb out of debt, Vlasenkov turned to his brother Igor and his coach Isaev for financial help. But his brother, who lived in Syktyvkar, was heavily in debt himself, while Isaev said he was ill and spending large amounts of money on expensive treatment. He died in 2023.
Vlasenkov then traveled to Moscow to seek help from the International Hand-to-Hand Combat Federation (IHCF). He was well known there: in 2009, he won the national Children of Beslan Memorial Tournament, took first place in the "My Republic Is a Sporting Republic" competition, and in 2015 became the Russian junior hand-to-hand combat champion.
In Moscow, Vlasenkov was received by Alexander Matovnikov, chairman of the IHCF supervisory board and a former member of Putin’s security detail. A colonel general, Matovnikov has served as deputy commander-in-chief of Russia’s Ground Forces since January 22, 2020. Pro-Kremlin media have described him as a “true Russian officer.”
However, the general told Vlasenkov that the federation had no spare money and advised him to volunteer for the “special military operation,” which Vlasenkov did. The State Duma only banned people suspected of pedophilia from signing contracts to serve in the “special military operation” in 2024.
Vlasenkov served as a reconnaissance sniper with the 200th Coastal Defense Brigade, attached to the Northern Fleet (military unit 08275). He was killed on Sept. 2, 2022, during fighting near the village of Udy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region.
The awards office
Vlasenkov’s story might have gone unnoticed, like the deaths of hundreds of thousands of other Russians who signed a contract with the Ministry of Defense. But General Matovnikov, the man who had advised him to volunteer for the front, changed all that.
After the disastrous start to the “special military operation,” Kremlin propaganda needed heroes, and Vlasenkov was an ideal fit: a young man from the provinces, practically an orphan, an athlete and a champion. That was when the campaign to build up his fresh image began.
Propaganda needed heroes, and Vlasenkov was an ideal fit: a young man from the provinces, practically an orphan, an athlete and a champion
Matovnikov himself began his career at the KGB’s Alpha Special Operations Center, eventually rising to become the unit’s first deputy commander. He took part in the storming of the hospital in Budyonnovsk in 1995 after it was seized by Shamil Basayev’s gang and was one of the commanders of the counterterrorism operations to free hostages at the Dubrovka theater in Moscow in 2002 (known as the Nord-Ost siege) and at the school in Beslan in 2004 (where hundreds of people were killed).
Matovnikov was later assigned to the security detail of Chechen head Akhmad Kadyrov as the FSB’s representative and acquired the nickname “Chekist.” On May 9, 2004, Kadyrov was killed in a bombing at Dynamo Stadium in Grozny. Matovnikov was in Moscow at the time, celebrating Victory Day.
Matovnikov’s immediate superior is Alexei Dyumin, who has been touted as a possible successor to Putin. After Dyumin moved to the Defense Ministry, Matovnikov took over his post as head of the Special Operations Service, serving as a deputy head of the GRU. In that capacity, Matovnikov repeatedly traveled to Syria on inspection missions. He did not take part in combat, but Putin awarded him the Hero of Russia title in 2017.
This past June, the Navalny LIVE YouTube channel published an investigation into how Matovnikov built his career under Putin, turning the war into a source of multibillion-ruble enrichment.
By the time of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Matovnikov was serving as deputy commander-in-chief of Russia’s Ground Forces. Through the Defense Ministry’s press service, pro-Kremlin media, and Z-bloggers, he set the propaganda machine in motion to promote Vlasenkov's memory.
On Oct. 22, 2022, a month and a half after Vlasenkov’s death, Putin issued a decree posthumously awarding him the title of Hero of Russia. His grandmother, however, was not invited to the Kremlin — the award was presented to her at the Komi Republic's regional administration building in Syktyvkar.
A source for The Insider in the Presidential Administration explained how such awards are processed:
“In short, Vladimir Vladimirovich doesn’t deal with routine matters — he has plenty of other things to worry about. State orders, medals, and certificates of honor are handled by Vladimir Osipov, head of the Presidential Directorate for State Awards. He is also a former KGB officer, and the president trusts him completely. Or they are handled by his deputy, Ivan Kalashnikov, who came to the Presidential Administration from the Ministry of Construction.
Before the start of the special military operation, there was stricter oversight: candidates were checked for criminal records and anything questionable in their backgrounds. But now all those checks have become pointless — the guys are overwhelmed. The Defense Ministry submits nominations for awards in huge batches, and half of those killed have criminal records.
Initial checks are carried out by the department responsible for preparing documents for state awards, headed by Irina Valyaeva, whose husband is a military pilot.
Heroes of Russia are a separate matter. If the candidates come from the FSB or intelligence services, their cases are handled by the department responsible for classified documents within the awards directorate. Irina Mitetele is responsible for processing the paperwork in those cases.
Sometimes a nomination may have a note attached saying, ‘Request from Slutsky, LDPR,’ or ‘From Zhdanov, SVR,’ or ‘Vavilov, Almaz-Antey,’ or simply ‘from Rotenberg.’
The documents then go to the presidential administration office. Its computers already contain completed, numbered forms bearing seals and Vladimir Vladimirovich’s facsimile signature — all you have to do is enter the surname. Award ceremonies at the Kremlin are timed to coincide with various dates. For the most part, the documents are sent to military enlistment offices in the deceased recipient’s place of residence. That’s the whole process.”
"He asked us to call him Shurik"
State propaganda went into full gear to glorify Vlasenkov. A monument was erected in his hometown, and at the school he attended, a museum was opened with funding from Transneft-Sever JSC. Among the exhibits is the desk used by the slain mercenary.
A postage stamp was issued soon afterward, and a photo of Vlasenkov was posted on the website of the All-Russian Federation of Applied Hand-to-Hand Combat (AFPRB). He appears alongside Matovnikov, Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov, and Alexei Katerinichev, a former FSB officer who was killed near Kherson in September 2022 in a Ukrainian missile strike.
In December 2022, the Komi Republican Television Channel (YURGAN) released a documentary titled Alexander Vlasenkov’s Last Height, produced in the style of a Soviet propaganda film.
The film makes no mention of the fact that Vlasenkov had effectively fled to the front to evade police supervision and court bailiffs. Instead, it dwells on the purported details of his final battle near the village of Udy:
“When Vlasenkov saw that the nationalists had decided to surrender, he believed: here it is, another victory! So he stepped forward toward the raised white flag. Perhaps Vlasenkov wanted to save the lives of those who had realized that there was no point in resisting. But the enemy proved treacherous and, instead of surrendering, met our soldiers with bullets. The hero shielded his comrades with his body.”
“He asked us to call him Shurik. I still keep his poems,” his first teacher, Nina Torlopova, says in the film.
“One of Alexander’s favorite subjects was history. The Order of the Patriotic War made an indelible impression on him,” the narrator says.
“He was never afraid to take responsibility and always tried to help. And patriotism was not just a word to him,” says Abdusator Niyazov, the military commissar for Udorsky District, reading from a teleprompter.
The propaganda piece ends on an equally bombastic note: “He always strove for the heights, and he conquered this height too, although it turned out to be his last.”

articles.title: Ukraine is experiencing a severe shortage of "air-to-air" missiles for F-16s - media
articles.body:
Ukraine is experiencing a severe shortage of "air-to-air" missiles for F-16s - media
Kyiv • UNN
Due to the acute shortage of "air-to-air" missiles, Ukrainian F-16s sometimes rely solely on guns. Weapons supplies are being rationed.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots are facing such an acute shortage of air-to-air missiles that during some daytime sorties they rely exclusively on the fighters’ internal cannon to counter Russian aerial threats. This was reported by a journalist who recently spoke with a senior commander of Ukraine’s Air Force, UNN reports, citing the TWZ Newsletter.
The publication notes that the shortage of air-to-air missiles means that available weapons stocks are currently being rationed.
This information offers a striking insight into the everyday reality of Ukrainian F-16 operations. Although aircraft may be available, pilots may be ready, and Russian drones and cruise missiles may be approaching, there may simply not be enough missiles to equip the fighters.
According to Newsmax journalist Shelby Wilder, Ukraine’s Air Force can track missile shipments as they cross the country’s border, with personnel counting not only the hours but also the minutes until the weapons reach the aircraft. The concern is whether the missiles will arrive in time for the next Russian airstrike.
A Ukrainian commander who identified himself by the call sign "Phantom" and said he was the commander of the 107th Wing confirmed the fundamental problem when asked directly whether Ukraine was experiencing an acute shortage of missiles for its F-16s.
"Yes, it is true. Any aircraft without weapons… is useless," Phantom said.
The publication notes that this straightforward assessment is particularly striking given the tasks Ukraine assigns to its F-16s and the relentless Russian bombing of Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
We would add
The fighters have become an important part of Ukraine’s multilayered air defense system, hunting Russian drones and cruise missiles, as well as providing a potential counter to Russian combat aircraft and conducting sorties against ground targets. Ukraine has operated F-16s since the summer of 2024.
"We are focused on protecting our airspace from Russian drones in order to protect our infrastructure inside the country," Phantom said. "Our priority target is cruise missiles."
Missiles are needed to destroy as many of the approaching threats as possible before they reach Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, and the F-16 fighter is primarily armed with medium-range AIM-120 (AMRAAM) air-to-air missiles and shorter-range AIM-9 Sidewinders.

articles.title: Putin and Zelenskyy issue threats as strikes rock Ukraine, Russia
articles.body:
Putin and Zelenskyy issue threats as strikes rock Ukraine, Russia
Putin accuses Zelenskyy of ‘terrorism’, while Ukraine warns foreign airlines against using Russian airspace.
Russian drone attacks across Ukraine have killed at least one person and wounded more than a dozen others, as Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin threatened to escalate the conflict.
Between Tuesday and Wednesday, Ukrainian authorities reported attacks in the capital, Kyiv, in the southern city of Odesa and in eastern Dnipro, where the body of a man was retrieved from under rubble.
The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as the conflict stretches into its fifth year following Moscow’s invasion of its neighbour. The front line in eastern and southern Ukraine remains largely deadlocked, and US efforts to negotiate a peace settlement have yet to produce a path to peace.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy exchanged threats late on Tuesday over what their next steps might be.
Zelenskyy warned foreign airlines that the skies over Russia are not safe for flights due to Ukrainian long-range drone attacks, saying that “Russian airspace will effectively be closing”. He said Ukrainian military pressure aims to compel Russia to accept peace negotiations.
Putin accused Zelenskyy of “state terrorism” and said: “We don’t negotiate with terrorists.”
At a late-night news conference on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin also addressed reports that the Ukrainian military had used British-made drones to strike targets inside Russia.
Asked whether Russia would strike British military facilities if the UK government continues to provide Ukraine with weaponry, Putin declined to rule it out. With a small smile, he told reporters it was “a military secret”.
China and North Korea, meanwhile, have provided military support for Russia, as has Iran in previous years.
The Russian and Ukrainian leaders’ comments came as European officials weigh their response to the latest in what they say is Moscow’s campaign of continental sabotage and disruption aimed at weakening European support for Ukraine. Germany on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport last month using a drone laden with explosives.
Odesa power outage
Russia fired 174 attack drones, about half of them jet-powered drones that are hard to stop and are increasingly being deployed by Moscow, as well as two ballistic missiles and two plane-launched missiles at Ukraine overnight, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.
Officials in the southern Ukraine region of Odesa reported that the attack damaged a 24-storey residential building, destroying apartments on several floors and wounding eight people, including a child.
Odesa office buildings and two educational facilities were also damaged, Serhiy Lysak, head of the Odesa city military administration, said. The barrage also caused a power outage that halted electric-powered public transport, the city council said.
A man and a woman were wounded by shrapnel in morning attacks on the Kyiv region, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.
It was the seventh straight day Kyiv came under attack, although the latest barrage wasn’t as heavy as in previous days. The assault started a fire at a warehouse, officials said. Russian forces have targeted civilian facilities in what Ukrainian officials say is an effort to disrupt daily life and sap public morale.
A fire broke out at an educational facility and a medical practice was also damaged, the Kyiv city military administration said.
Meanwhile in Russia, air defences destroyed 130 Ukrainian drones overnight, the Defence Ministry said on Wednesday. The drones were shot down over 11 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea, it said.
Ukrainian drone attacks killed two people in Russia’s Belgorod border region and wounded 16 more, acting governor Aleksand Shuvaev said. Ukrainian forces hit the region 140 times over the course of 24 hours, he said.
Ukraine’s domestically developed long-range drones have repeatedly targeted Russia’s oil sector, hoping to dent the economy and the warehouses of online retailers to make the Russian public feel the effects of war.
