articles.title: US army is grappling with profound crisis
articles.body:
There were also disagreements between the White House and military commanders during Donald Trump's first term, but according to the Washington Post, the level of changes and tensions in the command structure during the current Trump administration is unmatched. The removal of more than 20 senior officers and the blocking of dozens of commanders' promotions have raised concerns about the stability of the US military's command structure.
This is especially significant when the US military is also engaged in a long and costly war in the Middle East. The resignation of US Army Secretary "Dan Driscoll" is the latest sign of this tension. Driscoll left his post after growing differences with US War Secretary Pete Hegseth. The differences between the two officials were not just personal or administrative, but also related in part to the way the military command is managed and to widespread changes at the top levels of the military.
The departure of a few commanders or a political official may not seem so important, but in a military structure, the stability of command is part of combat power. The army is not just a collection of planes, missiles, ships and tanks. The experience of commanders, coordination between forces and trust between the political and military structure are part of the same power that must be demonstrated during the war.
From this perspective, the Iran war has put additional pressure on the US military. Of course, we cannot yet speak of the "collapse" or "impotence" of the US military. The United States still has the most powerful military in the world in terms of technology, air and naval power, intelligence, space power, and logistical capacity. But the problem is that even the most powerful military in the world does not have unlimited resources. One of the most important limitations is weapons stocks.
The White House has put the direct cost of the war at about $37.5 billion, but that figure is only a fraction of the true cost of the war. The cost of replacing spent ammunition, repairing equipment, long-term deployment of troops, and rebuilding military capabilities is not fully reflected in this figure.
The United States has used up a significant portion of its precision munitions and interceptor systems during the war. Reports of dwindling stocks of Patriot missiles and other air defense equipment have raised concerns among military officials and US allies. The importance of this issue becomes clearer when we realize that the United States is not just stockpiling weapons for the Middle East. Washington must also have military capabilities for Europe, the Pacific, and other regions of the world. So every interceptor missile fired in the Middle East is not just spent ammunition; it is part of a stockpile that could be used in another crisis.
This is where the Iran war directly ties into America’s competition with China and Russia. If the war in the Middle East is prolonged and the US is forced to keep significant amounts of troops, aircraft, ships, ammunition, and defense systems in the region for months, the US military’s flexibility to respond to other crises will be reduced.
This concern is particularly important for America’s Asian allies. Washington’s East Asian allies are not just looking at America’s political promises; they are also looking at how many planes, ships, missiles, and munitions the United States has at its disposal in a real crisis, and how quickly it can get them to the region. So the depletion of military reserves can become a political issue.
The longer the war drags on, the more resources the US will have to devote to rebuilding its stockpiles. This means more pressure on the defense budget, increased arms orders, and years to restore some stockpiles to pre-war levels.
But the cost of war is not just equipment; manpower is also depleted. The US military structure needs experienced commanders and a stable chain of command to maintain readiness in several regions of the world. Extensive changes at the top of the military, while American forces are still engaged in military operations, can have a cost that is very difficult to measure in financial statistics. That is why the Iran war has become a strategic test for the United States.
A war that was supposed to showcase American military might has now become a debate about the limits of American power. Washington is forced to simultaneously consider the cost of war, the depletion of weapons stockpiles, the attrition of forces, the stability of command, and the ability to counter threats from China and Russia.
This does not mean that America no longer has the military power it once had. In fact, the opposite is true; America still has enormous power, but the Iran war has shown that even that power has limited costs and capacity. Military power is not just the ability to start a war; it is the ability to continue it, to replace ammunition, to maintain the readiness of forces, and at the same time to be ready for the next war.
If the United States is forced to reduce its capabilities on other fronts to win on one front, then a regional war becomes a global issue. For this reason, the true cost of the Iran war to the United States may not be apparent today but in a few years, when Washington will have to rebuild its weapons stockpiles, train new commanders, and prove to its allies that it can still manage multiple crises simultaneously.
The Iran war has perhaps questioned the concept of "unlimited American power" more than it has challenged American power in a specific operation. And for Washington, this is perhaps one of the most important strategic consequences of this war.
MNA

articles.title: Russian specialists aiding Iran's development of supersonic cruise missiles, FT reports
articles.body:
Russian specialists aiding Iran's development of supersonic cruise missiles, FT reports
Russian missile specialists have been working with Iran on a covert program aimed at advancing Tehran's ability to develop supersonic cruise missiles, the Financial Times (FT) reported, citing leaked correspondence, travel records, and an analysis of military patents.
The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and involves Russian experts assisting Iran with the development of ramjet propulsion, according to the FT. The technology allows cruise missiles to maintain flight at several times the speed of sound and is likely intended for anti-ship and land-attack weapons.
Iran has already built and flight-tested a ramjet propulsion system, though the FT said there is no evidence that a supersonic cruise missile developed with Russian assistance has entered service.
Such missiles could pose a new threat to U.S. naval vessels in the Middle East. Their high speed and ability to fly at low altitudes can reduce the amount of time available for air and missile defense systems to detect and intercept them.
Russia's state arms exporter Rosoboronexport coordinated the program with NPO Mashinostroyenia, a Russian missile manufacturer sanctioned by the United States in 2014.
Travel records reviewed by the FT showed that Russian arms export officials and senior NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers repeatedly traveled to Iran before Rosoboronexport signed a contract with Iran's Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics in November 2023.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received Iranian technical material related to the ramjet system. Russian engineers subsequently analyzed data from an Iranian flight test and sought additional information from Tehran about the system's fuel supply, combustion stability, air intake, engine nozzle, and other aspects of its performance.
According to the FT, the exchanges show Russian engineers assessing a system Iran had already constructed and tested and using their expertise to help address technical problems and improve the design.
The cooperation continued into 2026, after the beginning of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Correspondence reviewed by the FT showed Russia preparing technical reports for Tehran while the two sides discussed a possible next stage of the program as recently as June. It remains unclear whether that stage has begun.
The Kremlin, Rosoboronexport, NPO Mashinostroyenia, and the Iranian government did not respond to the FT's requests for comment.
The program comes amid deepening military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran. Iran supplied Russia with Shahed attack drones used extensively in its war against Ukraine and helped Moscow establish domestic production of the drones.
Ukraine and Western officials have also accused Russia of assisting Iran during its war with the United States and Israel, including by providing satellite imagery, drone support, and weapons components.

articles.title: Camp Titin: Iran’s strike on a US Marine facility signals a wider strategic challenge
articles.body:
Camp Titin: Iran’s strike on a US Marine facility signals a wider strategic challenge
TEHRAN — Iran’s ballistic-missile strike on the US Marine Corps facility known as Camp Titin in Jordan could prove far more consequential for Washington than the damage inflicted at a single military site. The attack demonstrated that Iranian forces could reach a US position on the Gulf of Aqaba, hundreds of kilometers from the main theater around the Persian Gulf, while simultaneously striking or threatening American military infrastructure across several regional countries.
The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday that it had launched an intensive ballistic-missile attack against Camp Titin in southern Jordan in retaliation for recent US strikes inside Iran. The IRGC stated that the attack killed several US personnel and destroyed several facilities and helicopters.
Jordan, meanwhile, claimed its air defenses intercepted 10 of 13 ballistic missiles entering its airspace and did not confirm a strike on the US facility or American casualties.
The conflicting accounts make it premature to assess the physical damage at Camp Titin. But the strategic significance of the attack does not depend entirely on whether the base suffered extensive destruction.
Why Camp Titin matters
Camp Titin is located near Aqaba, at the northern end of the Red Sea and close to Jordan’s borders with Israel and Saudi Arabia. The location gives the facility particular importance for US-Jordanian military cooperation, Marine Corps training, and rapid-response activities.
Its targeting is significant because it represents a geographic expansion of Iran’s ability to threaten US military positions. Tehran has previously focused much of its military leverage on the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. By striking at a US position near Aqaba, Iran demonstrated that moving American forces farther from the immediate Persian Gulf theater does not necessarily place them beyond the reach of Iranian missiles.
That has implications for the broader US force posture in West Asia. American forces are dispersed across a network of bases in Jordan, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. These installations provide Washington with the infrastructure needed for air operations, intelligence, surveillance, logistics, and rapid reinforcement.
Iran's latest response sought to turn that network into a vulnerability.
A coordinated pressure campaign
The Camp Titin attack was not an isolated event. Within the same period, Iran announced missile and drone operations against US positions in Kuwait and Iraq, while the Iranian Army reported attacks involving loitering munitions against US-linked positions and radar installations in the UAE and Bahrain.
The geographical spread is what makes the latest escalation particularly important.
For Washington, protecting one base is manageable. Protecting a dispersed military architecture stretching from the Gulf of Aqaba to the Persian Gulf and northern Iraq is considerably more demanding. It requires continuous air-defense coverage, intelligence and surveillance, interceptor missiles and the ability to rapidly reinforce threatened installations.
The latest attacks therefore confront the United States with a difficult strategic equation: its military superiority remains overwhelming, but its regional footprint also provides Iran with multiple targets.
That distinction matters because the United States does not need to lose large numbers of personnel for the attacks to become strategically costly. Repeated attacks can force Washington to disperse aircraft, move personnel, reinforce air defenses, alter flight patterns, and spend expensive interceptors to defend relatively fixed installations.
The Hormuz factor
The pressure is compounded by the continuing confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz.
Before the war, roughly one-fifth of globally traded oil passed through the waterway. Although Washington has argued that its military operations have restored greater freedom of navigation, commercial traffic remains substantially below prewar levels, while the latest escalation has again pushed oil prices higher. Brent crude rose above $95 a barrel as fighting intensified.
This gives Iran a form of leverage that is difficult to eliminate through air strikes alone. Tehran does not have to defeat the US military conventionally to impose strategic costs. It can threaten shipping, attack regional military infrastructure and force Washington to devote increasing resources to protecting its personnel and partners.
 
  
Iran’s strategic position
The latest developments have revived a debate among Western analysts over whether Iran has retained — or regained — a degree of strategic leverage despite the damage inflicted on its military and economy.
Analysts believe that Tehran had gained the upper hand by May, citing its ability to rebuild offensive capabilities and exploit the strategic leverage provided by the Strait of Hormuz.
Former US Defense Secretary Mark Esper similarly said in August that Iran’s negotiating posture suggested Tehran believed it had the upper hand and had become more emboldened.
Those assessments do not imply that Iran has achieved conventional military superiority over the United States. Rather, they point to a different measure of power: the ability to deny an adversary an easy path to victory.
Iran has demonstrated that it can remain militarily relevant despite sustained US pressure and can impose costs outside its own territory. The United States, by contrast, faces the challenge of maintaining a large regional military presence while protecting that presence from increasingly dispersed Iranian attacks.
===A surprise for Trump?
For President Donald Trump and his administration, the developments of the past two days could be particularly uncomfortable because they challenge the assumption that renewed American military pressure would narrow Tehran's options.
Washington has vastly greater airpower, intelligence capabilities and financial resources. Yet the latest Iranian response has shown that those advantages do not automatically translate into control of the regional battlespace.
The Iranian army and IRGC's attack on Kuwait, Bahrain, Erbil, the UAE, and other US bases in the region indicates that Iran may not have superior equipment but does hold a strategic advantage.
The surprise is not necessarily that Iran retaliated — Tehran had repeatedly warned that US attacks would trigger a response. The more important surprise is the breadth of the response and its geographical reach, extending from Jordan and the Persian Gulf states to Iraq in a matter of hours. Reuters described the latest exchange as the most intense direct US-Iran fighting since July.
For the Trump administration, Camp Titin is therefore more than another military target in an expanding war. It is a warning that attempts to push US forces farther from the Strait of Hormuz may not remove them from Iran's strike envelope — and that Washington could face a widening contest in which protecting its regional military network becomes almost as important as striking Iran itself.
The central strategic question is consequently no longer simply whether the United States can inflict greater damage on Iran. It is whether Washington can convert that military superiority into a sustainable political outcome while Iran retains the ability to expand the battlefield, threaten US forces across the region, and keep Hormuz as a source of strategic leverage. The events of the past two days suggest that, despite its enormous military advantages, the Trump administration may have underestimated how difficult that task would be.

articles.title: Russia launches mass production of electronic warfare systems to counter Starlink, but analysts say its capabilities are overstated
articles.body:
Russia has begun mass production of the Volna Kupol Garant system, designed to jam SpaceX’s Starlink, state-controlled news agency TASS reported late last week. Russia claims the system can “collapse” the operation of Starlink satellites in orbit. However, military analysts interviewed by The Insider are highly skeptical of Moscow’s statements regarding the Volna Kupol Garant’s capabilities.
What do we know about Volna Kupol Garant?
News of a Russian military system called “Volna Kupol Garant” began circulating this past June, with Ukrainian communications and electronic warfare specialist Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov one of the first to report its existence. Around the same time, footage began appearing on social media showing Ukraine’s destruction of similar systems.
The complex consists of several trailers with satellite antennas. Beskrestnov described how it works: The antennas “look” into the sky, toward a passing Starlink satellite, and emit interference toward it so that it cannot receive signals from ordinary terminals. Eight such dishes were enough, he said, to “deafen” a satellite and destabilize terminal operation across an area of about 20 square kilometers.
A TASS source in Russia’s defense industry later described the same operating method for Volna Kupol Garant: a “narrow, directed” signal that “blinds the receiving antennas of satellites.”
“Several devices can close off an entire region. Dozens of devices switched on simultaneously could cause a temporary collapse in Starlink’s operation,” the state news agency quoted the source as saying.
In an interview with Spain’s El Mundo, Ukrainian troops acknowledged that Russian electronic warfare systems of this sort reduce the effectiveness of Starlink, which has been widely used by the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) in recent years. Ukrainian serviceman Ihor Lutsenko described the creation of Ukraine’s own satellite communications system as representing the most reliable solution to the problem.
After that report, the Kremlin-aligned Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper quickly rushed to label Volna Kupol Garant a “Starlink killer.” But the system is far from that.
The system’s actual effect
The system’s effectiveness has predictably been exaggerated by the Russian side, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) wrote last week. Experts interviewed by The Insider agreed with the ISW’s assessment.
Volna Kupol Garant has several major limitations:
- It is not mobile
- It costs about $1.5 million per system
- It has a relatively small coverage area
The relationship between the presumed cost and range makes the system financially unsustainable, said Dr. Thomas Withington, an associate fellow at the UK’s Royal United Services Institute (RUSI):
“Twenty square kilometers isn’t that much. It’s a range of 2.5 kilometers, which is nothing. And $1.5 million dollars to jam 20 square kilometers — that’s very expensive. How many thousands of square kilometers of the occupied area is there? How many of those systems are you going to need, taking into account its cost? This isn’t really a solution. And even if you cover 20 square kilometers — it’s not much. You just fly around the jammer.”
The claimed coverage area of the Volna Kupol Garant is indeed in line with the capabilities of tactical electronic warfare systems already used by Russia’s armed forces, said Anton Zemlianyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center. From that standpoint, he explained, it is not a fundamentally new threat. Scaling up production also does not mean the balance of forces on the front will change as a result. What matters is how Russia integrates the systems and how quickly Ukraine adapts to them.
Zemlianyi said such systems will most likely initially be placed near critical sites in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories and in border areas.
“That will probably become the main task, since Russia will not be able to create continuous electronic warfare coverage over large areas,” he said. “Mass saturation of the front and rear areas with such systems would require significant resources.”
Still, both Zemlianyi and Samuel Bendett, an expert in the U.S.-based research organization CNA, acknowledge that the system has proved effective on some parts of the front. That is supported by Ukrainian troops’ own accounts of interference with Starlink terminals, including in the El Mundo report.
Bendett also noted another important nuance: by emitting a jamming signal, Volna Kupol Garant itself becomes a “powerful beacon.” Like many combat systems that emit signals, including some types of radar, it becomes detectable, trackable and, ultimately, a target for enemy strikes.
A Starlink “killer”?
Russian state media and military bloggers (1, 2, 3) have emphasized that the system acts against the source of the signal: the Starlink satellite itself. Ukrainian bloggers have also reported about this, but military analysts are skeptical of such claims.
“Personally speaking, I don’t believe that claim of the Russians,” Withington said. “The reason why I don’t believe it is because you’ll need a very, very powerful signal to affect a satellite in orbit. Those satellites orbit the planet about a thousand kilometers above. To get the signal there, it must be very powerful. Think of this as running a marathon: before the marathon [runners] eat a lot of food, they drink a lot of water, but at the end of the marathon they’re very weak and exhausted. It’s the same with radio signals. For the signal to be powerful enough to jam a signal in space, you need a huge amount of power on the ground. And it not only needs to reach space, but also do the damage.”
Withington also noted that such a powerful signal could reveal the location of the systems, and its generation would place an extremely heavy load on electrical systems that they may not be designed for.
There is still no solid basis to claim that Volna Kupol Garant can directly affect the operation of Starlink satellites in orbit, Zemlianyi said. Such electronic warfare systems can jam or distort a satellite signal, limiting the effect of the satellite system for the user on the ground, but they do not interfere with the satellite itself.
“The main task of such a system is to create interference and overload the necessary frequency range,” Zemlianyi said. “Simply put, it creates ‘white noise’ over a specific area. That can either make it harder for a terminal to receive the signal or interfere with the satellite’s ability to receive the signal transmitted by the terminal. Roughly speaking, this can be compared to a classic electronic warfare system affecting the communications channel between a relay and a strike drone. As a result, the drone may lose a stable signal, its control channel, or data transmission.”
A jammer for export
The TASS source in Russia’s defense industry also hinted that Moscow is considering selling technologies like Volna Kupol Garant abroad.
“The most interesting thing is that Russia reserves the right to spread this technology among all interested countries around the world. Tools of similar purpose and power have already appeared in China. This is only the beginning,” he said.
CNA expert Samuel Bendett called the statement about selling such systems to Russia’s partners around the world “concerning.” The Financial Times recently reported that Moscow since at least 2023 Russia has secretly helped Tehran develop and produce supersonic cruise missiles. Russia has also been suspected of helping Iran carry out drone strikes on CIA facilities in the Persian Gulf region.

articles.title: Russia now hunts Kyiv by daylight too, Flash explains why
articles.body:
Russia has started launching its strike drones during the day, not only after dark. The reason is the new jet-powered Geran drones, which fire groups cannot take down, so for Russia there is no longer any difference between attacking by day or by night, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, President Zelenskyy's adviser on defense technologies, told Glavcom.
The near-hourly daytime raids are the new face of a campaign that culminated on 1 September, Knowledge Day, when Russia hit Kyiv and its region with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones and killed 12 people. That strike culminated a six-day assault on the capital that began on 27 August, two days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow. However, even after that, the attack continued. Sirens now sound across Kyiv and the surrounding oblast roughly once an hour, around the clock.
Why the shift to daylight
The daytime raids carry an added economic and psychological weight, he said. The threat of strikes forces shops and businesses to open and close unpredictably, snarls transport, and can halt rail service.
"They understand perfectly well that daytime attacks hurt the population and business," Beskrestnov said, adding that the state railway Ukrzaliznytsia is paralyzed.
Keeping the defenders on their feet
A further aim is to hold Ukraine's air defense in a permanent state of readiness, Beskrestnov said. Round-the-clock attacks mean radar stations and generators must run without pause.
"Radar stations and generators run constantly, and that also puts a strain on our troops," he added.
Kyiv remains a Russian prime target because it carries symbolic as well as military weight, as the capital houses the government, business, and warehouses, and a strike there would resonate far more than terrorizing a small town.
Russian forces first concentrated on districts nearer the drones' launch corridors — Kyiv's Left Bank, and the Brovary and Boryspil raions — before switching to the other bank to hunt for targets. As the cold season approaches, he expects Russia to intensify strikes on the energy infrastructure it has so far spared.

articles.title: NATO warns Russia over submarine build up ‘We see them’
articles.body:
NATO says it is closely monitoring the expansion and modernisation of Russia’s submarine force in the High North, including new-generation nuclear-powered cruise missile submarines operating from the Kola Peninsula, according to Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum.
In a statement published on X, the NATO command drew attention to developments around Russia’s Northern Fleet and said the Alliance was treating the growth of its undersea forces seriously.
Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum stated: “Something is moving beneath the surface. Russia is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet.”
The Kola Peninsula in north-west Russia contains several of the Northern Fleet’s principal naval bases and provides access to the Barents Sea and wider North Atlantic. The area is central to Russian submarine operations in northern waters and hosts both nuclear-powered attack submarines and strategic ballistic missile submarines.
NATO specifically referred to the development of newer nuclear-powered guided missile submarines, saying: “Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial capabilities into the High North.”
Something is moving beneath the surface. 🌊
Russia 🇷🇺 is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet.
Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial… pic.twitter.com/UneKonlDon
— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) September 2, 2026
SSGN is the designation commonly used for nuclear-powered submarines equipped primarily for cruise missile operations. Russian boats in this category can be employed against surface ships and land targets, depending on their weapons fit and tasking, while retaining the endurance associated with nuclear propulsion.
The command stated: “They may be invisible beneath the waves. But not for us. We see them, we watch the developments closely and yes, we take these developments seriously.”
The Northern Fleet is responsible for Russian naval activity across the Arctic and High North and operates from bases concentrated around the Kola Peninsula. Its submarines can reach the Norwegian Sea and North Atlantic through waters bordering NATO members Norway and Iceland and areas routinely monitored by allied maritime patrol aircraft, surface vessels and submarines.
Undersea activity in the High North has remained an important part of NATO maritime planning because the region connects Russia’s northern bases with the wider Atlantic. Allied forces regularly conduct anti-submarine warfare training in northern European waters, while maritime patrol aircraft and naval units contribute to surveillance and tracking activity.
Joint Force Command Brunssum is one of NATO’s operational-level joint headquarters and is responsible for planning and conducting activities across part of the Alliance’s northern and eastern area.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadets: ‘Literally they’re kids’
articles.body:
A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border.
On Monday night, Hegseth posted on X a photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor.
However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted a summer camp in July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base.
Its subjects are not members of Canada’s frontline military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18.
The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense.
Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario by executive order, Carney told reporters it was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to de-escalate trade tensions.
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said.
David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said.
The civilian Army Cadet League of Canada accused Hegseth of online harassment. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the group said in a statement.
Adam Kinzinger, the former Republican US congressman and a military veteran, was even more outspoken in a post on X.
“Literally they’re kids. This is a cadet program and our ass hat of a Secdef is making fun of children,” he wrote. “MAGA [Make America Great Again] males are betas who have to punch down to feel big.”
Ruben Gallego, the Democratic Arizona senator and a former marine, called the post “stupid” and “disrespectful”.
Danny O’Regan, a Canadian veteran writing on X, also criticized the post. “The Secretary of Defence is body shaming cadet groups,” he said. “This is not a military unit. They are kids looking for adventure, test themselves and align themselves with the values of service. Don’t be a Pete.”
The Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth. On Tuesday, Jacob Bliss, the defense department’s deputy press secretary, said: “The X post speaks for itself.”
The incident comes as Hegseth faces increasing pressure on several fronts. The US army chief Dan Driscoll resigned this week, reportedly after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. Democrats have accused the defense secretary of having “hollowed out” the military’s senior ranks.
On Wednesday, Iran accused the US of a “war crime” after four people were killed, including a four-year-old child, and dozens injured in a reported missile strike on a wedding at a home in the south of the country.
The ongoing Iran war has also left the US with a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors, the Associated Press reported, sparking fears among Nato allies of increasing vulnerability to a potential Russian military attack.
Hegseth has previously been critical of body shapes in the US military, telling senior commanders in Virginia last year that “fat troops are tiring to look at”.
Ordering military officials to crack down on a lack of physical fitness, he said: “It’s tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops.”

articles.title: For first time, Ukraine shows its British Rapid Ranger air-defense system mounted on Spanish off-road chassis. Its crews call it “close-range storm”
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has released photos of the RapidRanger air defense system mounted on a URO VAMTAC armored vehicle. The troops themselves described the system as a “short-range storm.”
The system defends the sky in areas where radar cannot spot a target and other weapons cannot reach it, filling the gap between mobile fire groups and heavy, less-mobile air-defense systems. That niche — fast, cheap, and radar-independent — is exactly where Russia's Shaheds and small reconnaissance drones have been slipping through.
The images show a crew of the 1030th "Aquila" Anti-Aircraft Missile-Artillery Regiment arming the launcher with missiles before going on combat duty for the first time, RBC-Ukraine reports.
Light enough to ride a pickup
Rapid Ranger weighs only 500 kilograms and has a modular design that allows it to be mounted on pickups, armored cars, or even tracked platforms.
The systems in Ukrainian service ride Spanish URO VAMTAC tactical off-roaders, which reach 135 km/h, drive on public roads, and can change position quickly or cover long distances.
That mobility is the point: a launcher that can shoot and move is far harder for Russian forces to find and destroy than a fixed battery.
Laser guidance beats the decoys
The system's LMM Martlet missiles are 1.3 meters long, weigh 13 kilograms, and reach 1,800 km/h, striking targets up to seven kilometers away. Crucially, the missiles use laser guidance, not only infrared, so Rapid Ranger can hit targets with a low thermal signature or those carrying heat-emitting decoys. That makes it effective against Russian reconnaissance drones like the Orlan-10, whose small heat trail slips past heat-seeking weapons.
A 360-degree electro-optical surveillance suite gives the crew all-around coverage, and the system detects targets out to about 15 kilometers, which is more than twice its engagement range, giving the crew time to track a threat before firing.
Rapid Ranger reached Ukrainian units as part of a British military aid package, and Euromaidan Press reported in April that the system was already downing Shaheds from its Spanish mounts. The 3rd Corps' photos are the newest confirmation that Ukraine's newest Western air-defense hardware is now integrated and standing combat duty at the front.

articles.title: E.U. Chief Says Alleged Russian Drone Plot Had 'Hallmarks of State-Sponsored Terrorism'
articles.body:
An alleged Russian drone plot at a German airport last month had “all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism,” European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas asserted Wednesday, a day after Germany said Russia was responsible.
“We have already summoned Russian ambassadors,” Kallas told reporters in Ireland, ahead of a meeting with European foreign ministers. Kallas said E.U. member states would consider adding further sanctions on Russian military assets, in addition to working with Ukraine on efforts to put additional pressure on Moscow to end the war.
Germany’s Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Russia was responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August, which saw the discovery of an explosive-laden drone close to a runway. Germany's Bild newspaper reported that the drone had been found lying near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Federal police and a bomb disposal unit were deployed to safely dispose of the drone.
Leipzig/Halle has served as a European base for Ukraine's Antonov jets since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The airport is also used by NATO for transportation needs, as well as by the German military.
Wadephul said “the means used to commit the attack, including the drone’s configuration, various components, explosives and ignition technology, are familiar to us from other Russian hybrid operations and from Russia’s war against Ukraine.”
He described the technology found at the airport as “professional” and said the drone’s components demonstrated “a high degree” of technical expertise. “Through the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership consciously chose to damage further our already severely strained bilateral relationship,” he alleged.
Wadephul announced retaliatory measures, relaying how Germany intends to close the Russian consulate in Bonn from Sep. 18. The lease for the Russian House in Berlin, an institute showcasing Russian culture, will be terminated.
There will also be tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and additional pressure will be placed on Moscow's shadow fleet.
Russia has denied responsibility for the drone plot.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that no evidence for the allegations had been presented, and that “under a completely far-fetched and far-fetched pretext, Berlin has once again escalated bilateral relations,” according to Russian state news agency TASS.
In response to the retaliatory actions taken by Germany, Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko told reporters Wednesday that Moscow “will respond as we deem necessary, when we are ready for it.” This came after Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German response a “grave mistake” that “clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people,” according to TASS reporting.
TIME has approached the Russian Foreign Ministry and the Kremlin for comment.
European officials lead support for Germany
Europe has rallied behind Germany and vowed to display a strong, united front.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said “the United Kingdom stands in full solidarity with Germany following Russia’s egregious and reckless attack in Leipzig. Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail.”
French President Emmanuel Macron said Russia's alleged involvement “cannot go unanswered,” calling for European allies to remain united and stand in support of Ukraine.
Further afield, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said "attacking a Ukrainian cargo plane on German soil was an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence—and it will fail."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had discussed the incident with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. “This is yet another Russian escalation, and it is important that Germany responded,” Zelensky said. “I assured him that Ukraine is ready to help—with expertise, experience, or in other areas where Germany may need it.”
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, meanwhile, expressed “full solidarity” with Germany. “The evidence is clear,” he said, voicing his backing of Berlin’s measures against Moscow. “Russia’s attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail.”
The U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said the U.S. "stands in solidarity with Germany and all allies in the face of efforts to cause harm and chaos on NATO territory."
Since President Donald Trump’s return to Office, Washington has maintained that European allies must do more to prop up its defensive capabilities, rather than relying heavily on the U.S.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a review of U.S. troops stationed in Europe in June, expressing the Trump Administration’s disappointment over the “shameful” response from allies to the war with Iran and the lack of support for Washington’s military actions.
NATO has largely heeded the call, with members pledging higher defense spending, but there have still been clashes over key issues, such as Trump’s expressed interest in annexing Greenland.

articles.title: Republican senator calls on Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Hegseth
articles.body:
Republican senator calls on Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Hegseth
Senator Thom Tillis accuses Pentagon chief of ‘inept mismanagement’ as US military is strained by war on Iran.
United States Senator Thom Tillis has called on President Donald Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth for creating a “leadership void” within the military amid the ongoing war with Iran.
In a social media post on Wednesday, Tillis contrasted Hegseth unfavourably with former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who submitted his resignation on Monday amid reported disagreements with the Pentagon chief.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll submits resignation, media reports say
- list 2 of 3Why are US Republicans losing faith in War Secretary Pete Hegseth?
- list 3 of 3Iran targets American bases in Jordan in retaliation to US strikes
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” the North Carolina senator wrote.
“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”
Tillis is a member of Trump’s Republican Party. But in recent years, he has become an increasingly vocal critic from within the party over policies he fears harm democracy.
In June 2025, amid criticism from Trump, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in November’s congressional midterm polls. His term ends in January.
Early in Trump’s second term as president, Tillis was among the senators who voted to confirm Hegseth, a military veteran and former TV host, despite criticisms of his conduct towards women and his past work.
Tillis only confirmed his vote in favour of Hegseth at the last minute, appearing to share some of the concerns being debated in the Senate.
Since taking office as defence secretary, Hegseth has pursued controversial changes to the Pentagon, including attempts to limit journalistic access to the Defence Department.
He has also undertaken a wide-ranging effort to root out what he calls “wokeness” from the military.
That effort has reportedly included firing top military leaders, blocking promotions, removing transgender service members and reviewing admissions standards for top military academies.
In Wednesday’s post, Tillis pointed to some of those efforts, questioning why Hegseth appeared fixated on culture war issues rather than modernising the military.
He pointed to evolving forms of warfare in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and in the US-Israeli war against Iran.
“Our understanding and assumptions of warfare are being challenged in places like Ukraine and Iran, and Dan [Driscoll] understands the old way of doing business no longer applies,” said Tillis.
The senator then proceeded to imply that Driscoll’s departure was a direct result of Hegseth’s mismanagement.
“If we had a Secretary of Defense who maintained the same priorities and forward-thinking, he would be fighting to retain talented leaders like Dan and the many flag officers he has forced into retirement. Instead, he is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks,” Tillis added.
Hegseth has faced growing scrutiny in recent months as the US struggles to achieve its goals in the war on Iran, launched on February 28. The war hit its six-month mark last week with no end in sight.
Media reports indicate that the war has left the Pentagon struggling with shrinking munitions stockpiles that could hinder the US military in future actions.
The war has also taken a toll on the popularity of the Trump administration, which has seen approval numbers sink ahead of the November congressional election.
Since the war began, fuel prices have skyrocketed, and the conflict has spread across the Middle East.
More than two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the administration’s handling of the war, according to a University of Massachusetts poll released on August 31.

articles.title: Von der Leyen, Rutte say Russian ‘intimidation will not work’ to stop Ukraine aid
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen speaks as NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte listens during a press statement at EU headquarters on September 2, 2026, in Brussels. | Omar Havana/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The EU and NATO will not back down from supporting Ukraine despite attacks against European countries blamed on Russia, the leaders of the two institutions said Wednesday.
The rare joint statement came after Germany said Russia was behind a foiled attack on an airport used as a key logistics hub for military aid to Ukraine.
“This was an attack using military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil — we will not tolerate it,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels. “If the intention was to make us think twice about supporting Ukraine, I can tell you it has only strengthened my resolve; intimidation will not work.”
Advertisement
“If Russia thinks we will be divided by the threat, or if they think we will be deterred from supporting Ukraine, they are mistaken,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said. “Our unity is unshaken — our support to Ukraine is clear.”
He slammed Russia's moves as “reckless,” describing a series of recent actions including “drones and missiles” intruding into NATO airspace, “malign activities” such as fires allegedly set at factories producing defense equipment for Ukraine and Russia's “hybrid attack” against the east German Leipzig-Halle airport.
“The dangers Russia poses are clear,” Rutte said.
On Tuesday, Berlin attributed an attempted Aug. 4 attack in Leipzig to Russia. Three drones carrying explosive material were spotted at or near the airport, including one that was found near a Ukrainian Antonov plane used to ship munitions.
The remarks underscore growing tensions between Moscow and Ukraine’s Western allies as they increasingly blame Russia for sabotage and other hybrid attacks on their territory while continuing to send military aid to Kyiv.
Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia would “adopt much harsher methods to destroy everything that enables the West to fuel Kyiv’s war machine.”
Advertisement
Von der Leyen said the EU would send “rapid response teams” to help countries impacted by similar incidents and was “ready to impose” further sanctions against Russia. The bloc’s foreign ministers, who are meeting in Ireland on Wednesday, will discuss further measures against Moscow, she added.
The leaders also signaled that the response to Russian pressure would include more support for Ukraine.
Von der Leyen also confirmed EU countries were examining a new payment request of “several billion euros” by Ukraine to fund its air defenses, including buying advanced U.S.-made PAC-3 Patriot interceptors. Ukraine is complaining of a critical shortage of air defenses that's allowing Russian ballistic missiles to hit targets across the country. The request, first reported by POLITICO, will be examined by Commission experts on Sept. 7.

articles.title: Spy planes swarm Russia’s borders in rare surge
articles.body:
Two RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft, at least two P-8A Poseidons and American tanker support are operating across the High North in a concentration of intelligence-gathering flights rare in both scale and composition, according to open-source tracking.
The account DefenceGeek, run by one of our team members Jon, logged the aircraft operating from the United Kingdom and Iceland, watching across the border into Russia. Among them were the Royal Air Force Rivet Joint ZZ666 using the callsign ASCOT 7202, an American RC-135W as JAKE 17, and a KC-135R tanker as RAKE 67 providing refuelling.
A United States Air Force Rivet Joint is operating within the European Command area for the first time in a while, flying near Russia’s naval base complex at Murmansk. It is likely to be operating with fighter escort given an active tanker bridge in the area. A second Rivet Joint, this one British, was tracked along the border between Russia and Finland, with a Poseidon monitoring the Baltic at low altitude. American Rivet Joint aircraft have concentrated elsewhere in recent years, which is what makes an appearance over the Barents notable.
NATO Eyes on Russia Continues
Two RC-135 “Rivet Joint” SIGINT platforms and at least 2 P-8A “Poseidon” aircraft are operating out of the UK & Iceland today in the high north, watching across the border into Russia, supported by US tankers:
🇬🇧 RC-135W “ASCOT7202” ZZ666 #43C39D… pic.twitter.com/dqKU3KIQuv
— DefenceGeek 🇬🇧 (@DefenceGeek) September 2, 2026
What they are looking at
Murmansk and the wider Kola Peninsula hold the Russian Northern Fleet, including the ballistic missile submarines that carry the sea-based portion of the Russian deterrent, along with the attack boats that transit south into the Atlantic. It is the single most concentrated collection of Russian naval power anywhere, and the point from which any submarine deployment towards the Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom gap begins.
The RC-135W does not take photographs, no, it is an electronic surveillance aircraft, and its crews survey the electromagnetic spectrum to collect communications, radar emissions and other signals, building a picture of what is switched on, where it is, and how it behaves. Flying a track along a border allows the aircraft to map air defence radars and communications networks without entering the airspace they cover.
The P-8A Poseidon does a different job, of course. It hunts submarines, using sonobuoys dropped into the water and its own radar and acoustic processing, and the Royal Air Force operates nine of them from RAF Lossiemouth in Moray. A Poseidon working the Baltic at low altitude is looking at what is on and under the surface.
Britain operates three Rivet Joints from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, converted from KC-135 airframes under a co-operative programme with the United States Air Force, which flies a larger fleet of the type from Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska.
The flights come at the end of a fortnight of unusually heavy allied air activity along the Russian frontier. Around 25 aircraft from several nations operated over the Baltic region on 18 August in a package overseen by the United States, including an EA-37B Compass Call electronic attack aircraft and an ARTEMIS II intelligence platform, with further flights on the two days following. NATO E-3A Sentry aircraft and Multinational MRTT Fleet tankers have been operating over Lithuania and Poland since.
Germany formally attributed the attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russian intelligence on Tuesday, announcing the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn along with new sanctions and entry restrictions, in a step Estonia’s prime minister described as Russia taking its hybrid attacks in Europe to a new and dangerous level.
Surveillance flights of this kind are deliberately visible, as readers will know. Aircraft on these missions generally transmit, and their tracks appear on civilian monitoring platforms, which is a choice rather than an oversight.
The Russian Navy has meanwhile had no presence in the Mediterranean since June, with a NATO official telling us last week that allied warships outnumber Russian vessels in European waters by roughly three to one.
Neither the Ministry of Defence nor United States Air Forces in Europe comments on individual intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sorties.

articles.title: How 9/11 Shaped My Life
articles.body:
Twenty-five years later, Sept. 11 remains a watershed moment, one with both personal and global implications. To mark the anniversary, TIME spoke to people with very different connections to the day, to hear about what they experienced at the time as well as the ripple effects. For some, the legacy of the date is one of profound loss. Others know about the tragedy mostly from history class. One thing is clear: The attacks that changed the world also changed lives.
I was 4½ when my dad died. I have only brief memories of that day. I remember my mom taking my twin brother and me out of preschool. I remember watching the TV at home and then going over to one of her friends’, whose husband was also a firefighter, and watching it there. We were so young, we didn’t really grasp what was actually going on. But as you get older, you start to realize what you’ve missed out on. It’s not quite the same as being sad because you miss someone close to you. It’s more like you’re sad because you didn’t really get to be close to them.
My dad was a cop for 12 years and a firefighter for only 18 months, but joining the FDNY was always his plan. For as long as I can remember, I also wanted to be a firefighter. I did the entry exam when I was 18, even though they don’t take anyone until 21. I went to college, but I think I was just killing time. I dropped out after two years, as the process ramped up. My mom kept encouraging me to consider other things, but she knew I had put all my eggs in that basket. I loved the routine and discipline of the academy, and I really tried to earn my spot; I didn’t want to feel like I was getting special treatment.
A lot of things about the fire department don’t change, and I remember thinking my dad might have stood right where I was standing, worrying about getting yelled at by some drill instructor for having a button undone. I don’t have many shared memories with him, but that came close. He worked in Brooklyn, just on the other side of the tunnel from the World Trade Center. I wanted to go to a different firehouse, to let the guys make up their mind about me without having known his reputation, so I’m in the Bronx. The firefighters I meet that knew him, I feel like they're happy to see that I'm on the job.
On 9/11 I usually go to Mass at my firehouse and then drop by Ladder 101, where Dad worked. Last year for the first time I met someone who was actually riding that day, and he gave me the full rundown. They were staged at the mouth of the tunnel right under the towers, and as they sat there on the rigs, they watched the second plane come in. They could feel the impact and then they went straight in. From what I understand, his group went up a way, came back down, and were in the lobby when the building collapsed.
Dad was also a lifeguard at Overlook Beach in Long Island, and the lifeguards there put up a little memorial for him. My mom is not big on going to the firehouse or the ceremonies in the city on the anniversaries. I think it’s just too overwhelming. So we do a more casual gathering in the afternoon. It’s less somber, more a reason for everyone to just get together.
Sometimes the attention that comes with being a legacy firefighter is uncomfortable, but not for the reasons you might think. I don’t have trouble talking about it; it was something that happened when I was young, but I had a happy childhood and a very fortunate life. I’m not looking for sympathy—I feel lucky to have had that role model of selflessness and self-sacrifice. On the other hand, I do miss having had a real relationship with my dad.
Do I wish he was still alive? Of course. I sometimes wonder if I’d be different if I’d known my dad. But that event shaped my way of thinking and shaped me. I’m very proud of what he did, and I think it’s a very admirable and honorable way to die. And I wouldn’t want someone else to have been in his place because I don’t think that’s what he would have wanted. –As told to Belinda Luscombe
Kelsey Griffin
My journey of becoming a pilot started when I was 14, when I went to a youth summer camp sponsored by the Organization of Black Aerospace Professionals (OBAP). When I first told my parents that I wanted to be a pilot, of course they were a little bit concerned about the dangers that come with flight training at a young age, but they were also very supportive.
I took my first discovery flight with an instructor in 2022. At first I was definitely nervous, because there was so much going on in the plane at once. But once we were at around 2,000 feet, everything became incredibly peaceful. Looking down at the scenery gave me a sense of freedom that I never really experienced anywhere else. I knew at a young age that I never wanted to work a traditional nine-to-five job. I was also really big on traveling, and that discovery flight showed me that being a pilot was something I could do every day and enjoy. I took my first solo fight in 2024.
Flight training is expensive, but my parents made sacrifices to support me financially as I sought out scholarships and opportunities. I was drawn to the LeRoy W. Homer Jr. Foundation Scholarship, because of their mission to empower future aviators. He was an African American pilot, and a first officer for United Airlines on Flight 93. I wasn’t alive when 9/11 happened, so my understanding comes from learning about it through documentaries and conversations with my parents and grandparents and others.
The tragedies definitely impacted not only the lives of everyday people, but also caused major disruption in the aviation industry. When my mentor just started his career as a pilot, he got furloughed soon after 9/11 because the airline industry was completely devastated over Americans’ fear of flying. I have a family member that is still afraid to fly on aircrafts.
Before I went to college, I became a private pilot and a licensed drone pilot. I briefly stopped my training after one of my friends passed away, but getting the scholarship lifted my spirits and gave me an extra push to continue my goal. The scholarship exists because of somebody who lived with courage, professionalism, and commitment to serving others. Knowing that I’m representing his legacy motivates me to work harder and fly with integrity, and never take opportunities for granted.
At Middle Georgia State University, I'm enrolled in aviation courses to finish out my remaining ratings and license and also to, as we call it in the industry, time build. I have to get at least 1,000 flight hours before I can go to a regional airline. It will probably take me about six more years of training to become a major airline pilot. African American women make up less than 1% of professional pilots in the U.S. I have had the privilege of connecting with several of them through organizations such as Sisters of the Skies, OBAP, Aviation Career Enrichment, Pink STEM, and Youth in Aviation. Having this support gives me a sense of comfort and understanding that through hard work, I can also achieve it. –As told to Philip Wang
Alka Pradhan
I was infamous as an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins for choosing classes in the afternoon so I could sleep all morning. My more diligent roommate would try to wake me so she’d have someone to talk to. On 9/11, I thought that’s what she was doing. Maybe a minute or so after she got me to the TV, the second plane hit. It was terrifying.
Even at 19, I was on track to study the intersection of human-rights law and international humanitarian law. When it became clear in early October that we, the U.S., were going to strike Afghanistan in a way that seemed not entirely targeted and seemed to conflate the Taliban with al-Qaeda, that began my interest in all this. But to me, our actions didn't seem to comply with the law of war that I had been studying. I really did not anticipate that I would eventually use my specialization to litigate as hard as I possibly could against my own government. But that is what I have done for the past 13ish years in my work at Guantánamo.
I was already working with Guantánamo detainees when, in 2015, I got a call from a friend at the Department of Defense, who said the military commissions, which are prosecuting those actually alleged to have organized the attacks on 9/11, were hiring civilians. He asked if I’d be interested in representing Ammar al-Baluchi, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed’s nephew. I thought, well, there's nothing I can do that is deeper in the heart of this morass than the military commissions, because the CIA torture programs are at the heart of these cases. So I've been a defense attorney for Ammar al-Baluchi’s 9/11 case since 2015. It has been in pretrial hearings for 14 years.
For 9/11, the actual fact allegations against al-Baluchi are that he transferred money to people who ended up being the hijackers. We have never contested the fact that he transferred money. He was in Dubai, he was asked to transfer money, he transferred money. The $10,000 question is: What did he know at the time? And the government has no evidence that is not derived from torture that indicates he had any knowledge of what was happening on Sept. 11.
The 9/11 case really is all day, every day. It is the biggest criminal case in U.S. history. I hold a top-secret security clearance, and I still don’t have all the information I need about the torture at the black sites that impacted how Ammar is today and the statements he gave later. The trial has just been scheduled for June 2028, but I don’t know if it will ever happen, and I think that is a very hard truth, particularly for the victims’ family members. Witnesses have passed away, evidence has been destroyed by the government. The men themselves are deteriorating because the U.S. refuses to give them the medical care they need as undisputed torture victims. Millions and millions of dollars have been wasted on this exercise so far. It’s the Jarndyce v Jarndyce of the United States.
However I also think this is one of the most important things I will ever do because it shows fellow Americans that this is what dissent looks like, and I know it sounds trite, but this is also what patriotism looks like. I am both grateful for and have great contempt for what the Department of Defense has done over these 25 years. On 9/11 I will reach out to the victims’ family members who I am in touch with and convey my very deep sadness and anger over what happened. I will watch the commemorations. I will contemplate. Then I will start speaking again about everything that we are continuing to do wrong. –As told to B.L.
Jukay Hsu
I was student-body president at Stuyvesant High, three blocks from the World Trade Center. I had an early meeting that day with the principal about the plans for the year. So normally I’d be walking to school when the first plane hit. We evacuated, I think, just as the first tower fell, and I remember looking through these two-story plate-glass windows at this billowing black-gray kind of fog coming from one way as we went out the other way into a sunny sky.
I grew up in Queens. My mother was a social worker. I was lucky to get full financial aid to Harvard, and signed up for ROTC, then went to Iraq. I always thought service was public service. I was a second lieutenant leading a platoon of 40 men in Salahuddin province, kind of at the mid-end of the surge. Even with combat patrols, I ended up doing a lot around civil governance because counterinsurgency involves that. It was a very different kind of learning.
When I got out of the military, all my classmates were going into tech. I was like, If New York is going to become a tech sector, how can more people be included in that? All the soldiers I worked with never went to college. That's the difference between officer and soldier. Even though my platoon sergeant was 20 years older than me, I was in charge because I went to college. It really got you thinking: All these companies and jobs and wealth are being created, but two-thirds of Americans and two-thirds of New Yorkers don’t have a four-year college degree. In 2011, I ended up creating Pursuit. Our idea was to train working-class people in the skills tech companies tell us they need. The average student arrived making $16,000 and a year later has a job paying $94,000.
I left Pursuit to start a research organization called Bright Future to focus on AI alignment for the benefit of humanity. There’s this idea that AI is going to be so dominant, so superpowerful, not just tools, but creating a being—we’re trying to create like a god, essentially, right? It's kind of crazy. So what does that mean for humans? This year I also joined the New York City Economic Development Board, which oversees and shapes AI policy.
Perhaps the future is not college versus noncollege. Perhaps it’s going to be AI and non-AI. But hopefully, there’s a way to democratize that and enable cooperation. We're creating these new digital minds, so you have to consider their power and impact. Early on in high school, it was imprinted on me that what’s most important is what happens to all of us. And the ability to have agency in that. 9/11 helped cement that. Important critical junctures really can bring out the best in humanity, if we choose to respond.
Marc Rivera
I was born in Puerto Rico but have lived all but the first three months of my life on the Lower East Side of Manhattan. Next year, it will be 50 years that I'm pastoring down here. Primitive Church is within eyeshot of the towers. On 9/11, I saw the towers fall and then didn’t set foot outside lower Manhattan until March the following year.
I had just dropped my younger son at high school a block away from the Trade Center and I was going into the church office when I saw my secretary outside. She simply says, “Look.” Sure enough, there was a gaping hole in the north tower. I could see what I thought was debris falling. Later on, I discovered it may have been people. I turned around to get my son, but the police wouldn’t let me through, so I went back to the church, and all of a sudden, a sea of people filled with soot and stuff came walking down our street. We opened the church to them. We had four landlines that were somehow still working. Eventually my son walked in with a bunch of friends, all covered in soot. My older son also arrived from midtown. That was a rebirth moment for me. I was able to shift my attention to helping the helpers and healing the healers.
By day two after the collapse, I was doing what I've always done: galvanizing people and starting to help individuals, raising money to pay people's rent and medical bills and for funerals. We established the Ground Zero Clergy Task Force, which was simply clergy of different faiths, denominations, and traditions who gathered together to help at the site and to coordinate churches with FEMA and the New York City government. Every day, anywhere from 15 to 50 clergy would meet in the sanctuary, and then go down to the hole, to ground zero, to see what we could do. About a year afterward, I established a Northeast Clergy Group, which was broader and longer-standing. It tried to run the same program for people at the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania.
We closed those organizations eventually, but through them I saw the importance of not being so rigid or immovable in my theological training. Many religious people, regardless of faith tradition, tend to think that we have the patent on truth. This event broadened my perspective and really challenged me to make that change intellectually and also in my practice. When tragedy strikes, no one cares how much training you have, how many books you have written, how large your congregation is. Because the bottom line is love. I saw a fireman who looked so tired and I asked if I could pray for him. I didn’t ask what he believed first.
The most painful consequence for me personally was that my oldest son, Tim, was diagnosed with Stage IV colorectal cancer, one of the cancers that is covered by the 9/11 fund. He fought it courageously for three years, but this September will mark one year since his passing. He would have been 46. We believe he probably got it because we live down here.
One of my greatest concerns today is that there are still people in our congregation and in this community who may qualify for assistance through the 9/11 fund that the federal government set up, but some remain reluctant to apply. They’re more afraid of the system than they are of getting sick. So, more than two decades later, part of our ministry is still helping people understand that the consequences of Sept. 11 did not end on Sept. 11. We are still caring for people. We are still encouraging people to seek the help that is available to them. And we are still learning what that terrible day taught us from the very beginning: when people are hurting, our first responsibility is to love them.
Connie Stevanus
That day, I was working at a bank, and as I went from department to department, they were bringing this up on their computers. On my way home, it’s just a two-lane country road, and there was so much traffic. Cars were passing me in either direction. They were state police cars. When I finally got home, I see my husband picking things out of the yard, and I didn’t know what he was doing until I went to pull into our driveway. It was black, totally black, with small pieces of burnt debris. And it just hit me then what I was looking at. Flight 93 carried mail. We had mail in our trees, in our yard. The neighbor across the road from us had a piece of the United Airlines magazine in her yard.
We started volunteering at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pa., after my husband had retired from work, like five years after 9/11. People come from all over—Europe, Australia, different countries. They like to tell you where they were and their experiences of that day. And then they always ask, “Where were you when this happened?” We get a lot of school students, and they're very alert to what happened here, so they're usually very quiet and very respectful. My 21-year-old grandson wasn't born yet. And when he was in eighth grade, I think it was, his school came out.
I never get tired of talking about it. Probably 99% of them still feel the pain and show their emotions easily when we're talking. Sometimes it’s a little hard to be there, because I’m that person—I might not be able to say the right thing to you, but I can cry right alongside of you. At the Visitor Center, we have those three phone messages. You know that some of the passengers on Flight 93 had to leave messages because they didn’t get an answer? Those are very powerful.
Can I share one little story with you? This was just after they were done with the excavation and the road opened up. So it was about two weeks later. My husband and I stopped there after work one evening. And it was just like the day of 9/11. Sunny, bright blue sky, not a cloud in the sky. There was nobody around, just me and my husband. We looked down through the field, and you could just see where the crash site was, the fresh soil that covered that area. And we just stood there. And all you could hear were birds, the rustling of the high grass, and just silence. And there wasn't a flag. There was nothing where you would think something like this happened. You could see the little fence that they had around the debris field. But that is a moment that I'll never forget. –As told to Karl Vick
Shams Frough
I was going into fifth grade when 9/11 happened. I remember, because it was two days after a famous Northern Alliance commander was assassinated. Obviously, there was no TV in Kabul, but our ears were wide open and we did hear about it on the radio. (From a very young age, I was listening to BBC Persian.) Then came the bombings, and life in Kabul became a bit hard, so for a short period, I went back to my village, Kapisa, which is 100 km from Kabul, where I had shepherding duties. I remember very well the big difference when we returned to school; girls were going too, and we no longer had to wear black turbans. Everybody wanted the Taliban to go, but we didn’t know that eventually all these American soldiers would come and there would be a hot war again. We all thought the Northern Alliance would take over.
My mother died when I was young, and my father really worked to make sure his children did not have to work on the farm. I went to an elite Turkish-run high school; out of 6,000 applicants, only 100 were accepted—and some of those places were reserved for the children of government ministers. Most lessons were in English, but we also learned Turkish. I wanted to go to medical school, but I was young and male and I believed the hype, and in the last year of school I began working with the U.S. Army. I was sent to Kandahar as an interpreter. After I was nearly killed twice, I was transferred to the Department of Procurements in Kabul and ended up doing simultaneous translation for colonels and generals who were advising the Afghan military and police. I reported what looked like corruption in the Afghan procurement process, and then I knew I had to leave. It took three years, until 2014—a week or so after I resigned—for my Special Immigrant Visa to be processed.
My wife and I were initially assigned to Albuquerque, N.M., which was funny, because my Army friends always made fun of the mud huts in Afghanistan and there they were in America, only it was called adobe. When we moved to Chicago, I went to community college and so I took up driving taxis and Ubers. I’d study all week and then sleep in my taxi at the airport, because there was always a three-hour wait for a fare. Then in 2021, I started a business called Kapisa Rugs; it was rebranded as Rugistan in 2024, and we directly source hand-knotted rugs from Afghanistan. It’s not easy with Amazon and other competition, so to keep prices down, I’m here seven days a week. Right now we have two locations, but this is not the goal.
I love rugs. I'll always cherish them. But hopefully, in about a year, it will be profitable enough, and my wife will have taken over and I will be able to fire myself. Some of my high school friends who didn’t join the Army are already doctors here, so I sometimes feel like I haven’t lived up to my capacity in the way I could have in Afghanistan. I am currently completing my master’s of public health at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, and I hope to start medical school in 2028. I joke with my wife that I’ll probably graduate alongside our sons. –As told to B.L.
Sari Beth Rosenberg
My first day of student teaching was supposed to be 9/11. I was 26, in grad school, planning to observe a teacher teaching U.S. history at LaGuardia High School. My alarm-clock radio played Z Morning Zoo, a show known for its goofiness, but the hosts were talking about a plane crashing into the Twin Towers and I thought, “That’s not funny.” I turned on the TV, and that’s when I was like, “Oh my, no, this is actually real.” I got a phone call from one of my best friends who worked on Canal Street near the Twin Towers, and when I saw the first tower buckle, I yelled to her, “You have to run!”
The next semester, I was placed at Stuyvesant High School by what was once the Twin Towers. The air was constantly being tested in the cafeteria. And yet 9/11 never came up in the classroom. In the years that followed, I would have students interview a friend or family member about that day as a lesson in how history is remembered, showing them that they just collected primary sources.
Nowadays, students are more clued into current events on their devices and TikTok, so they’re asking really interesting questions about 9/11, like “Why did we attack Afghanistan?” Many students don’t understand the difference between why we went into Afghanistan in the early 2000s versus Iraq. Many adults don't know the difference if they don't really pay attention to the news or recent current events. How do you understand what’s going on in Iran now if you don’t understand the history of Iraq, Iran, the Middle East?
Kids don’t talk about the fear of terrorists coming from the Middle East. The thing that kids are more scared of today is what they see as domestic terror coming from ICE agents. I’ve had to explain that ICE was created in 2003 as part of the new Department of Homeland Security, which was established in response to 9/11, and now it’s being used to, in my opinion, terrorize communities.
I’m definitely going to bring up the 25th anniversary in class this year. They were born so long after 9/11, it’s history to them. We need to find ways to cover more recent history. In a U.S. history class—or any history class—there’s so much to cover, and we don’t get to the recent history, from 1980 to the present, because it’s not emphasized on tests and also you run out of time. –As told to Olivia B. Waxman
Allison Turkel
On Sept. 11, I was outside of Albuquerque, N.M. I worked for a not-for-profit then called the National Center for Prosecution of Child Abuse, and we were running a conference. And the receptionist where we were holding it said a plane just hit the World Trade Center, and you could go into our break room to watch it on TV. I went in just in time to see the second plane hit. Luckily I was able to reach my dad, who had a meeting downtown that day. I got him right before the phones went out in New York, and then we started driving back. We looked on our map. We tried to avoid missile silos because we thought that those might be under attack or shooting things. We had no idea. I drove crying. Not the whole time, but a lot. It’s a skill.
I lived in the D.C. area at the time, but I grew up in Manhattan, up in Washington Heights. I worked down in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which was actually in the zone. So all of it translates well into how and why I’ve been the Special Master of the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund for the last 3½ years.
We want as many people as possible to know, one, we’re still here. We are in business until 2090. We have as much funding as is necessary to pay every eligible claimant. And two, we serve people beyond first responders. We serve people that lived, worked, went to school in the New York exposure zone, who were at Shanksville and at the Pentagon.
