We really encourage people if they were there, to register with the VCF. In order to file a claim, folks need to get certified that they have a 9/11 illness from the World Trade Center Health Program, which is our sister program that runs out of HHS. We are receiving over 700 new claims a month.
Since 2011, when we reopened, we have received over 110,000 claims. We've paid out $18.5 billion compensation. [The original VCF closed in 2004 after paying out the $7 billion appropriated for those killed or physically injured on 9/11.] The CDC estimates that in New York alone, over 400,000 people may have been exposed to the toxins.
Remember “America Strong”? “Let everybody return”? “Let's begin to live, work, go to school, start over again”? People went back into the New York zone, and the consequence, of course, is they were exposed to these toxins that have made them ill. And people have died from it. On that day, 2,977 people perished at all three sites and on the planes. Since we reopened, we’ve had 6,100 of our claimants die from exposure to the toxins. And unfortunately, every year there are more people becoming ill. Today, 63% of our claimants have a cancer, and those cancers, because of the unique nature of what people were exposed to, may have long latency periods.
Every Sept. 11, the memorial and museum in New York City does the reading of the names of the victims, and there’s always six moments of silence, to mark the four moments of impact and two tower collapses. This year, they’re adding a seventh, to honor the people that have become ill from the toxins. I think that’ll help spread awareness that so many are still suffering and that the 9/11 VCF is here to help.
Christopher Ashley
I actually didn't behave that great that day. I almost got into a fistfight.
It was the first day of rehearsal for the play Wonder of the World, which I was directing. We canceled rehearsal for that day and the next, and I ended up walking back home to the West Village. Late that night, there was a very drunk man who put himself in front of me and asked if I was an Iraqi. He kept putting himself in front of me, and I kept trying to get away. Then he took a swing at me, and I punched him in the face.
It’s not automatic that people are their best selves in these moments. I think one of the things people do with traumatic situations is move on, so it was really meaningful to me to dig back into the feelings that that day created while directing Come From Away, a musical about 38 planes grounded in Gander, Newfoundland, and the people who took care of strangers at this moment of real terror. Telling that story around the world, onstage, on Apple TV helped me heal.
In 2011, the play’s authors, David Hein and Irene Sankoff, went to a 10th anniversary event reconvening a lot of the people who had been diverted there on 9/11. They expected to be there for a couple of days and ended up staying for weeks and weeks. Claude Elliott, the mayor of Gander, used to joke, "Wait, you guys are making a musical about making sandwiches?”
In the current world we're living in, it almost seems mythical that people would take this good care of each other because there are just so many things that pull us apart and make us suspicious of each other. We're all vulnerable. Nobody’s safely apart behind a wall. We're all going to have to figure out how to share the world and the space together. The world keeps changing, but the show remains about the responsibility we have to each other and the value of kindness and connection. Twenty-five years ago, if more people thought like the people in Gander—“these people are my problem, my responsibility, and I will take care of them, despite the fact that I didn't meet them until today”—I think we'd be in a better place. –As told to O.B.W.
Nancy Gibbs
Moments after 8:46 a.m., attention fixed on one incomprehensible event. As first responders scrambled and survivors fled, the rest of us skidded to a stop and watched.
At TIME, editor Jim Kelly launched a reporting army: correspondents around the world tracked the attacks and reactions in real time. White House correspondent Jay Carney was with President Bush in the press pool; writers and editors in the New York City headquarters headed downtown, or to city hospitals and command centers. My job was to curate and condense it all into a single story for a special issue of the magazine. “I just want you to tell the story of today,” Jim told me. “Think of it as a time capsule.”
In one sense we all saw something different. If you lived in New York City, not only did you see the smoke, you smelled it, tasted it. You heard the sirens, felt the fear. Elsewhere, the alerts jolted large towns and small. Local landmarks shivered and then shut down: Disney World and the Sears Tower, Congress and the Supreme Court, the Space Needle. Also, the entire airspace of the United States.
But at a deeper level, we all saw the same thing, a once unimaginable attack on what we soon started calling the Homeland, as though we were all residents of the same reality. No matter how different our individual experiences of that day, we lived through it together and emerged more united: By October, 60% of people said they trusted the government to do the right thing all or most of the time, a three-decade high.
It’s easier to put a jigsaw puzzle together when you can see the whole picture on the lid of the box. Yes, there were toxic rumors and conspiracies even without the yet-to-be-invented Facebook and X. But compared with what has transpired since then, the information landscape looks practically pristine. The demolition of the business model for traditional news sources corresponded with sinking institutional trust across the board. Journalism’s self-inflicted wounds and technological upheaval radically changed how people make sense of the world. Trust in government now sits around 17%. Trust in the media has hit an all-time low.
If you had told me 25 years ago, as we color-coded the threat level, cast a wide surveillance net, launched a Global War on Terror, that we would manage to avoid further terror attacks, I would have found it hard to believe. But I also couldn’t have imagined the maceration of the media as our news channels filled with content of all kinds streaming in from all corners. This year for the first time, more people globally rely on social and video platforms for news, rather than TV or news websites. As audiences migrate from broadcast and cable, print and radio, to creators on TikTok and YouTube, the very notion of a shared reality feels quaint. Eight in 10 of us say Democrats and Republicans can’t even agree on basic facts, which makes reasoned discussion of everything from security threats to education reform all but impossible.
Twenty-five years ago, like journalists everywhere, I focused on how to tell this story, in the belief that stories are stickier than bloodless fact. But what has happened since makes me wonder if I missed the actual war. Sept. 11 did not cause 21st century truth decay, but it coincided with it. Jolted out of the snug 1990s, people went searching for answers they could trust, tribes they could join, distraction as an antidote to alarm. We no longer hear the same stories and too many leaders are counting on that. We can each collect the puzzle pieces, but it's harder to see the full picture. Even when the country is broadly united around key values—reject political violence, protect the safety net, get money out of politics, regulate AI—the sense of division abides and people on both sides see mainly a caricature of their opponents.
Strong societies need good information; communities benefit from shared stories. On Sept. 11, many of those stories were of quiet, reflexive heroism, sacrifice, service. First responders and random strangers modeled courage under fire, and the rest of us were swept up in a wave of gratitude that helped drain the fear. Those are stories worth retrieving now. –Nancy Gibbs
Keira Unterzuber, Eric Johnson, and Freya Johnson
Keira: My first child was due on Sept. 3, and my doctor was going to induce me on the 13th. So the 11th was any other day, really. I was getting ready for work when my husband, who is a pilot and was home on family leave, said, “Keira, come here.” He explained that a plane had crashed in the World Trade Center, and I said, “But it's so sunny!” He's like, “Yeah, that's really weird.” And while we were watching the TV, the second plane hit. As the morning went on, I started to feel unwell. But then I don’t think anybody felt well that day.
Eric: We live near the Pentagon, and suddenly, it was like somebody pushed over a piano in the room next to us. It shook the whole house. The cats jumped off the bed and hid. I went outside and saw smoke. Sometime in there, Keira said, “I’m having the baby today.” I drove 80 to 90 miles an hour all the way  to the hospital. There was zero traffic. It was eerie, like driving somewhere in the middle of the night. 
Keira: Because of construction, we had to go through the emergency-room entrance and I remember all these emergency medical staff just waiting, and not for me. In the delivery room, Eric started to say he was ready to join the military and go fight the terrorists and because of the mood that he was in, he suggested several new names for the baby: Phoenix, America, Freedom, Liberty. I just said no, no, no. Eventually he picked Freya, who is goddess of war and love and a very strong woman. 
Freya: When I was young, I didn’t really understand the significance of the day. But around the 10th anniversary, I realized, “Oh, this is huge,” and then it became very depressing. On the morning announcements at school, they’d show a video tribute, and those videos were obviously very sad. In middle school, some kid told me that I was the reincarnation of Osama bin Laden. So I used to wish I was born on the 10th or the 12th. I actually didn’t celebrate my birthday from ages 10 to 13. It just felt inappropriate and weird to be so happy when everyone else was not. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve told people my birthday, and it becomes a whole conversation. When I need ID at a bar or when I have to pick up a prescription, and they ask me for my birthday, they’re like, “Really?” I’ve even had people ask me, “What was that like for you?” And I have to say, “Well, I was not even born yet so I was not aware of anything.” I’ve learned to just say my birthday is in September. However, as I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized that I like my birthday. It’s such a beautiful time of year. I’m at the point where I can acknowledge that it was sad, but I can also celebrate myself. All my friends tell me that when they think of 9/11, they think of me as their first thought. 
Keira: When something tragic happens, it’s a beautiful thing to be around a newborn baby. My brother’s wife lost her first husband on the 10th, and his funeral was on the 13th. She adores Freya because, in her world, she’s a bright light at a dark moment. We have a lot of friends who say that year after year: She was the shining light that day. –As told to B.L.

articles.title: NATO has no plans to deploy nuclear weapons to additional countries — Polish official
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. NATO is not considering the deployment of nuclear warheads to additional countries as part of its Nuclear Sharing program, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said.
"As of today, the deployment of nuclear warheads beyond the places already hosting them is not on the [NATO] agenda," he told RMF FM.
However, the Polish defense official clarified that Warsaw sought to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence concept and that it was one of the issues on the agenda. "For the first time, we have been able to make sure that NATO countries are willing to include Poland in the nuclear sharing program, which is a very serious one," Zalewski noted.
On August 27, Zalewski said at a press conference at the NATO headquarters in Brussels that Poland had neither the desire nor plans to host nuclear weapons. He explained that Warsaw would like to be part of NATO’s nuclear deterrence strategy without having nuclear arms stationed in the country.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki said in an interview with Polsat television in mid-February that Warsaw should seek access to nuclear weapons. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, in turn, stressed that the authorities were not considering such an option. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke of the country’s interest in the "nuclear umbrella" project proposed by French President Emmanuel Macron.

articles.title: India news: Foreign Minister Jaishankar begins Poland, Ukraine visit
articles.body:
India news: Jaishankar offers help to end war in Ukraine
Published September 3, 2026last updated September 3, 2026
What you need to know
Here is a roundup of the latest developments from India on Thursday, September 3.
- India's foreign minister on tour of Poland and Ukraine
- US Secretary of State has responded to a key meeting between Indian PM Narendra Modi and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian
- A retired Air Marshal of the Indian Air Force has been tapped to be the first CEO of the controversy-mired Ram Temple in Ayodhya
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
India ready to help end Ukraine war, Jaishankar says during Kyiv visit
India is ready to help end the war in Ukraine, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said as he arrived in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Thursday.
"If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there," Jaishankar said as he addressed the media alongside Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Sybiha welcomed Jaishankar for what he described as the "first-ever dedicated bilateral visit" of an Indian foreign minister to Ukraine.
"India is a global power and we welcome Prime Minister Modi's call to move from an endless war towards an end to the war. Ukraine stands ready for diplomacy," Sybiha wrote on X, referring to comments the Indian leader made during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan earlier in the week.
Jaishankar's trip to Ukraine comes more than a week after he attended the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation in Moscow with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
The Indian foreign minister also met Putin during the Russia visit.
Since the start of Russia's war in Ukraine, New Delhi has been under pressure from Kyiv's Western partners over its cooperation with Moscow, India's decades-long ally.
"This historic moment takes place amid escalating Russian attacks against our cities, port infrastructure, and civil shipping. Our capital is constantly under attack and I appreciate my colleague's brave visit," Sybiha said as he talked about Jaishankar's Kyiv visit.
The Ukrainian minister added that he and Jaishankar discussed the need to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, global food security, and bilateral cooperation.
"From infrastructure and pharmaceutical sector to technological innovation and digitalisation, we are ready to realise our full potential," Sybiha said.
Air Force veteran to be Ram Temple's first CEO
A trust that runs India's grand Ram Temple in Ayodhya has roped in an Indian Air Force veteran to be the Hindu shrine's first chief executive officer (CEO) in a leadership shake-up following a donation embezzlement row, Indian media reported.
Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, who retired from the Air Force in April 2026, was appointed CEO of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust on Wednesday.
According to news agency ANI, more than 5,000 applicants were vying for the post.
The temple in Uttar Pradesh was inaugurated in 2024 by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, fulfilling a key Hindu nationalist pledge.
The temple site has been a controversial flashpoint because it was built on grounds where the 16th-century Babri Masjid, or Mosque of Babur, once stood. The mosque was demolished by Hindu mobs in 1992, triggering bloody riots that left nearly 2,000 people dead.
Mishra's appointment comes after the Ram Temple became embroiled in controversy in recent months following allegations of theft involving donations and offerings worth millions of rupees.
Mishra served as chief of the Indian Air Force's Western Command during the 2025 Indian military strikes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, which New Delhi said targeted "terrorist infrastructure" in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
"I also consider this the blessings of Lord Ram that after 43 years of service to the nation in the Air Force, He has given me the opportunity to serve Shri Ram Mandir (temple) and Shri Ram bhakt (devotees)," Mishra told news agency ANI.
Opposition slams move
The appointment has also drawn political criticism, particularly in the wake of the donation-related allegations surrounding the temple trust.
The opposition Congress party has questioned Mishra's appointment.
"Will appointing a new CEO or bringing in new people in the Trust bring back the donations by devotees? Has action been taken against the thieves?" Uttar Pradesh Congress chief Ajay Rai said in an interview with ANI.
"Will the retired Air Marshal take action against these thieves and send them to jail? When will the action be taken and the stolen money be brought back?" he added.
Congress leader Imran Masood told news agency PTI that the job was for "saints and seers."
"Now, instead of saints and seers working inside the Ram Temple, a retired Air Marshal will be doing the work," he said.
US Secretary of State Rubio reacts to Modi- Pezeshkian meeting
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said he does not believe India and Iran are discussing a trade deal, two days after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modiheld a bilateral meeting with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the SCO in Bishkek.
The Monday meeting between Modi and Pezeshkian was their first since the start of the Iran war.
Rubio reacted to the leaders' meeting during an interview on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" on Fox News Radio on Wednesday.
When asked by the host whether New Delhi and Tehran were pursuing some form of trade deal, Rubio said: "Well, I don't think there's a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously, there are - countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime."
Later in the interview, the secretary of state issued a sanctions warning and reiterated US President Donald Trump's stance that no nation should help Iran evade sanctions.
"No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we're going to have to sanction them too," Rubio said.
Foreign Minister S Jaishankar arrives in Poland, next stop Ukraine
India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has reached the Polish capital of Warsaw as he kickstarts an official visit to Poland and Ukraine on Thursday.
During the three-day tour, which runs until Saturday, Jaishankar is scheduled to meet Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha for bilateral consultations, the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement.
The ministry added that the visit is focused on "enhancing bilateral relations" and will also provide an opportunity to "exchange views on regional developments and issues of mutual interest."
The foreign minister was greeted at the airport in Warsaw on Wednesday by India's ambassador to Poland, Neeta Bhushan.
Jaishankar's trip to Poland comes amid speculation about a visit by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to India.
Earlier in August, Poland's top envoy to India said that Tusk's visit, which would be his third to New Delhi, would send a strong signal for cooperation.
There is yet to be formal confirmation of Tusk's India tour.
The visit also reflects broader efforts by New Delhi to deepen engagement with Central and Eastern European partners.
Following the Poland leg of his tour, Jaishankar will head to Ukraine.
Jaishankar's Ukraine visit comes after key Modi-Putin meeting
The Ukraine leg of Jaishankar's tour comes days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday. During the meeting, Modi urged an end to the war in Ukraine.
Ahead of Jaishankar's arrival in Kyiv, Ukraine's First Deputy Head of the Office of the President, Sergiy Kyslytsya, said on Tuesday that he had met India's Ambassador to Ukraine, Anjani Kumar, to discuss Kyiv-New Delhi ties and India's role in efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Kyslytsya said he discussed with Kumar Modi's message to Putin in Bishkek, in which the Indian prime minister urged a "move from endless war to end of war" in Ukraine.
"We look forward to continued dialogue with India and to translating this shared interest in peace into concrete steps," Kyslytsya added.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily roundup of the biggest headlines making a splash in India.
India's Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar is embarking on a trip to Poland and Ukraine today, where he is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with his counterparts.
Jaishankar's visit comes on the heels of a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) earlier this week, where Modi urged close ally Putin to move from an "endless war" to "an end of war" in Ukraine.
In more diplomatic news, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reacted to a meeting between Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
Meanwhile, in domestic news, Ayodhya's Ram Temple will now have an Air Force veteran as its first chief executive officer following a donation theft controversy.
We will cover that and more in this blog.

articles.title: Lebanon disarmament plan stalls as Hezbollah shifts to guerrilla tactics
articles.body:
It is now clear that something is not working in the mechanism that was supposed to bring calm to the northern border. The pilot program in southern Lebanon, designed to pave the way for Hezbollah’s disarmament south of the Litani River, an IDF withdrawal and the transfer of responsibility to the Lebanese army, is not progressing as expected.
Israel’s defense establishment has identified significant difficulties facing the Lebanese army, which is not operating in accordance with the targets set for it. Because of a legal limitation, its soldiers avoid searches inside homes and terror infrastructure in villages, preferring to focus only on open and public areas.
Beyond the difficulties on the ground, the root of the problem lies at the diplomatic level. So far, no agreement has been reached on who will supervise the Lebanese army’s work, what criteria it will be required to meet and what exact conditions the IDF will need to approve before beginning a withdrawal.
About two months ago, ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported on a proposal under which Italian military forces would supervise the process, but that plan has yet to get off the ground.
The deadlock has two sides. On the one hand, it gives the IDF vital room to complete its mission on the Ali Taher ridge, where dozens of Hezbollah terrorists are currently trapped. It also allows the forces to improve their holding model, establish better command infrastructure and continue clearing the area and denying Hezbollah the infrastructure it developed over the years.
On the other hand, a prolonged stay in southern Lebanon raises familiar concerns, foremost among them a return to the difficult and bloody days of the past.
Meanwhile, the fighting on the Ali Taher ridge is progressing well and creating considerable tension within Hezbollah. That was evident overnight, when the terror organization launched two explosive drones toward forces operating in the area. The incident ended without casualties after one drone was intercepted and the other fell.
A study published by the Alma Research and Education Center, which researches security challenges in northern Israel, points to a significant change in Hezbollah’s operational pattern as the organization adapts to the new reality.
After the threat of an invasion of the Galilee suffered a severe blow and Radwan Force infrastructure was destroyed, the organization abandoned broad operational plans and shifted to decentralized guerrilla activity by small cells, in a format similar to that now familiar from the Gaza Strip.
Security officials say Hezbollah continues to gather intelligence on IDF troops, study how they operate, map locations and identify methods of operation in preparation for a scenario in which fighting resumes in the form of infiltrations, ambushes, explosive-drone launches and the laying of explosive devices.
To pull the pilot program out of the deadlock, Israel is trying to apply American pressure on the Lebanese government and army, based on the assessment that completion of the IDF’s operation on the Ali Taher ridge, together with diplomatic contacts mediated by the United States, will force the sides to move forward, formulate an agreed enforcement force and set clear criteria.
Northern Command is preparing the area for the holiday period and the onset of winter. The preparations include driving drills, opening routes and combat training for extreme weather conditions.
At the tactical level, the main focus is on dealing with the threat posed by explosive drones.
“We will come to the next round better prepared when it comes to the drone threat,” a security official told ynet.
In the absence of a broad technological solution, troops are being trained in protective procedures, the deployment of defensive nets and interception methods, alongside several new systems that have already become operational in the field.
It is important to note that the work carried out by the IDF in the current maneuver, which began with Operation Roaring Lion, has been highly significant and has struck nearly all of Hezbollah’s systems.
Ultimately, the situation on the northern border remains a direct result of the balance with Iran.
Israel’s defense establishment assesses that if the situation between Washington and Tehran escalates further and Israel is drawn into it, that will have an immediate impact on the Lebanese arena as well.
The Middle East pressure cooker is once again approaching boiling point just as the already tense holiday period begins, with the confrontation between the United States and Iran escalating again and putting Israel’s defense establishment on the highest level of alert.
All this is taking place against the backdrop of an escalation across the various arenas, from aggressive activity in Gaza and the West Bank to increased pressure in Lebanon. At the same time, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been holding tense talks with the U.S. ambassadors to Israel and Lebanon over the southern Lebanon pilot plan, which, as noted, is not progressing as expected.

articles.title: Berlin’s latest Russia panic is reckless even by its own standards
articles.body:
Berlin’s latest Russia panic is reckless even by its own standards
When you’ve burned all your bridges, go and burn some more.
That seems to be the unspoken strategy of Berlin’s policy toward Moscow, which is the only plausible interpretation of Germany’s fresh efforts to damage its already abysmal relationship with Russia. Not that they have come as a surprise. Since the odd drone incident at the Leipzig/Halle airport at the beginning of August, the German political establishment and its always compliant mainstream media have been preparing the ground for explicitly blaming Moscow.
The German public has been subject to what looks like a systematic campaign of escalating innuendo for almost a month. The story emerging from this barrage of unfounded claims and speculation masquerading as self-evident certainty has been changing: the role of an airport bus driver merely discovering the drone sitting quietly on the tarmac next to an extra-large Ukrainian transport plane or kicking it to the ground with a Bruce-Lee-type flying kick, as initially claimed, has remained unclear and contradictory. Initial reports of another drone colliding with a plane in flight had to be retracted when traces of birds became too obvious.
Now, clearly, the time has come to make things official. The German government, represented by Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt and foreign policy chief Johann Wadephul, has blamed the drone incident on Russian intelligence services and announced retaliation measures, such as closing a consulate and cultural center in Berlin, even more travel restrictions and individual sanctions on Russians, and fresh attempts to go after Russian ships by, in effect, piracy. The Russian ambassador has been called in, various EU governments, the EU commission, and NATO – though not the US – have made a grand show out of supporting Germany.
Moscow has roundly rejected Berlin’s accusations, called in the German chargé d’affaires, and promised a symmetric response to Germany’s actions. President Vladimir Putin has plausibly described them as a “grave mistake” and, equally plausibly, surmised that it is due mainly to attempts to shape elections and distract from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s historically sensational unpopularity.
So far, so bad: Berlin has managed to reach a new low-point in a relationship that is crucial for Germany but which it loves to tear apart. As Sarah Wagenknecht of the new-left BSW party has noted, the drone did not do any damage, regardless of the question of where it came from. The German government, though, has deliberately chosen a massive over-reaction. The new-right AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund, likely to soon make history by winning the AfD’s first state elections, has also called for moderation and dialogue instead of escalation. In today’s Germany, reason is literally on the political margins, while the self-declared Center has gone nuts.
What is even worse, however, is that no proof has been presented of Russian involvement. It is true that after the announcement of Berlin’s official blame game, conveniently timed leaks to the mainstream media have conveyed unsubstantiated claims about two holders of Russian passports being involved. But this conspicuous combination of a specific accusation presented without evidence and clearly coordinated leaks merely hinting at it makes the impression of manipulation even worse.
Not to speak of the fact that these passports – if they exist and if they actually belong to real perpetrators – are extremely flimsy and, frankly, bizarre pieces of evidence: Why would Russian intelligence services make sure their agents carry Russian passports? If anyone had an interest in making it that easy to point fingers at Moscow it would surely be either Ukraine, which has a vile record in terrorist false flag operations, lying, and subterfuge of the worst sort. For Kiev, it would have been ideal to place a drone that creates hysteria in Berlin but fails to destroy an asset as valuable and rare as the AN-124 Condor transport aircraft.
The fact that the West in general and Germany in particular already has a long record of proven false alarms about Russian drones has also made no difference. As the Germans say, where there’s a will, there’s a way. And the will to deepen tensions with Russia is boundless among the current German establishment.
Speaking of which, it is impossible not to be stunned by the difference between Berlin’s treatment of a devastating terror attack which did actually work and one that either failed or was staged to begin with: We now know that Ukraine – most likely with the help of one or more NATO states – committed the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline attack, that is the single worst sabotage of postwar Germany’s vital infrastructure, economy, and environment while blaming Russia.
Yet Berlin has shown a consistent pattern of tolerating or even helping with the cover-up, while going as slow as possible on investigation and prosecution, while Ukraine’s leader Vladimir Zelensky keeps boldly lying. That is the state of the art almost four years after the attack. That and a relentless and unceasing flow of gazillions of German taxpayers’ money to the Kiev perpetrator regime. So much for “not rewarding the aggressor”: National masochism is too kind a term.
After the Leipzig/Halle incident it has taken less than a month to come to sweeping conclusions and reach for strong retaliatory measures while not presenting evidence. What a contrast. Clearly, those commentators are right who guess that Berlin’s newfound capacity for rapid over-reaction is rooted in several aggressive policy agendas: the current push to turn the German foreign intelligence service BND into an instrument of sabotage paramilitary operations; the new militarism which aims to build the most powerful conventional army in Europe and is explicitly targeting Moscow, and, last but not least, turning hatred and fear of Russia into a distraction in a country in deep economic crisis.
If Berlin is not preparing for open war with Russia, it is certainly doing its best to leave precisely that impression. Many Germans do not agree with this road-to-perdition course. For all of Europe’s sake, let’s hope that they will finally manage to change it.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Denmark's intelligence agency warns Russia 'actively' preparing acts of sabotage
articles.body:
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilising European nations.
Russia is "actively" preparing sabotage operations against Denmark, particularly its defence industry, Danish intelligence agency PET told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
"The Russian intelligence services are actively preparing acts of sabotage targeting the defence industry in Denmark," Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) said in a statement to AFP.
They are recruiting "ordinary Danes" on social media to take photos that can be used in planning acts of sabotage, it said.
Emil Graesholm, PET head of counterintelligence at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, told newspaper Berlingske in an interview on Thursday that the agency was sharing details about the methods "because they don't need to look like a spy movie."
The warning came after EU countries summoned Russia's envoys and discussed fresh sanctions after an explosive-laden drone incident in Germany that the bloc's foreign policy chief said bore the marks of "state-sponsored terrorism."
European Union ministers weighed how best to respond to the attempted drone attack on Wednesday but struggled to find new ways to meet the challenge without resorting to military means.
"It is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism. The question is: what do we do about this," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters before chairing a meeting of the bloc’s foreign ministers in Ireland.
The EU has already slapped almost two dozen packages of sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine, hitting more than 3,000 officials, oligarchs and entities including banks, energy companies and drone makers.
Russia has in recent months been accused of ratcheting up sabotage attacks against European backers of Ukraine, as Moscow's forces stall on the front line of the war launched by the Kremlin in 2022.
Back in 2024, PET said that the Russian threat against Denmark, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, had grown stronger.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Denmark has provided Ukraine with at least €10 billion in military support and around €1 billion in civilian contributions, the Danish foreign ministry said.
In June, Copenhagen announced its 30th military aid package for Kyiv worth around 4.4 billion kroner (€577 million) which would include ammunition, arms, equipment and training for Ukrainian soldiers.

articles.title: They came for a wedding dance, Trump gave them the dance of death
articles.body:
They came for a wedding dance, Trump gave them the dance of death
TEHRAN – A fresh wave of deadly missile strikes carried out by United States military forces against civilian infrastructure and residential gatherings across southern Iran on Tuesday night has left over a dozen people dead and scores of others wounded, triggering widespread outrage and renewed calls for international criminal accountability over blatant violations of international humanitarian law.
The overnight aggression struck three separate locations in the vicinity of Ahvaz and Aghajari in the southwestern province of Khuzestan, alongside a series of lethal bombardments across the southern coastal province of Hormozgan.
The most egregious atrocity occurred in the coastal town of Kouhestak, situated in Hormozgan’s Sirik County, where American ordnance struck an active family wedding ceremony at around 8:00 p.m. local time on Tuesday. The horrific blast turned a peaceful gathering into a scene of carnage, killing at least five civilians and severely injuring 68 others, with women and children making up a large share of the casualties. Local medical personnel confirmed that a four-year-old child was among those killed on the spot.
Following the massacre, the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) issued an official statement attempting to justify the fatal strikes, falsely claiming that American forces had launched attacks exclusively on targets belonging to Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC). CENTCOM attempted to link the aggression to what Washington described as recent Iranian actions against commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and alleged security threats to US forces stationed in the region.
Provincial officials and local witnesses vehemently dismissed Washington’s narrative, stressing that the struck site in Kouhestak was a clearly identifiable residential and social venue hosting a traditional family wedding reception with hundreds of non-combatants present.
The devastating strike on the Kouhestak wedding has drawn swift and unequivocal condemnation from legal observers, human rights defenders, and Iranian humanitarian bodies. In an official letter submitted to the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) demanded immediate legal action and a formal investigation following the US missile attack on the ceremony.
In its statement, the IRCS emphasized that given the reported civilian character of the location as the venue of a family wedding ceremony, as well as the presence of civilians at the site, the incident raises serious concerns under international humanitarian law and warrants an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation.
The IRCS underscored that the Kouhestak massacre, which left innocent families devastated, constitutes a clear war crime under all established legal frameworks.
Senior Iranian officials have reacted with sharp indignation to the latest wave of American aerial assaults. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf forcefully condemned the attack on the wedding ceremony, stating that the deliberate targeting of civilians at schools, sports complexes, and social gatherings shows that Washington is operating and killing “like Satan.”
In a post on social platform X on Wednesday, Qalibaf stated that the Kouhestak bombing represents an indivisible part of a sustained campaign against defenseless civilians, referencing earlier high-casualty strikes against an educational center in Minab and a sports facility in Lamerd. He wrote: “Minab school: children massacred. Lamerd sports hall: kids slaughtered. Kouhestak wedding: children killed with families. If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan.”
Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, also questioned how the United States military could claim advanced reconnaissance capabilities while repeatedly hitting soft civilian targets. Ghashghavi stated that a regime which claims to utilize comprehensive satellite coverage to monitor even the smallest movement on Earth cannot credibly claim it failed to distinguish military installations from a school, a sports venue, or a wedding ceremony. He added that the United States has for decades dropped bombs and missiles on defenseless populations while routinely leaving the justification of its crimes to post-facto inquiry committees.
The latest strikes on Khuzestan and Hormozgan are part of an intensifying military confrontation that began on February 28, when joint military escalation by the United States and Israel plunged the region into active hostilities. During 39 days of war, Washington and Tel Aviv carried out repeated air and missile incursions across Iran, resulting in widespread civilian bloodshed that contradicts Western claims of precision targeting. A Pakistani-mediated memorandum of understanding reached between the US and Iran on June 17—designed to underpin the ceasefire that had paused hostilities since April 8—was violated by the administration of President Donald Trump.
The tragedy in Kouhestak follows earlier high-casualty attacks that shocked the nation. On the first day of the war on February 28, a catastrophic US strike hit a school in the city of Minab in Hormozgan province during peak school hours, killing 168 people, the vast majority of whom were young school children attending class alongside their teachers and school staff. The horrific loss of 168 lives in Minab triggered instantaneous global outrage, prompting protests across international capitals, emergency statements from international legal bodies, and direct condemnations from human rights watchdogs that denounced the carnage as a flagrant breach of the Geneva Conventions and international legal protections afforded to educational facilities.
That tragedy was compounded shortly afterward in Lamerd, Fars Province, where an aerial strike blasted a community sports hall during scheduled youth sports training sessions. The attack in Lamerd killed young athletes, coaches, and spectators, critically wounding scores more and reducing a vital public recreation center to rubble.
The deliberate bombing of the Minab school, the Lamerd sports hall, and now the Kouhestak wedding ceremony underscores a continuous and documented pattern of attacks on protected civilian sites. Legal experts note that the sheer scale of non-combatant casualties across Minab, Lamerd, and Kouhestak dismantles any pretense of collateral damage and demonstrates systemic negligence and criminal disregard for human life.
Shortly following the latest aggression in Khuzestan and Hormozgan, Iran’s Armed Forces responded by staging a series of combined retaliatory operations featuring precision ballistic and cruise missile strikes alongside advanced long-range drone barrages targeting regional American military installations and strategic interests.
Iranian military and diplomatic officials have reiterated that the Islamic Republic will exercise its legitimate right to self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, affirming that unprovoked aggression against Iranian soil, citizens, and civilian infrastructure will be met with decisive responses and relentless pursuit of justice through international legal tribunals.

articles.title: Russian Volunteer Corps deputy commander alleges SBU detention, pressure over suspected FSB ties
articles.body:
Deputy Commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK) Stepan Kaplunov stated that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) detained and interrogated him on suspicion of cooperating with the Russian FSB.
As Kaplunov recounted in an interview with NV, on August 23 he was attacked by unidentified individuals who presented themselves as police officers. Afterwards, he was taken to a secret facility, where he was kept in a cell on chains and subjected to psychological pressure.
Kaplunov claims that under this pressure, he was forced to agree with the version regarding his connections with Russian special services and to redirect suspicions toward his own commander, Dmytro Ivanov.
Nine days after his disappearance, Kaplunov was brought back to the site of his detention for a search of his apartment, during which no prohibited items were found.
"However, when I, the SBU officers, and the investigator arrived at the location, security was already inside the apartment. That is, our unit was providing security for the residence to ensure that under no circumstances would any incidents occur during the search—for instance, to prevent anything from being brought in or planted, so that everything went as cleanly as possible," Kaplunov recounted.
While in the apartment during the investigative actions, Kaplunov observed through the window a shooting that took place on September 2 in the Bereznyaky residential area in Kyiv between SBU officers and GUR servicemen. After the incident concluded, a GUR special forces unit evacuated him from the scene. Kaplunov expressed conviction that his abduction was an attempt to discredit the intelligence special unit and the commander with the callsign "Timur" due to longstanding interagency rivalry.
As reported, on September 1, the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) received an application from attorneys of Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine serviceman Stepan Kaplunov regarding the soldier’s alleged disappearance; investigators are examining it for legal classification.
Earlier, information appeared on social media that Deputy Commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK) Stepan Kaplunov was abducted in the courtyard of his own home by unknown individuals. Subsequently, a video was published on social media in which the individuals who allegedly abducted the soldier introduced themselves as employees of the National Police of Ukraine.
Later, the SBU reported the detention of servicemen from one of the units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine during a special operation, which thwarted an FSB terror attack against a leader of the Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine on the occasion of Independence Day. According to their data, during the suppression of armed resistance, law enforcement officers used weapons, resulting in injuries.
In connection with the incident, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that the Prosecutor General’s Office and the SBI would conduct an investigation.
He stated in his evening address on Wednesday that they would clarify all the details, with all testimony and statements from the participants of the event to be checked, as well as the entire situation step by step.
The president also dismissed Head of the SBU Department for the Protection of State Secrets and Licensing Oleh Khramov.

articles.title: Iran strikes Kuwait, warning US that all-out war could return
articles.body:
Amid questions over the future of US presence in the region, China is expanding its military and diplomatic footprint across the West Asian and North African region, writes Sabena Siddiqui.
Read more below:
Welcome,
Here are the key updates:
And so we continue our live coverage of the day....
The State of Qatar condemned "in the strongest terms" the renewed Iranian attacks on Kuwait, considering it "a blatant violation of its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and a flagrant violation of international law, the Charter of the United Nations, and the principles of good neighborliness."
The Qatari Foreign Ministry affirmed in a statement that "the continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts aimed at containing tension and undermine political and diplomatic efforts aimed at achieving security and stability in the region," holding Tehran "full legal responsibility for these attacks and their resulting repercussions and consequences."
Qatar renewed its full solidarity with Kuwait and its support for all legitimate measures it takes to preserve its sovereignty, security and territorial integrity.
The ministry stressed "the necessity of an immediate and complete cessation of all military actions and attacks that threaten the security and stability of the region, and to refrain from everything that would expand the circle of escalation, and to return seriously to the path of dialogue and negotiations, and to adhere to the understandings achieved through diplomatic efforts."
More than $1bn in oil revenues entered Iran during the first 11 days of the period ending September 2, Iran's semi-official Fars agency reported.
It also reportedIran’s oil sales during the first five months of the current fiscal year generated revenues equivalent to more than 80 percent of the oil income projected in Iran’s 2026-27 budget, from 21 March 2026 to 20 March 2027.
Iran's army on Thursday said it targeted US bases in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by US President Donald Trump.
"This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base in Kuwait with missiles and drones," the army said in a statement carried by state TV.
It added that "the location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad Air Base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army".
Kuwait's foreign ministry lambasts Tehran after the latest overnight attack targeting the tiny Gulf state, as hostilities between Iran and the United States reignited over the past days.
In a statement, the foreign ministry calls the strikes "a direct threat to its [Kuwait's] security and stability, and the safety of its citizens and residents on its territory, and a grave breach of the rules of international law."
Oil prices sank Thursday after Donald Trump suggested the latest US attacks against Iran would likely be short-lived.
The move helped most equities higher and eased pressure on bond yields, providing much-needed relief to markets, while the yen extended gains after a spike Wednesday fuelled fresh intervention talk.
Trading floors have been jolted since US strikes on Islamic republic targets in the Strait of Hormuz sparked tit-for-tat exchanges between the two and sent crude rallying as much as 10 percent.
The flare-up, which broke weeks of relative calm around the waterway fanned fears of another step up in already elevated inflation and put pressure on central banks to hike interest rates.
It also came just days after a hawkish speech by Federal Reserve boss Kevin Warsh that was seen by investors as a pivot towards a possible tightening of monetary policy.
Sentiment was given a much-needed boost Wednesday after the US president said the latest round of strikes could be over soon.
Asked how long the bombing campaign could last, he told reporters: "I don't think too long."
Meanwhile, CNN cited US officials as saying the military escorted 40 commercial ships loaded with 18 million barrels of crude through the strait, a wartime high.
The two main contracts Brent and West Texas Intermediate pared their gains Wednesday and on Thursday snapped their recent rally to drop more than one percent.
Yields on 10-year US Treasuries and Japanese government bonds of the same length both dipped.
The latest developments helped all three main US indexes higher, and while most of Asia followed suit in the morning traders turned a little more cautious in the afternoon.
Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on a mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah fighters, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.
The message, delivered last month, highlights Iran's continued direct involvement in the ground fighting in southern Lebanon and its readiness to retaliate against Israeli attacks there as the regional war enters its seventh month.
Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon, according to Lebanese security sources, and has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.
In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher. In response to Reuters questions about the message, or whether the US had put pressure on Israel not to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate." There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the US Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.
Two of the officials said the message was delivered via Oman, which has played a mediating role. Those two regional officials, briefed by Tehran, said over a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, including at least two senior officers, were with Hezbollah fighters.
The third source, a foreign official with direct knowledge of the message, said it was delivered around mid-August and that as a result of US pressure, Israel had put off storming Ali al-Taher.
Contacted by Reuters, Hezbollah's media office neither confirmed nor denied Iran's message but said it was a "natural conclusion" that such a warning would have been sent about the ridge.
"Iran considers any Israeli move on the ground in southern Lebanon, especially territorial expansion, a major violation of the Islamabad Agreement," Hezbollah's media office said, referring to the June US-Iran memorandum of understanding that included a Lebanon ceasefire.
United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan received a phone call from President Trump.
The two leaders discussed the latest developments in the region, according to the Emirati state news agency.
Talks included "ways to further strengthen ties" in support of their "mutual interests", it said.
US President Donald Trump said that the United States is achieving "very good results" in its confrontation with Iran, claiming that his country currently controls the Strait of Hormuz, and stressing that it will continue to work to keep the situation that way.
Only six commodity vessels were able to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, down from 11 the day before, according to the latest ship-tracking data from Kpler, according to Reuters.
The vessels included two very large gas carriers, two long-range tankers, one Supramax tanker and one Panamax tanker, the data showed.
The figure is well below the current 10-day average of about 13 ships a day.
The Iranian Health Ministry reported at least 18 people were killed and 142 wounded in attacks by the United States between 30 August and 2 September.
61of the injured were women and 44 victims were below the age of 18. Among those killed were two women and one child, the ministry added.

articles.title: Trump aides seek 'quiet' in Iran war before November elections
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump aides seek 'quiet' in Iran war but say attacks may intensify after November elections
Top aides to President Donald Trump are pushing to keep the Iran war from escalating before November's midterm elections to staunch Republican electoral losses, four people familiar with the discussions said, a strategy already under strain as the US and Iran exchanged back-and-forth attacks overnight.
White House officials will consider ramping up military action after the 3 November vote, said the sources, who requested anonymity to describe internal thinking, though any return to full-scale conflict is far from a given. The US military said its latest strikes were retaliation for recent attacks on American forces and marine traffic in the region.
For now, the sources said, the administration wants to rely on applying more economic pressure on Iran in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that months of military action failed to secure.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
Keeping the war mostly contained until then would help prevent the unpopular conflict from dominating the news as Trump's Republicans campaign to defend thin majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, said the sources, three of whom are White House officials.
Only 31% of Americans approve of the war, while some 63% disapprove, according to a late August Reuters/Ipsos poll, and voters are particularly unhappy about high gas prices.
A tactical pause could also give the US military some breathing room to replenish its heavily depleted munitions stockpiles, the sources said.
But pulling off the play-it-cool strategy looks more difficult by the day. While the conflict remains much less intense than it was during the spring or during a flare-up in the middle of the summer, both sides have exchanged tit-for-tat strikes in recent days.
Iran's leaders, emboldened after months of disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and facing little internal unrest, will likely keep striking at US and allied Gulf targets, including military bases, vessels and energy infrastructure, at least periodically, analysts said.
The US will face pressure to retaliate, potentially leading to an escalatory spiral that brings both sides back to a full-scale air war—whether the administration wants it or not.
Over the weekend, the US struck rocket launchers on Iran's Larak Island, prompting Iran to fire missiles toward Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. The US hit more Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in the biggest outbreak of fighting since July, a fresh outburst of violence that killed military personnel and civilians in Iran.
"The regime has every incentive to disrupt the 'calm'—which is no real calm, after all, since the administration's explicit aim is to increase economic pressure massively on Iran," said Barbara Leaf, who served as the top State Department official for the Middle East under former President Joe Biden.
Another wild card is Trump himself.
The president's approval rating has fallen from 40% to 33% since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling. Sources said he is not currently interested in escalation, but he is famously prone to changing his mind and could change course in response to events.
Trump threatened on Tuesday to escalate the conflict if Iran hits back against the latest US strikes.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Trump on Wednesday said he did not think the renewed military campaign would last long. He also reiterated his position that the upcoming elections were not factoring into his Iran strategy.
"Number one, I'm not running. My party is running, and I'm going to help my party," he told reporters in the Oval Office. "But I think my party respects the fact that we're not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
Constrained by logistics and politics
As the US-Israeli war on Iran enters its seventh month, his White House finds itself increasingly constrained by logistical and political realities, however.
"The timetable has changed," one senior White House official said. Another added that the "calendar is driving Iran."
Reuters reported in August that the military had used "virtually all" of its supply of certain precision missiles. The Washington Post reported on Sunday that the heads of the Army, Navy and Air Force warned Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth in a written assessment that prolonging the war was unsustainable and would diminish the military's readiness in other theaters.
The Pentagon has said the military had "everything it needs to execute" its mission.
“President Trump has destroyed Iran’s military capabilities and is crippling what’s left of its abysmal economy with the most powerful naval blockade in world history and crushing sanctions," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said. "The President will continue to advance America’s interests at home and abroad and will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."
America's Gulf allies—some of whom had pushed for aggressive action against Iran earlier in the war to weaken their main regional adversary—roundly urged the White House to de-escalate after a recent round of attacks in late July, regional diplomats said.
Currently, two White House officials said, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are among the high-ranking Trump aides who are on board with the idea of trying to keep the Iran conflict relatively "quiet" until November.
In recent weeks, administration officials have instead intensified an economic isolation campaign, during which the US has threatened to slap countries that trade with Iran with massive sanctions, while maintaining its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
The trade-focused strategy, however, has its own limits, analysts and officials said.
Iran has spent decades under layers of US and international sanctions that have battered its economy but have not deterred its leadership.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that the pressure campaign may cause Iran to lash out militarily, raising the prospect that the economic campaign could itself stoke military escalation.
Additionally, some major world powers, like China, have not joined Washington's bid to isolate Iran, prompting questions about the campaign's effectiveness.
"The purpose of the new sanctions package is meant to add economic pressure on top of that being caused by the blockade to force Iran back to the table, after the administration determined it was a better option than returning to kinetic action," said Alex Plitsas, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council. "Iran is concerned about it, but China has already indicated that it's not willing to play ball, which calls into question how effective it will be."

articles.title: Houthis target Yemen's western coast with 14 ballistic missiles: Army
articles.body:
Ikram Kouachi
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Houthi fighters targeted populated districts along Yemen's western coast in Taiz and Hodeidah provinces with 14 ballistic missiles and drone attacks, the Yemeni Armed Forces Media Center said Thursday.
 
Air defenses intercepted several drones in the Taiz front and others over districts along the western coast, the center quoted a military source as saying.
The source praised the "high combat readiness" of Yemeni armed forces, saying morale remained high and military units across different sectors maintained a high level of vigilance and preparedness.
The ballistic missiles did not hit positions of forces deployed along the western coast, the source said.
It added that Yemeni forces suppressed sources of hostile fire and threats in the Al-Kadaha sector of the Al-Barh front in western Taiz province, amid reciprocal ground clashes in the area.
Yemen has witnessed a relative lull since April 2022 in a war that began nearly 12 years ago between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa and other cities and provinces since September 2014.
Fighting has resumed in several provinces in recent weeks, including Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhalea and Taiz, as the country continues to face one of the world's worst humanitarian and economic crises.
A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government supports government forces, while Iran is accused of backing the Houthis. The Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia in July.

articles.title: Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel
articles.body:
Berlin approves $930 million in weapons sales to Israel
The German government approved nearly €800 million ($930 million) in weapons exports to Israel between January and June, Der Spiegel reports, citing a government response to a parliamentary inquiry. The sum is already four times higher than the total value Berlin greenlighted last year.
Around one-fifth of the exports was linked to German-Israeli defense-industry cooperation benefiting the German Armed Forces, according to the government. Just over two-thirds of the approved value is tied to the INS Drakon, a nearly 70-meter-long Dolphin II-class submarine built for Israel by German shipbuilder TKMS. The vessel, which can remain submerged for weeks, left Kiel on Tuesday and is reportedly on its way to Israel.
Berlin said the remainder covered equipment not classified as ‘weapons of war’, including small arms, ammunition, explosives, and drones, according to Der Spiegel.
The Left Party accused Berlin of “boundless double standards” over the deals.
“As [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz was supposedly outraged by [Israeli Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir’s inhumane statements, his federal government was pushing ahead with cooperation with a government and an army facing genocide charges before the International Criminal Court, supporting settler violence in the West Bank, and continuing to occupy southern Lebanon,” MP Lea Reisner said.
The controversial Israeli minister stated last month that he considers the enclave “to be ours” and urged the IDF to carry out dozens of “targeted assassinations” there every night, claiming that some in the Palestinian enclave “are not people.”
Germany’s War Weapons Control Act requires licenses to “always be denied” where weapons risk being used in “peace-disturbing acts” or where Germany’s obligations under international law could be impaired.
Berlin temporarily halted weapons exports to Israel in August 2025 over West Jerusalem’s plans to occupy Gaza City, but lifted the restrictions in November after a US-backed ceasefire with Hamas. Israeli forces have since continued operations in Gaza and against Hezbollah in Lebanon, where they still occupy parts of the south.
Germany is meanwhile expanding military cooperation with Israel. On Wednesday, the German Navy said it had successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic with a range of up to 500 kilometers. Germany has no ballistic missiles of its own, with Taurus cruise missiles being its longest-range missile systems.
Germany’s unwavering support for Israel, which is facing genocide accusations before the International Court of Justice in a case filed by South Africa, has arguably cost Berlin international support, as it failed to secure a seat on the Security Council in June.

articles.title: ‘Enemy Did Not Take a Vacation’: Russia Escalates Attacks Across Ukraine, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had begun a new escalation of its aerial campaign, early morning on Thursday, Sept. 3, after overnight attacks caused damage in 13 Ukrainian regions and wounded 17 people in Odesa.
In a Telegram post, Zelensky said emergency crews were responding to attacks in several parts of the country while air raid alerts continued almost without interruption in many cities and communities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A Russian drone hit a residential high-rise in Odesa, damaging apartments between the 10th and 17th floors. At least 17 people were wounded, including three children.
Emergency services remained at the scene on Thursday morning. The building has 21 stories, according to Reuters.
Authorities were also working to address the consequences of attacks in the Obukhiv and Boryspil districts of the Kyiv Region. State Emergency Service rescuers were battling a fire at a pharmaceutical company’s warehouse.
Zelensky reported additional attacks on Nikopol, Kherson, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia and Khmelnytskyi. He said damage had been recorded in 13 regions during the night.
Zelensky said Russia was intensifying its attacks and increasingly using jet-powered drones to keep Ukrainian cities under prolonged air raid alerts.
“The enemy did not take a vacation – the Russians have found a new escalation and have no plans to slow it down,” Zelensky said.
Jet-powered drones travel considerably faster than conventional Shahed-type attack drones, reducing the time available for air defenses and civilians to respond.
Tusk Calls Polish Drone Component Plant Fire Sabotage
Ukraine has faced almost continuous Russian aerial assaults in recent days. The attacks have targeted residential buildings, transport facilities, energy infrastructure and other non-military sites across the country.
Ukraine seeks air defenses from Europe
Zelensky urged Ukraine’s partners to step up their response and accelerate European production of air defense systems, particularly weapons capable of intercepting missiles and drones.
He argued that Europe has already developed much of the capacity needed to become stronger and more self-sufficient in defense but must increase production to protect its population and way of life.
“Europe can be self-sufficient and strong – a great deal has already been done for this over the past years,” Zelensky said.
The president added that Ukraine was working with its partners every day to secure new defense packages as Russia expands its use of drones and maintains pressure on cities and economic activity.
