articles.title: How Iran disabled the largest US naval base in West Asia
articles.body:
How Iran disabled the largest US naval base in West Asia
TEHRAN — The strategic architecture of the Persian Gulf underwent a seismic realignment with the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began on February 28. In a rapid and calculated operational response to the aggression, the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran executed precision retaliatory strikes against key military hubs across the region, dealing a severe and crippling blow to Washington’s forward-deployed infrastructure.
At the very center of this collapse is Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain, the largest and most critical US naval installation in West Asia. For decades, the sprawling facility served as the operational headquarters for the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet and the primary command-and-control node for American naval hegemony across the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Arabian Sea, and the Red Sea. Constructed and expanded to project American power directly onto Iran’s doorstep, the base housed thousands of military personnel, advanced command centers, logistical stockpiles, and deep-water berthing infrastructure. It was treated by the Pentagon as an untouchable fortress capable of sustaining carrier strike groups, guided-missile destroyers, and amphibious ready groups indefinitely.
However, when the US-Israeli war on Iran commenced on February 28, Iran’s targeted missile and drone salvos shattered that assumption within the opening hours of the conflict. By striking critical command facilities, logistical depots, and support infrastructure at NSA Bahrain, Iran effectively neutralized the base’s ability to function as a forward headquarters. The strike stripped the US Navy of its secure onshore rear-echelon support, forcing an immediate evacuation of personnel and cutting off the Fifth Fleet from its primary logistical lifeline in the region.
The lingering consequences of this operational setback were brought into sharp relief during a recent worldwide town hall held by the US Navy’s top brass, including Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman. Speaking before an audience of sailors at Fort Meade, Maryland, and connected remotely to personnel worldwide, Caudle faced direct questions regarding the ongoing crisis resulting from the strikes.
The first question of the day came from a seaman who asked about household goods displaced by an Iranian attack on Bahrain at the start of the war with Iran. Caudle said a return to the base was not imminent.
“We’re not getting back in there anytime soon,” he said. “I just want to be completely honest with that. But we’re working real hard to develop a scheme of maneuver in order for you to get your things.”
This direct statement from the Chief of Naval Operations serves as official recognition of the operational void created by Iran’s defensive strikes. Rather than discussing force projection or operational readiness out of Manama, the Navy’s highest-ranking admiral was reduced to addressing how displaced sailors might eventually retrieve their abandoned household goods through a scheme of maneuver.
The disabling of NSA Bahrain has triggered a domino effect across US naval operations throughout the theater. Stripped of their primary port of call and sustainment facilities, US carrier strike groups have faced unprecedented operational friction. Deployments have stretched past 250 days without standard port calls, causing acute supply deficits in basic food and hygiene goods, compounding maintenance backlogs, and eroding crew morale and readiness. Furthermore, the loss of secure basing in Bahrain has forced the Pentagon into chaotic asset reshuffling, including deploying the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Arabian Sea to relieve the USS George Washington.
Ultimately, the neutralization of NSA Bahrain proves that forward US bases, long utilized to encircle and intimidate sovereign regional states, have turned into acute tactical liabilities under the precision envelope of Iranian deterrence. By knocking the largest US naval installation in West Asia offline from the earliest days of the war, Iran demonstrated that the era of uncontested American military footprint in regional waters has effectively come to an end.

articles.title: Pentagon limits classified access amid Iran war concerns - report
articles.body:
The Pentagon has restricted access to decades of classified military documents on an internal computer system, The Washington Post reported on Wednesday, days after the newspaper reported that senior US commanders had raised concerns about sustaining large-scale military operations against Iran.
Documents associated with the Secretary of Defense Orders Book (SDOB) were removed from an internal web portal on the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke to The Washington Post on condition of anonymity.
It was not immediately clear whether the documents remained available to US personnel through other means or how the reduction in access could affect military planning, according to the report.
SIPRNet contains information classified as "secret," while top-secret information is held on more highly classified networks with fewer people granted access.
US military leaders raised concerns over Iran operations
The SDOB contains information on the location and availability of US warships, military units, weapons systems, and other resources. It also allows senior military leaders to formally register reservations about orders while continuing to carry them out through a process known as "non-concurring," The Washington Post reported.
The Jerusalem Post previously reported, citing the Washington Post, that several senior US military leaders raised concerns in the classified August 14 edition of the SDOB about continuing operations against Iran.
The officials warned that prolonging the war could weaken the US military's ability to respond to threats elsewhere. The SDOB reportedly called for some US troops deployed in the Middle East to remain in the region through September, while others would remain until 2027.
Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, head of US European Command; Gen. Francis Donovan, head of US Southern Command; Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of US Pacific Command; and Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, were among those who registered reservations with a "non-concur," according to people familiar with the discussion who spoke to the Washington Post.
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach and acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve agreed with Hegseth's plan to extend some unit deployments but emphasized that doing so would carry significant risks, according to the report.
Pentagon declines to discuss access change
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declined to discuss the reported change with the Washington Post on Wednesday but did not dispute that it had occurred.
"As we have previously stated, the Department of War does not publicly discuss internal operational deliberative processes, including the management, handling, or access protocols for the Secretary of War Orders Book (SWOB)," Parnell said in a statement to the newspaper.
"The success of our service members is Secretary Hegseth's top priority, and for that reason, decisions regarding operational processes, force posture, and deliberative staffing are managed through appropriate security channels to ensure mission security and operational integrity," he added.
Following the Washington Post's Sunday report, Parnell said on social media that much of what the newspaper published was "inaccurate," though he did not specify which details he disputed.
"Non-concurs are standard," Parnell said. "The Secretary sees them constantly. That's how you run a real military. We are in great shape around the world."
Restricted access could complicate military planning
A former defense official who routinely reviewed the documents told the Washington Post that removing the SDOB from SIPRNet or moving it to systems with higher levels of classification would "dramatically reduce the number of people who have direct access to it."
Commanders and their staff rely on access to the SDOB for time-sensitive decisions and notifications, the former official told the newspaper.
Moving aircraft and weapons from one command to another, for example, requires urgent logistical work to redirect equipment and resources. Restricting access to the relevant information could make that process slower and more difficult, according to the former official.
The change does not make it impossible for personnel to access strategic and operational documents, but doing so is now "certainly more difficult," the former official said.

articles.title: Ukrainian helicopter gets new AI-assisted gun module against Shaheds
articles.body:
- The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation delivered a Khyzhak combat module for aviation use, funded through a joint project with Uklon.
- The module fires a stabilized 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and uses AI-assisted tracking to help engage drones, including Shahed-type strike drones.
The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation says it has delivered a remotely operated “Khyzhak” combat module for use in Ukrainian aviation, and that the system is now being used against Russian targets.
The foundation announced the delivery on social media, saying it purchased the module through a joint project with the ride-hailing company Uklon called “Pidsvity Voroha 2.0” (“Light Up the Enemy 2.0”). Video accompanying the post shows the module mounted on a helicopter and used against Russian Shahed-type strike drones.
“We are complicating flights for Russian Shaheds,” the foundation wrote. “The video shows the remotely controlled Khyzhak combat module, which the Foundation delivered for aviation. We purchased it as part of a joint project with Uklon, ‘Pidsvity Voroha 2.0.’ And now this module is successfully working against enemy targets, thank you for that!”
The Khyzhak module is built around a 7.62 mm PKT machine gun and can rotate 360 degrees horizontally and elevate up to 75 degrees vertically. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense codified the module and cleared it for use in the Armed Forces. The ministry said the machine guns mounted on the module can be loaded with either Soviet-pattern or NATO-standard 7.62 mm ammunition and that the platform is stabilized, allowing accurate fire while the vehicle carrying it is moving.
The module’s developers designed it to be modular. It can be installed on robotic ground platforms, mounted stationary, adapted for use on vehicles, or fitted to naval systems. The version shown in the foundation’s video represents an adaptation for aviation.
The module includes an artificial intelligence system for automatic target recognition and tracking, including automatic detection of drones. That capability allows operators to use the Khyzhak to engage small first-person-view drones as well as larger Shahed-type drones, which are roughly the size of a small Cessna aircraft, at close range.
The foundation did not disclose how many Khyzhak modules it has funded, which unit or units are operating the system, or the cost of the purchase made through the Uklon partnership.

articles.title: US and Iran Trade Strikes as Fighting Resumes in Gulf
articles.body:
U.S. Central Command launched a wave of strikes against Iran on Sept. 1, and President Donald Trump said forces are “prepared to do another one” as Iran launched retaliatory attacks Sept. 2.
Fighting resumed Aug. 30, as CENTCOM officials announced strikes on “minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz.” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has been using land-based launchers to lob floating mines into the Strait.
Speaking in the Oval Office on Sept. 2, Trump said he ended the roughly monthlong pause in hostilities because of sea mines.
“They were trying to rebuild their radar systems and a missile system and … to build a rocket that drops mines,” Trump said at a White House event. “They were building it, it was almost finished, so we took it out. We saw that they were building it, we see everything that they’re doing.”
Iranian forces countered with ballistic missile attacks on U.S. forces in Jordan and on civilian ships transiting the Strait. A number of U.S. Air Force personnel and assets are stationed at the base in Jordan that has previously come under attack.
On Sept. 1, CENTCOM announced additional strikes on IRGC targets in retaliation for “attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.” The command indicated its targets included “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
Trump called the U.S. strikes “a very heavy attack” that “took out all of the new equipment that they tried to build along the Strait of Hormuz: some defensive, some offensive.”
Iranian state media outlets alleged the strikes also hit a wedding party in a coastal town, but those claims remain unconfirmed.
Iranian forces launched their latest retaliatory strikes Sept. 2. Officials and media outlets in the Middle East reported attempted strikes in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, and Iraq. Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry also said Iran targeted a Saudi tanker in the Strait of Hormuz and killed members of its crew.
As of 4 p.m. Eastern time and 11 p.m. in much of the Middle East, CENTCOM had not announced additional strikes. Trump told reporters that the U.S. is “prepared to do another one anytime we want.”
CENTCOM continues to enforce a blockade of Iranian ships and ports and said in a Sept. 2 social media post that it has redirected 86 commercial vessels, disabled three, and boarded two as part of the blockade.

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks stall
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks remain stalled
Israeli strikes killed one person and wounded another in the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh on Wednesday, according to Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency, after the Israeli military said it had struck the area in response to an alleged Hezbollah drone attack on its forces.
The NNA said the casualties resulted from an Israeli drone strike on the al-Ruwaiss and al-Maasouma Garden neighbourhoods of Nabatieh. Further Israeli strikes later hit the Nabatieh area, with local media reporting heavy explosions around Kfar Tebnit and circulating footage of a large column of smoke.
The Israeli military claimed that Hezbollah had launched two explosive drones overnight towards soldiers operating near the Ali al-Taher Ridge, close to Nabatieh. It said troops fired at and intercepted one of the drones and that no Israeli personnel were injured. Israel said it subsequently targeted what it alleged to be "Hezbollah infrastructure" used to plan attacks on its troops and civilians.
Hezbollah had not publicly commented on the Israeli allegation by Wednesday afternoon. The group has not claimed responsibility for attacks on Israeli targets in recent weeks.
Air raid sirens sounded briefly on Tuesday night in Tuval and Ma’ayan Baruch in northern Israel, near the Lebanese border, amid the alleged drone incident. Lebanese media later reported additional Israeli attacks across the south, including in Mansouri, Houla and Qantara.
The Ali al-Taher Ridge, a high point near Nabatieh overlooking areas of south Lebanon and northern Israel, has become a particular focus of Israeli operations. Israel has alleged that Hezbollah maintains underground military infrastructure in the area, while the elevation gives forces operating there a wide view of the surrounding border region.
Rome talks remain deadlocked
The attacks came a day after US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem. Israeli National Security Adviser Shmuel Ben Ezra also attended the meeting, according to images issued by Netanyahu’s office, which did not disclose the substance of the discussion.
The meeting took place before an anticipated eighth round of US-mediated Lebanese-Israeli talks in Rome. No official date has been announced, though Lebanese broadcaster MTV reported that the next session could be held on 15-16 September. In a statement on X, Huckabee claimed Hezbollah was the only obstacle to progress in the negotiations.
The talks are based on a US-brokered framework agreed on 26 June, under which Israeli forces would withdraw in phases from southern Lebanon while the Lebanese army deploys to designated areas and non-state armed infrastructure is dismantled. The arrangement has been slowed by disagreements over the sequencing of any Israeli withdrawal, the scope and pace of the Lebanese army’s deployment, and how compliance would be independently verified.
Israel has demanded assurances that areas transferred to Lebanese state control are clear of Hezbollah weapons and military positions. Lebanon, meanwhile, has sought a further Israeli withdrawal and resisted proposals that could amount to a permanent "security belt" or buffer zone inside its territory. Hezbollah has rejected arrangements affecting its weapons, leaving the army’s role in any eventual implementation politically sensitive.
Separately, the Lebanese Armed Forces said it was responding to what it described as "fabricated claims" by Israeli media concerning the army’s positions and operational role in southern Lebanon. In a statement issued on Wednesday, it said the reports sought to undermine internal cohesion and public confidence in the institution and its leadership.
The statement did not identify a specific report or outlets. But it appears to be intended to counter claims often by Israeli media outlets to cast doubt on the Lebanon army’s performance, loyalties or ability to carry out its southern missions at a moment when it is expected to be central to any eventual Israeli withdrawal and security arrangement. The army said its personnel remained committed to the command’s directives and to defending Lebanese sovereignty, security and stability.
Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed at least 8,920 people since hostilities erupted in October 2023.

articles.title: Ukraine takes Zelenskyy’s Russian airspace warning to UN aviation body
articles.body:
Ukraine formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) on 2 September that Russian airspace is unsafe for civilian flights because of increased military activity, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said. The letter behind the notification asks the organization to urge its member states to stop civil flights over Russia altogether, ZN reported.
ICAO, the UN aviation agency, cannot close Russian airspace or order carriers to reroute. European and US airlines already avoid Russia's airspace, while carriers from China, Türkiye, and the Gulf states have kept flying through it. Those remaining airlines must assess the safety of flying amid drone and air defense operations. Drone alerts during reported Ukrainian attacks have repeatedly shut Russian airports and delayed hundreds of flights.
The notification follows a 1 September warning by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who told airlines, insurers, and other aviation stakeholders that Russian skies were becoming unsafe as Ukrainian drones reached deeper into the country.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's Foreign Ministry would pass information about the risks to international organizations. The letter to ICAO came from another office—Mykola Kalashnyk, Ukraine's minister for recovery, infrastructure, and transport, whose portfolio covers aviation.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Zelenskyy's statement amounted to "a bid for state terrorism" and that Moscow would find a way to respond if civilian "tragedies" followed.
Sybiha urged airlines to avoid Russian airspace and said the notice was meant to prevent unintended incidents, arguing that Moscow was failing to disclose the dangers its war had created. He invoked Ukraine’s inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, the provision that recognizes states’ right to defend themselves against an armed attack. The foreign minister further stated that the war was “returning home to Russia.”
In its separate statement, ICAO warned of rising threats to civil aviation worldwide. It did not mention Russia, endorse Ukraine’s assessment, or say Kyiv’s notification had prompted it.
The UN aviation body identified long-range weapons, drones, navigation-signal interference, and advanced air-defense systems as growing dangers to civilian aircraft. It reiterated that international aviation law prohibits the use of weapons against them.
ICAO urged member states to assess airspace under their control, share threat intelligence quickly, and improve military-civilian coordination.
Russian airports were already facing repeated closures
Russian airspace has not been legally or completely closed. The disruption has instead taken the form of temporary restrictions at individual airports.
From 5–7 May 2026, restrictions during reported Ukrainian attacks delayed more than 450 flights at Moscow airports, while limits at Vnukovo remained in place for nearly 18 hours.
On 6 July 2025, Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport canceled 171 flights, while airports in five other cities suspended operations. During an earlier wave on 22 May 2025, Domodedovo halted flights four times in one day and Sheremetyevo three times, while Vnukovo and Zhukovsky also restricted operations.
Airports in Kaluga, Nizhny Novgorod, Saratov, and Tambov were temporarily closed during a 27 May attack in which Moscow claimed 99 drones were intercepted. Two days later, another alert delayed 20 arrivals and 14 departures at Vnukovo, pro-Kremlin Telegram channels claimed.

articles.title: How Israel kidnapped a senior Hamas security official in Gaza
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Israeli forces kidnapped a senior Hamas security official from Gaza City
Israeli forces kidnapped a senior Hamas security official from his home in western Gaza City on Tuesday during an armed operation that killed his wife and wounded his son, according to Palestinian and Israeli sources.
Moen al-Arabid, head of Hamas' internal security apparatus in the Gaza Strip, was kidnapped after an Israeli special forces unit entered the area near the Katiba in western Gaza City, according to a Hamas source who spoke to The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The source said the Israeli force, dressed in civilian clothes and travelling in two vehicles, including a white bus, entered the densely populated area before being discovered and engaging in an exchange of fire with Palestinian fighters.
Israeli drones subsequently carried out several strikes around the area, the source said, adding that the airstrikes provided cover for the Israeli forces during the operation.
According to the source, al-Arabid and his wife, Samah al-Khalidi-al-Arabid, confronted the Israeli soldiers inside their home.
Samah was killed during the confrontation, while their son, Obaida, was wounded, the source said, who added Obaida had been scheduled to celebrate his engagement on Wednesday.
The Israeli forces later arrested al-Arabid and removed him from the area while he was wounded, according to the source.
The source described the operation as a kidnapping rather than an attempt to kill al-Arabid, saying the Israeli forces had entered the area specifically to capture him alive.
One video appeared to show al-Arabid crawling along the ground while attempting to find cover. An Israeli bus then approached, and several projectiles were thrown in his direction.
The Hamas source said the projectiles were sound grenades rather than offensive grenades and were intended to distract the wounded man and prevent him from taking cover, facilitating his capture.
Israeli media later published a photograph purportedly showing al-Arabid after his arrest, depicting a handcuffed man who appeared to be injured.
Meanwhile, Palestinian sources also said that a vehicle attempting to leave the area toward eastern Gaza City came under attack about 200 meters from the site of the operation, causing additional casualties, including children.
Videos and photographs circulated on social media showed damage around al-Arabid's home, including a white bus with damaged windows and what appeared to be bullet marks.
Israel confirms arrest
Israeli officials confirmed that al-Arabid had been abducted during an operation in Gaza City.
Israeli Defence Minister Yisrael Katz said in a televised statement that Israeli forces were continuing their operations in Gaza City and had recently arrested a senior Hamas official.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that al-Arabid was one of the "most prominent Hamas leaders in Gaza."
Netanyahu accused al-Arabid of helping hide and transport Israeli captives, attempting to rebuild Hamas' capabilities, participating in efforts to restore Hamas' rule over the Gaza Strip and spreading what Israel claimed was misinformation concerning the disarmament of Gaza.
"My directives are clear," Netanyahu claimed, saying that Israel would continue pursuing Hamas leaders and those involved in the 7 October 2023 attack.
Israeli Channel 12 reported that al-Arabid was wounded during the operation and transferred to Israel for medical treatment.
The Israeli Broadcasting Corporation, Kan, also quoted a security official as saying, "The target was wounded during the operation in the Gaza Strip and transferred to Israel for medical treatment."
According to Israel's Channel 11, the operation was planned and approved in recent days by Netanyahu and Katz. Kan reported that the Shin Bet security agency managed the operation.
Israeli sources cited by the channel said the operation was intended not only to obtain intelligence but also to send a message to senior Hamas leaders that they remained subject to Israeli pursuit despite the ceasefire.
Casualties in residential area
The operation caused casualties and damage in the surrounding neighbourhood in Gaza, which includes shelters for displaced Palestinians and is located near an American field hospital and a kindergarten.
Zaher al-Wahidi, director of the Information Centre at Gaza's Health Ministry, told TNA that ambulance and civil defence crews recovered four bodies and treated eight wounded people following the Israeli operation.
He said two children and two women were among those killed, including Samah al-Arabid, al-Arabid's wife.
The dead and wounded were transferred to al-Shifa Medical Complex, he added.
For residents living near the site, however, the operation was experienced not only through its casualties but through the sudden fear it caused among families, particularly those with children nearby.
Marwa Ezzat, a resident of the area, said her children were inside a nearby kindergarten when the clashes began.
She told TNA that the sudden gunfire and airstrikes sent residents into panic as families rushed to reach their children and move away from the area.
"We were terrified because our children were inside the kindergarten and we could hear the gunfire and explosions around us," Marwa said. "Everyone was trying to find a way to reach their children and get them to safety."
"After the operation subsided, displaced families gradually returned to their shelters and homes," she added. "Some found their tents and belongings damaged by shrapnel, while many children remained frightened by the possibility of renewed gunfire or airstrikes."
Intelligence and security objectives
Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim told TNA that the operation appeared to have several objectives, including demonstrating Israel's ability to reach senior Hamas figures inside Gaza.
"Israel could have targeted al-Arabid from the air if its objective had been to kill him but instead chose to send a ground force to capture him alive," he said.
He added that the decision could indicate that Israeli security agencies wanted to obtain information from al-Arabid while he was alive, given his senior position within Hamas' security apparatus.
"The operation sends a message that the ceasefire does not prevent Israel from carrying out security operations inside Gaza," Ibrahim noted.
He explained that the arrest of a senior security official could give Israel access to sensitive information and create additional security risks for Hamas.
Hamas condemned the operation as a "serious crime" and accused Israel of deliberately endangering civilian lives.
The movement called on mediators and the U.S. administration to pressure Israel to stop what it described as violations of the ceasefire agreement.
In a press statement, Hamas said it had contacted mediators and Nikolay Mladenov, the UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, requesting "maximum pressure" on the Israeli government to halt its operations and implement the ceasefire agreement.
The operation came amid continuing tensions over the implementation of the ceasefire, with Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violations.
According to Gaza's Health Ministry, 1,326 Palestinians have been killed and 4,398 wounded in the Gaza Strip since an alleged ceasefire agreement took effect on 10 October 2025.
The ministry said the cumulative Palestinian death toll since the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war in October 2023 had reached 73,462, with 174,509 people wounded.
The kidnapping of al-Arabid adds another point of tension to the fragile ceasefire, as Israel says it will continue pursuing Hamas figures while the Palestinian movement and mediators seek to preserve the agreement and advance its implementation.

articles.title: Putin's 'global battle' against US & NATO: Russia 'testing' NATO since 2022 Ukraine invasion began
articles.body:
Putin's 'global battle' against US, NATO: Russia 'testing' NATO since 2022 Ukraine invasion began
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Anna Borshchevskaya, Senior Fellow at The Washington Institute. She interprets Russia’s reported missile support for Iran not as an isolated arms transaction, but as part of a broader geopolitical strategy in which Moscow treats Ukraine, Iran, NATO, and the United States as interconnected fronts. In her analysis, Vladimir Putin’s objective is less about pursuing direct military confrontation with Washington than about altering the strategic environment around it: strengthening actors hostile to the United States, increasing the costs of American and Israeli military action, and repeatedly probing Western thresholds for retaliation.
Putin relentlessly tests where Western “red lines” actually lie rather than where Western governments say they lie: Russian drones entering NATO territory, cyberattacks, disinformation, support for Iran, and the continuing war in Ukraine become different expressions of the same strategic logic. Her “bigger chessboard” metaphor captures this interpretation particularly well. It presents Putin as connecting geographically distinct conflicts through a common calculus of pressure, escalation, and opportunity.
There is also an important political dimension to her argument. Borshchevskaya suggests that Moscow has a strong interest in the survival of the existing Iranian regime, because the emergence of a pro-Western government in Tehran would represent a major strategic setback for Russia. On this reading, Russian military assistance does more than improve Iranian capabilities: it helps preserve a regional order advantageous to Moscow. Her broader warning is that insufficiently enforced Western red lines can themselves become strategically consequential, encouraging further attempts to determine just how far Russia could go.

articles.title: Russia attacked with 163 drones, up to half of them jet-powered: how air defense performed and the situation across the regions
Trump touts Hormuz control, credits US strikes for halting Iran’s nuclear programme
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that Iran must never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, crediting last year's US strikes with halting Tehran's atomic programme just before completion and adding, "We now control the Strait of Hormuz."
Speaking in a phone interview published on Wednesday, Trump said: "If we didn't do it, Iran would have a nuclear weapon."
"If we didn't send in the B-2 bombers a year ago to blow up their nuclear capacity, you know they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon," he said.
Warning of consequences, Trump argued that if Iran had "a nuclear weapon, Israel would be gone. The Middle East would be gone, and they would be hitting cities in the United States, absolutely, because they're crazy."
Turning to the latest strikes, Trump said, "We're doing very well. We're just annihilating them, but the bottom line on that is very simple: Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon."
‘Control of Hormuz’
He said US forces now dominate a key regional waterway, adding, "We now control the Strait of Hormuz. We control it. Last night, we took out 28 boats, 28 ships. We control it. They get nothing, and we took out ships."
Trump also suggested in a social media post renaming the Strait of Hormuz as "Trump Strait".
"Now that we have it under USA control, should we change the name of the Hormuz Strait to the Trump Strait??? Like America itself, it would be 'hotter' than ever before!" Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Regional tensions have escalated following US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began on Feb. 28 and Tehran's retaliatory missile and drone attacks against Israel and US interests in countries across the region.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled amid disagreements over security arrangements in the strait.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on 'special operation in Kyiv:' Accountability needed, incl personnel decisions by special service chiefs
articles.body:
There must be accountability and personnel decisions by the heads of the special services, as well as internal investigations within the SBU and the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ministry of Defense following today’s special operation in Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"Regarding today’s utterly shameful situation between certain units of the SBU and the Main Intelligence Agency, which took place in Kyiv, we spoke with Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko. The Prosecutor General and the State Bureau of Investigations will get to the bottom of all the details: all testimonies and statements from those involved in this incident will be verified, and the entire situation will be examined step by step," Zelenskyy said in an evening address on Wednesday.
"There must be accountability, including personnel decisions by the heads of the special services regarding those involved in what happened, and there must be internal investigations in both agencies," the head of state said.
He added that in Ukraine, "it is permissible to fire only at Russian occupiers in defense of Ukraine." "No other exchange of fire will ever be viewed by our state as something that anyone is permitted to do," Zelenskyy said.
As previously reported, the Security Service of Ukraine, in cooperation with the Main Intelligence Agency of the State Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, foiled a terrorist attack that the Russian FSB was planning against one of the leaders of the Russian opposition movement, who had arrived in Kyiv to mark our country’s Independence Day.
The SBU and the Prosecutor General’s Office of Ukraine reported the detention of service members from one of the units of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, as well as injuries sustained during the operation.
"SBU officers were conducting urgent investigative actions to collect and secure evidence. During a search at one of the addresses, a group of individuals carried out an armed attack on the SBU’s operational-investigative team. They attempted to obstruct the investigative actions… As a result of the incident, some of those who resisted were injured. The attackers were detained. Initial investigative actions established that the detainees belong to one of the units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces," the statement reads.
Weapons and documents were seized from the detainees. A pre-trial investigation has been launched into threats against and attempts on the lives of law enforcement officers.

articles.title: Iran, US trade threats as Tehran blames Washington for wedding strike
articles.body:
Iran, US trade threats as Tehran blames Washington for wedding strike
Iran and the United States traded threats on Wednesday after their heaviest military exchanges in weeks. Tehran accused Washington of striking a wedding party and called the attack a war crime. President Donald Trump threatened further US strikes, while Iran’s security chief warned Washington would face a “new strategy.”
Iran and the United States traded threats on Wednesday after some of the heaviest military exchanges in weeks, including a strike on a wedding party that Tehran blamed on Washington and branded a "war crime."
President Donald Trump said US forces staged a "very heavy attack" on Iranian targets overnight and are "prepared to do another one any time we want."
Iran's security chief warned that the United States would face a "new strategy" in the war that began in late February with US and Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X.
Besides threatening new attacks, Trump on Wednesday also suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz, the vital oil waterway that Tehran has effectively shut for six months, as "Trump Strait."
"Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???" the US president said in a post on Truth Social.
Read moreUS-Iran war: Old videos falsely claim to show new attacks on American bases
He later implied that he wasn't serious. "It was just thrown out there," Trump told an AFP reporter who asked about his post.
Iran targeted US bases in Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region after extensive US bombardment on Tuesday of sites across Iran.
Iran reacted with fury after the Iranian Red Crescent said four people including a child were killed and more than 50 people wounded by a US attack that hit a wedding in Iran's south.
"The truth of this unlawful war of choice -- and the true face of the war crime -- is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei posted on X.
The US military did not address the incident directly.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC," referring to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
'Acts like Satan'
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out at Washington over the wedding attack, calling the United States "Satan."
"If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan," he posted on X.
The latest round of fighting began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks.
Tehran's forces then targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks, one of which killed two Filipino sailors, according to a Saudi shipping company.
Trump said the US strikes were in retaliation for an Iranian attempt to plant sea mines in the Strait and for firing missiles at a base in Jordan.
Read moreIsraeli FM Gideon Sa'ar: 'I hope Iran will not make the mistake of attacking us'
Iranians expressed regret at the return to hostilities.
Hossein Moazami, 50, who is self-employed, called the attacks "truly distressing."
"I hope they all return to the negotiating table because the only people suffering from this are the Iranian people," he said. "The Americans are on the other side of the world and nothing happens to them."
A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Sirik following the US strike, with people heard screaming in the background.
"It is a very saddening incident...Thank God the casualties were not higher," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building that was hit, said in a video carried by state TV.
The war began February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
A fragile ceasefire collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Israel's defence minister said meanwhile that his country was prepared to respond "with great force" if attacked by Iran over the Jewish high holiday season, which begins in mid-September.
"For now, they are striking throughout the region except us," Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli media outlets.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Information campaign launched to discredit military intelligence, Ukraine's Defence Intelligence says
articles.body:
Information campaign launched to discredit military intelligence, Ukraine's Defence Intelligence says
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has said that a disinformation campaign aimed at discrediting the military intelligence agency and its units has been launched, with media outlets, bloggers and Telegram channels expected to be involved.
Source: DIU on Telegram
Quote: "Defence Intelligence of Ukraine is warning that a targeted disinformation campaign is being launched with the aim of discrediting military intelligence and combat units of DIU.
To carry out the campaign, its organisers plan to involve media outlets, bloggers and Telegram channels with questionable reputations, including in exchange for financial reward. We urge you to trust only verified official sources of information."
Details: DIU also urged media outlets, journalists and bloggers to contact law enforcement agencies immediately if they are asked to publish or distribute unverified and dubious information.
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that its deputy commander for combat operations, Stepan Kaplunov, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of a residential building. [The Russian Volunteer Corps is a military and political organisation established in 2022 that consists of Russian volunteers who have been fighting for Ukraine since 2014]
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between DIU and the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance.
- Meanwhile, the SSU said in the morning that, together with DIU, it had foiled a terrorist attack against a leader of a Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine.
- Later, Kaplunov's lawyer, Taras Borovskyi, said that the serviceman had been released, but his whereabouts were unknown.
- On the morning of 3 September, the SSU released a video in which Kaplunov admitted to having links to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) and said an attempt had been made to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian military personnel and other individuals. However, his lawyer insists that the confession was made under duress.
- Kaplunov himself said on 3 September that he had been abducted by SSU officers and described how he had been made to confess under duress.

articles.title: Britain wants laser armed ground vehicle drones
articles.body:
Britain is seeking counter-drone technology that could lead to autonomous laser weapons mounted on Army vehicles and, later, uncrewed ground vehicles, with £5 million available immediately through a new Ministry of Defence competition, the department has said.
Project PANOPTES, launched by UK Defence Innovation on behalf of the MOD, is intended to develop an integrated Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System force-protection capability able to deal with massed and low-cost aerial threats without rapidly exhausting conventional ammunition stocks.
The MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
Although the competition is open to a range of technologies, laser directed-energy weapons are specifically identified as an area of interest. The MOD said: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The intended configuration would place the counter-drone capability on a military ground platform. According to the procurement documents: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
The system is intended to protect deployed forces against complex and saturation attacks involving small uncrewed aircraft, including simultaneous threats designed to overwhelm local air defences or force troops to expend comparatively expensive missiles and ammunition.
The MOD stated: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus covers representative Class 1 UAS and other small aerial targets. These could include individual drones as well as repeated, sequential or simultaneous attacks used for surveillance, targeting, disruption or attempts to exhaust defensive systems.
A later objective would move the capability onto an unmanned ground platform. The MOD stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
UK Defence Innovation has confirmed that Project PANOPTES is open to UK-based innovators and that a share of £5 million is available immediately. Stage 1 will act as an initial screening process, with applicants outlining their proposed technology before successful teams are invited to develop more detailed proposals.
The first phase is not intended to produce a complete operational counter-drone system. The MOD said: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
Successful technologies could then be matured through later phases into demonstrable Minimum Viable Products before selected systems are developed into Minimum Deployable Capabilities for an initial operational user group.
The notice states: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record.”
The wider procurement has an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, rising to £150 million including VAT. That figure is not an approved programme budget. The MOD stated: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.”
Stage 1 submissions are due by midday on 23 September. A launch webinar will be held on 9 September to provide potential suppliers with further information on the operational requirement before the competition moves into its subsequent stages.

articles.title: Trump weighs ending Iran war as Pentagon extends deployments: Report
articles.body:
Muhammed Yasin Güngör
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
US President Donald Trump is privately considering declaring the war with Iran over, even as the Pentagon quietly extends troop deployments in the Middle East, according to a Wall Street Journal report Wednesday.
The newspaper reported that Trump has discussed with senior aides "whether to declare the Iran war over," a move the president reportedly "favors." He believes that maintaining intense economic pressure will eventually force Tehran to "either dismantle its nuclear program or collapse."
The US launched Operation Economic Outcast last week, targeting Iran’s key economic lifelines, including its oil, shipping, aviation, gold, technology and digital asset sectors.
Despite the private discussions, the Pentagon is extending deployments in a sign that the war could drag "well into next year.”
The military is maintaining 50,000 troops and 19 warships, including two aircraft carriers and 13 guided-missile destroyers, to provide the president with operational "flexibility."

articles.title: Air defense downs 135 of 163 Russian targets, hits recorded at 15 locations
articles.body:
On the night of Thursday, Ukraine’s Defense Forces neutralized 135 Russian targets, but hits were recorded at 15 locations and falling debris at four, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, 135 targets were shot down/suppressed by air defense: 135 Russian UAVs of the Shahed type (including jet-powered), Gerbera, and other types of drones," the report says.
In total, on the night of September 3 (from 18:00 on September 2), Russia attacked with 163 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (about half being jet-powered), S8000 Banderol, Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the directions of Millerovo, Orel, occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiyske in occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned system units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 15 locations, and falling debris from downed targets was recorded at 4 locations.

articles.title: Videos and debris raise questions over alleged US strike on Iranian wedding
articles.body:
Videos and debris raise questions over alleged US strike on Iranian wedding
On the evening of September 1, a barrage of US missile and drone attacks on a town in southern Iran allegedly struck a wedding ceremony, killing at least five people, including a four-year-old boy. FRANCE 24 geolocated a direct hit to the civilian building where local residents say the wedding was being held. The building was more than 135 meters from the apparent target, a communications tower.
Amateur videos showing the aftermath of a US attack on September 1 on the building show extensive destruction. The roof of the building, located in Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, along Iran’s southern Persian Gulf coast, appears to have been completely destroyed, with debris scattered for dozens of metres around the impact site. Videos from a hospital in Minab, 45 km to the north, also show people injured in the attack, including children being treated, as well as the body of a boy, covered with a blue sheet.
According to the Iranian Red Crescent, five people were killed and 68 others were injured in the attack.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
"There’s absolutely no military infrastructure near that house"
"Motahereh7", a resident of the town with a large following on Instagram, posted a video shortly after the airstrikes at around 9:30pm local time saying she had been attending a wedding at the site.
"Lots of you sent me messages asking, 'Have they hit Kuhestak?'. Yes, they hit the house where there was a wedding. It’s my husband’s cousin’s house. I don’t know yet how many people were there, how many people are under [the rubble]… God help us. There’s absolutely no military infrastructure near that house. Nothing…"
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
What do we know about the attack?
A CCTV video that captured the impact on the town shows at least six explosions. The apparent primary target was a communications tower on the edge of the town, on the shore of the Persian Gulf. Videos recorded by local residents also documented strikes on the tower.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
FRANCE 24 geolocated the communications tower and found it to be located in an urban area, just 30 metres from the nearest buildings.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Several videos showing the aftermath indicate that the building where the wedding was said to be taking place was directly hit, rather than damaged by shrapnel. Using several videos recorded by local residents, FRANCE 24 geolocated the building and found that it was more than 135 metres from the communications tower.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
According to several experts, photographs of the incident published by a local teacher showed components from an AGM-154 Joint Standoff Weapon, a US-made glide bomb.
However, FRANCE 24 could not independently confirm whether the debris was recovered from the site of the strike on the wedding, or from the communications tower.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Several Iranian officials reacted to the incident. Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and a key figure in negotiations with the United States, called the US government "Satan".
Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for US Central Command, said they were aware of reports of civilian casualties. He added: "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)."
This is the fourth reported incident in which US strikes have hit civilian sites in Iran since the US-Israel war against Iran began in February 2026.
On February 28, the first day of the war, a strike reportedly carried out by the United States killed about 170 people, most of them schoolchildren, as well as teachers, parents and others.
UPDATE (3/9/2026): The original version of this article published on September 2, 2026 cited experts who had said initial images of the debris at the alleged wedding site suggested it was from a US-made SLAM-ER cruise missile. After analysing further images that emerged of the incident, the experts said the debris contained components of a different weapon: an AGM-154 Joint Standoff Weapon, a US-made glide bomb.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drones Reach Moscow’s Doorstep, Hit Homes and Sochi Port
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones attacked targets across Russia overnight, hitting residential buildings near Moscow and a seaport in the Black Sea resort city of Sochi, Russian officials and monitoring channels reported.
In Kubinka, about 60 kilometers west of Moscow, a drone attack caused a fire on the eighth and ninth floors of an apartment building, Moscow Region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said. Ten people were evacuated. He said there were no casualties.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kubinka is home to a major Russian military airfield used by the country’s Russian Knights and Swifts military aerobatic teams. The town is also located near Patriot Park, a large Russian military-themed complex.
A second residential building was hit in Pavlovsky Posad, a town east of Moscow. A drone hit an apartment building on 1 Maya Street, blowing out windows in several apartments. Residents were evacuated, according to Vorobyov.
A separate drone attack reportedly caused a fire at a factory in Bolshoye Bunkovo, in Bogorodsky District, which borders Pavlovsky Posad. Vorobyov did not identify the facility.
At least 94 drones reportedly shot down
Russian officials claimed that air defenses destroyed 56 drones over Moscow Region overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin also reported dozens of drones flying toward the Russian capital.
According to the officials combined claims, Russian air defenses had shot down at least 94 drones since midnight.
The figures could not be independently verified.
Russia Strikes Ukraine's Largest Wine Retailer, Alcohol Importer
Sochi port also targeted
Farther south, Ukrainian drones reportedly attacked the seaport in Sochi, a major Russian resort city on the Black Sea.
Monitoring channels published footage appearing to show a fire at the port. No further details about damage or casualties were immediately available.
Neither the Krasnodar Krai governor nor the mayor of Sochi had publicly confirmed the reported attack.
Ukraine has increasingly carried out long-range drone assaults against military, industrial and energy targets inside Russia, saying such operations are aimed at degrading Moscow’s ability to wage its war against Ukraine.
Moscow attacks come as Russia keeps up Kyiv drone blitz
The attacks inside Russia came as Moscow continues a relentless drone campaign against Kyiv and the surrounding Kyiv region, now entering its eighth consecutive day since Thursday, Aug. 27.
For more than a week, Russia has repeatedly sent large waves of drones toward the Ukrainian capital, disrupting daily life far beyond the immediate damage caused by individual strikes.
Air raid alerts have repeatedly forced residents into shelters, while attacks and prolonged alerts have disrupted public transport, schools, restaurants, shopping malls and other businesses and public services across Kyiv.
The sustained barrage has increasingly appeared aimed not only at causing casualties and destruction, but at exhausting the city and disrupting its ability to function normally.

articles.title: Nigeria confirms US troop withdrawal
articles.body:
Nigeria confirms US troop withdrawal
Nigeria has confirmed that around 200 US troops deployed to support its fight against armed groups will begin leaving the West African country, with most expected to withdraw by late September.
A smaller advisory and intelligence team will remain, while cooperation in training and information sharing will continue, Nigerian military spokesperson Major General Samaila Uba said on Tuesday. “The deployment of United States personnel was tied to specific operational and counterterrorism objectives,” Uba said, according to AP.
The troops arrived in February to provide intelligence, targeting, and training support. Washington subsequently deployed MQ-9 Reaper surveillance drones to Bauchi Airfield in northeastern Nigeria. The mission came after US President Donald Trump accused the Nigerian authorities of failing to protect Christians and threatened military action.
Nigeria rejected claims that Christians were being systematically targeted, saying jihadist violence, banditry, and communal conflicts affect citizens of different faiths.
The two countries conducted coordinated airstrikes against alleged Islamic State fighters in Sokoto State in December 2025. In May, Nigeria’s Defense Headquarters and US Africa Command said a joint operation in the Lake Chad Basin killed senior Islamic State figure Abu-Bilal al-Minuki. Trump described him as the group’s second-highest-ranking leader globally.
US Africa Command chief General Dagvin Anderson announced in July that most of the American troops had been withdrawn, saying the campaign had successfully degraded Islamic State’s leadership and disrupted its wider network. Samuel Memeh, chairman of Nigeria’s Democratic Leadership Alliance, disputed that assessment. Memeh told RT that the deployment had produced no significant improvement in security and argued that foreign forces alone could not defeat the country’s armed groups.
Nigeria continues to face overlapping threats from Boko Haram and its Islamic State-affiliated offshoot in the northeast, armed bandits operating across the northwest and central regions, and intercommunal violence. More than 40,000 people have been killed since the insurgency began in 2009, UN News reported in January.
Major attacks continued during the US deployment. On August 21, gunmen attacked several communities in Niger State, reportedly killing 30 people and abducting hundreds of worshippers from a mosque. Residents put the number of captives as high as 600, although the authorities said the figure had not been verified. At least 2,000 people reportedly fled into neighboring Benin.
Lagos-based security consultancy SBM Intelligence said in a report last month that at least 7,825 people were abducted across Africa’s most populous nation between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase from the previous 12-month period.

articles.title: Xi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
articles.body:
Xi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday called on "the people of the Middle East" to oppose "externalinterference" and consider reshaping the region's security order during a visit to Egypt. The rare visit by the Chinese leader comes as Beijing aims to expand its influence in the region as the Iran war tests the reliability of the traditional US security umbrella in a vital geostrategic zone.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday urged countries to oppose "external interference" in the Middle East and said Beijing was ready to work with regional states to safeguard maritime shipping, jeopardised by the US-Iran war.
Xi's remarks to his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, come as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region, expanding investment while managing fallout from the war.
"We must uphold the principle that the people of the Middle East are the masters of their own affairs, oppose external interference [and] support regional countries in strengthening dialogue on peace and security," Xi said in a meeting with Sisi, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Xi was greeted by Sisi and a 21-gun salute for talks at the opulent Ittihadiya Presidential Palace in the Egyptian capital.
The talks covered the six-month US-Iran conflict, with both presidents urging "diplomatic solutions" to reach a "comprehensive agreement to end the war", according to a statement from Sisi's spokesperson.
Sisi's office also said the two BRICS members signed an agreement to launch the third phase of the Egyptian-Chinese industrial zone at the Suez Canal, which officials say already hosts 200 companies and investments worth around $4 billion.
The new investments – for which Egypt has not announced a figure – give Beijing even greater influence in the canal zone, a critical artery of global trade, as conflict in the region chokes other conduits.
Read moreGlobal shipping firms to avoid Suez Canal as attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels increase
Xi said China "stands ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation... and eliminate the breeding grounds for conflict".
A series of additional agreements were also signed, though Egyptian officials did not provide details.
'Independent foreign policy'
Beijing is eyeing a greater foothold in the Middle East, at a time when "the United States looks like it can't really make up its mind whether it wants to withdraw from the region or be more engaged", Mirette Mabrouk, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, told AFP.
China sees Egypt as a key partner and an entry point to more regional influence.
For Egypt, closer ties with China are part of a broader effort to diversify partnerships rather than align with a single power, Mabrouk said.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after the Emirati branch of Egypt's second-largest bank, Banque Misr, was targeted by US sanctions.
Washington vowed last month to isolate Iran economically, threatening expanded sanctions that could also hit Chinese banks, among others.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has vowed to safeguard its interests.
In the lead-up to an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month, it has also sought to shore up ties with US-friendly regional nations.
Cairo is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, and historically a key Middle East mediator.
Egypt – which under Sisi's administration became one of the world's top weapons buyers – hosted major joint air combat exercises with the Chinese military in August, featuring Beijing's powerful J-16 fighter jet.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Xi is expected to head to the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids later on Wednesday.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Iran threatens tougher strategy after US strikes kill 4 at wedding
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran threatens tougher strategy after US strikes kill 4 at wedding
Iran threatened to take a tougher line in its war with the United States on Wednesday after the heaviest exchanges in weeks left at least 19 Iranians dead, including four at a wedding -- an incident slammed as a "war crime" by Tehran.
A wave of Iranian attacks earlier targeted US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, after extensive US bombardment hit sites across Iran.
The flare-up deepens the ongoing impasse in the war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz oil export route and the US presses its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran reacted with fury after the Iranian Red Crescent said four people including a child were killed and more than 50 people wounded by a US attack that hit a wedding in Iran's south.
"The truth of this unlawful war of choice -- and the true face of the war crime -- is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei posted on X.
The US military did not address the incident directly.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC", referring to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
Iran's security chief warned the United States would face a "new strategy" from Tehran in the six-month war.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X.
'Acts like Satan'
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out at Washington over the wedding attack, calling the United States "Satan".
"If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan," he posted on X.
The latest round of fighting began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks.
Tehran's forces then targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks, one of which killed two Filipino sailors, according to a Saudi shipping company.
Trump said the US strikes were "in retaliation for the Iranians' failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait" and for firing missiles at the base in Jordan.
More US strikes came on Tuesday, with Iranian state TV reporting explosions along the Hormuz and on an island in the Gulf, as well as an attack on an airport in the southern province of Kerman.
Seven people were killed and eight others wounded in a missile attack in the southern Khuzestan province, IRNA reported.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four personnel were killed in a US strike in Kermanshah province, and three paramilitaries died on Lavan island in the Gulf. Another paramilitary was killed in the southern province of Fars, Iranian media said.
US President Donald Trump had warned of "much harder" attacks if Iran retaliated.
But Tehran's response was widespread, and included attacks targeting US interests in Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan, and a US Marine training camp in Jordan near the Saudi and Israeli borders, according to Iranian media.
In the Gulf, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain and Kuwait, where authorities said an Iranian drone set off a blaze at a residential complex.
'Very saddening'
Iranians expressed regret at the return to hostilities, including the deaths at the wedding. Hossein Moazami, 50, who is self-employed, called the attacks "truly distressing".
"I hope they all return to the negotiating table, because the only people suffering from this are the Iranian people," he said.
"The Americans are on the other side of the world, and nothing happens to them."
A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Sirik following the US strike, with people heard screaming in the background.
"It is a very saddening incident... Thank God the casualties were not higher," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building that was hit, said in a video carried by state TV.
The war began in late February with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
A fragile ceasefire collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Hormuz strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
Incidents in the strait have continued. Iran's Guards said Wednesday that two oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines due to "the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route".

articles.title: Estonian defence minister resigns in €70m EU-funded procurement scandal for Ukraine
articles.body:
Estonia's defence minister has resigned over an arms deal for Ukraine involving EU funds paid to an Indian company with no track record of making shells.
Estonia’s Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur announced on Wednesday that he would step down from his political post after it emerged that the government had used European Union funding to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine from companies with no previous track record of producing the weapons.
Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported on Wednesday that the government struck a deal in 2024 to acquire artillery shells for Ukraine, paying €70 million upfront from the EU’s European Peace Facility to fund the purchase.
The companies involved, however, had never previously sold a single artillery shell. Estonia is now disputing the contracts in a case before the European Court of Arbitration in Strasbourg.
Pevkur, who has served as defence minister since 2022, addressed the scandal while announcing his resignation on public broadcaster ETV. He said that, as minister, he must accept responsibility for the entire area under his authority.
“Although the minister does not count socks and ammunition or conduct contract negotiations, the National Audit Office’s criticisms, primarily concerning the activities of the Defence Forces and the Centre for Defence Investments, raise the question of political responsibility,” Pevkur said.
Estonia’s National Audit Office criticised the Baltic country’s defence spending last month, including investments made by its armed forces. It also raised concerns about the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments, the country’s military procurement agency.
Addressing the artillery contracts, Pevkur stressed that he had not read them, saying the defence minister is not traditionally involved in the details of individual procurement deals.
“The defence minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defence minister does not count socks and ammunition,” Pevkur said, adding: “The defence minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine.”
The European Peace Facility is an EU funding instrument established before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It aims to strengthen the bloc’s ability to prevent conflicts, build and preserve peace, and reinforce international security and stability. It has increasingly been used to support Ukraine through military assistance and procurement.
European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said Brussels was in contact with the Estonian authorities to investigate whether Estonia must pay back the €70 million of European Peace Facility funds.
“There are, of course, safeguards and there are recovery processes in place to make sure that taxpayers' money is well spent," he said, adding that he could not clarify when the talks would take place.
Pevkur’s resignation follows the high-profile departure of Latvia’s Defence Minister Andris Sprūds in May.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defence Ministry increases number of codified weapons and military equipment by more than 500 in one year
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defence Ministry increases number of codified weapons and military equipment by more than 500 in one year
Ukraine's Ministry of Defence has codified and authorised 1,526 new items of weapons and military equipment for supply to Ukraine's defence forces in the first eight months of 2026, which is 543 more than during the same period last year.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence
Quote: "During the same period in 2025, the Defence Ministry codified 983 items of weapons and military equipment, with Ukrainian-made products accounting for 86%."
Details: The share of Ukrainian-made products has also increased: this year, it stands at almost 91%, compared with 86% last year.
In particular, 565 Ukrainian unmanned aerial systems were authorised for supply.
Among the new unmanned aerial systems, the Defence Ministry highlighted long-range deep-strike and middle-strike drones, as well as high-speed interceptor drones.
The ministry also codified 256 types of ammunition, 139 communications systems, 86 ground robotic systems, 64 electronic warfare/electronic intelligence systems, 52 vehicles, 48 items of armoured vehicles and specialised armoured vehicles and 37 optical devices.
In addition, Ukrainian non-lethal equipment was authorised for supply to the defence forces. This included 26 items of rear-support equipment, 21 training simulators, 19 engineering and demining systems and items, 10 items for equipment maintenance and three items for radiological, chemical and biological protection.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that as of mid-June 2026, the Defence Ministry had codified 1,000 items of weapons and military equipment, 892 of which were Ukrainian-made. During the same period in 2025, the ministry had codified 659 items.

articles.title: Twenty Ukrainian firms are racing to catch Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds. This one’s interceptor is already flying combat missions
articles.body:
Twenty Ukrainian companies are now building jet-powered interceptors to down Russia's increasingly fast jet-powered drones. One of them, the Ukrainian-British startup Firebolt Engineering, already has an interceptor flying combat missions with two Air Force units and Ukraine's special operations forces, Defender Media reports.
Russia launched more than 2,500 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in August alone, straining air defenses built to catch the slower, piston-engine Shahed-136. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on 30 August 2026 that four interceptor systems have cleared field testing and are being scaled toward mass production. It is unclear whether Griffen, Firebolt's drone, is among them.
Grenadyr funds a spinout
Firebolt was spun out after the UK-based investment fund Grenadyr backed the team behind the interceptor project. Grenadyr's director, Tomasz Wozniak, told the outlet that a reliable way to intercept jet-powered Shaheds "has never been more important" as Russia scales up the faster drones.
Grenadyr and Firebolt have not disclosed the size of the investment, though the fund's check ranged from $350,000 to $1.3 million.
The new company employs up to 25 people across Ukraine and the UK, split into component manufacturing, final assembly, and calibration, plus a separate R&D unit. Its CEO, who asked to be identified only as Mykola, led the interceptor project prior to the spinout.
Griffen flies, but not against jets yet
Griffen, Firebolt's first product, is a fixed-wing, jet-powered interceptor that reaches speeds above 350 km/h, altitudes above 7.5 km, and a range of up to 120 km, according to Defender Media. Mykola said the team aims to push its speed past 400 km/h through aerodynamic changes. The drone currently costs an estimated $8,300–$10,500.
Griffen still flies on Chinese engines while its British partner, Dynamic Propulsion, develops a turbojet built specifically for the drone, with test samples expected by the end of summer. Firebolt can build 30 Griffens a month and is working to add more crews to fly them, Mykola said. The drone's first confirmed kill, however, was a conventional-engine Geran — not the jet-powered variant it was designed to catch.
Autonomy waits on Ukraine's radars
Firebolt is developing a homing system meant to let Griffen find and strike targets without an operator, a goal shared by rival interceptor makers The Fourth Law, SkyFall, and F-Drones. The system is in testing and expected to ship by default by mid-fall, Mykola said.
Full autonomy, he added, is bottlenecked by Ukraine's radar coverage, which he described as too thin and fragmented to reliably feed target data to an autonomous drone. Closing that gap, he said, depends on the state buying more radars — a decision outside Firebolt's control.
