articles.title: EU Countries Pledge More Air Defense to Protect Ukraine From Russian Missile Attacks
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
EU Countries Pledge More Air Defense to Protect Ukraine From Russian Missile Attacks
Several European Union member states pledged additional air defense systems for Ukraine during an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers and invited non-EU partners in Ireland, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, according to Ukrinform correspondent on September 2.
Speaking at a press conference following the meeting, Kallas said Russia had shown no indication of changing its war objectives, pointing to recent Russian strikes on Kyiv as evidence that Moscow was not seeking peace.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Against this backdrop, Kallas said the EU was focused on providing Ukraine with the capabilities necessary to defend itself against Russian attacks.
According to the EU foreign policy chief, €8.47 billion (nearly $10 billion) has already been allocated through the Ukraine Support Loan, while an additional €6.1 billion (about $6.7 billion) has been approved, including funding for air defense.
Kallas stressed, however, that EU-level financing alone was insufficient and needed to be supplemented by bilateral assistance from individual countries. She welcomed commitments made during the meeting by several member states to provide Ukraine with additional air defense capabilities to counter Russian missile attacks.
Kallas did not specify how many interceptor missiles had been pledged. She said details on the quantities and specific contributions would be announced separately by the countries that had committed to providing them.
The new commitments come as individual European countries continue to strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses through bilateral support. Germany, in particular, is expected to deliver additional air defense packages to Ukraine later this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced following talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian and German officials are also finalizing a bilateral Drone Deal aimed at strengthening the defense capabilities of both countries.

articles.title: Air defenses down 135 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Air defenses down 135 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this in a Telegram post.
Beginning at 18:00 on Wednesday, September 2, the enemy attacked Ukraine with 163 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (about half of them jet-powered), S8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodya-type decoy drones launched from the directions of Millerovo and Oryol, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The aerial attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:30 on Thursday, September 3, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 135 UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera drones, and other types of UAVs.
Hits were recorded at 15 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
As reported by Ukrinform, 17 people, including three children, were injured in a Russian attack on Odesa overnight on September 3.

articles.title: Moscow Airports Go Dark for Second Straight Night After Zelenskyy Warns Airlines to Stay Away From Russia
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Moscow Airports Go Dark for Second Straight Night After Zelenskyy Warns Airlines to Stay Away From Russia
Moscow’s Vnukovo and Sheremetyevo airports suspended operations for a second consecutive night amid drone threats, shortly after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines and insurers that Russia’s increasingly contested airspace poses a growing risk to civilian aviation, according to The Moscow Times on September 3.
Russia’s federal aviation authority, Rosaviatsia, again imposed temporary restrictions on aircraft movements at the two major Moscow airports on September 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Temporary restrictions have been introduced on the arrival and departure of aircraft,” Rosaviatsia said.
The disruption followed another night of severe delays across Moscow’s aviation network.
Three airports in the Russian capital temporarily halted operations the previous night. Flightradar24 data showed 21 flights canceled and another 235 delayed at Sheremetyevo, while Vnukovo recorded 22 cancellations and 94 delays.
The repeated shutdowns came after Zelenskyy issued a warning on September 1 to international airlines, aviation insurers and companies still operating through Russian airspace.
The Ukrainian President said Kyiv intends to intensify long-range drone operations inside Russia in response to Moscow’s sustained strikes against Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure, warning that the growing presence of drones over Russian territory must increasingly factor into commercial aviation decisions.
Ukraine has stressed that its forces do not target civilian aircraft.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine had formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization, or ICAO, that Russian airspace presents growing dangers to civilian aviation.
Ukraine has also asked the UN aviation body to urge member states to completely prohibit civilian aircraft from operating in Russian airspace.
According to a letter from Ukrainian Infrastructure Minister Mykola Kalashnyk cited by Reuters, Kyiv argues that stronger international measures are necessary to minimize the risk of a civilian aviation disaster as military activity inside Russia intensifies.
Ukraine’s position is that the consequences of Russia’s war of aggression can no longer be treated as confined to Ukrainian airspace while Moscow continues launching missiles and drones against Ukrainian territory and Kyiv expands long-range operations against targets inside Russia.
Previously, Türkiye’s largest private airline, Pegasus Airlines, turned several Moscow-bound aircraft around mid-flight and canceled dozens of services to Russia overnight on September 2, amid drone-related disruptions at Russian airports and warnings from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the growing risks of operating in Russian airspace.

articles.title: Zelenskyy reports destruction in 13 regions due to overnight Russian attacks
articles.body:
Attacks by Russian occupiers on Thursday night caused destruction in 13 regions of Ukraine, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported.
Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that necessary services continued to work in Odesa at the site where a drone struck a residential high-rise building, noting that due to damage to apartments from the 10th to the 17th floors, 17 people were known to have been injured, including three children. He reported that work to eliminate the consequences of the strike continued in Obukhiv and Boryspil districts of Kyiv region, adding that a specific number of State Emergency Service rescuers were fighting a fire at a pharmaceutical company warehouse. He noted that strikes also targeted Nikopol, Kherson, Sumy, Zaporizhia, and Khmelnytsky, with destruction reported across 13 regions during that night alone.
He noted that in many cities and communities across Ukraine, air alerts practically never ceased due to the threat of Russian jet-powered drones, emphasizing that the enemy had not taken a vacation, had found a new escalation, and did not plan to slow its momentum.
The president stated that there was a need to accelerate European production of defense systems, primarily anti-missile and anti-drone air defense. He added that Europe could be self-sufficient and strong, noting that a great deal had already been done toward that end in recent years, and emphasizing that only in that way could it protect itself and its way of life. He reported that they worked daily with partners on new defense packages.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill 5, injure 67 across Ukraine as drones target western regions
articles.body:
Russian attacks killed at least five people and injured at least 66 across Ukraine over the past day, as drones reached western regions including Khmelnytskyi and Vinnytsia oblasts, local authorities said on Sept. 3.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian attacks caused damage in 13 oblasts overnight, while air raid alerts remained active for extended periods in many cities and communities due to the threat of jet-powered drones.
"The enemy did not go on vacation – the Russians have found a new escalation and have no plans to slow it down," Zelensky said. "We need a stronger response and countermeasures, and faster European production of defensive systems, primarily air defense – both anti-missile and anti-drone."
In western Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Russian drones struck twice overnight, Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Drone debris fell on the grounds of an enterprise in the city of Khmelnytskyi, setting a truck on fire and damaging a warehouse. The driver suffered shrapnel wounds and was hospitalized. A second attack caused a fire at another enterprise in the oblast, according to the DSNS.
In neighboring Vinnytsia Oblast, two women were injured after what authorities described as the likely fall of drone debris in the regional capital. Residential buildings and surrounding property were damaged.
The largest number of injuries was reported in Odesa Oblast, where at least 17 people, including three children, were injured in a Russian attack. Twenty apartments on the 10th through 17th floors of a residential building and 12 nearby cars were damaged, according to Governor Oleh Kiper.
Overall, Russia launched 163 Shahed-type drones and other aerial targets overnight, around half of them jet-powered, according to Ukraine's Air Force. The attack also included S8000 Banderol munitions, Gerbera drones, and decoys. Air defenses downed 135 drones, while strikes were recorded at 15 locations and debris from intercepted drones fell at four others, the Air Force said.
In Kyiv Oblast, a man suffered shrapnel wounds in Boryspil district and was hospitalized following a Russian attack, local authorities said. Warehouses, an administrative building, a shop, and kiosks were damaged. A private house also caught fire, and a car was damaged.
The deadliest attacks were reported in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, where four people were killed and 13 injured as Russian forces struck six districts with drones, artillery, and a glide bomb, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Educational facilities, apartment buildings, a food warehouse, and cars were damaged.
In Kherson Oblast, one person was killed and 16 others injured in Russian attacks, according to local authorities. Three apartment buildings, six houses, an administrative building, a humanitarian aid distribution point, agricultural machinery, and cars were damaged.
In Sumy Oblast, eight civilians were injured as Russian forces carried out nearly 40 attacks against 24 settlements over the past day, local authorities said.
In Donetsk Oblast, six people were injured, including five in Kramatorsk and one in Sloviansk, as Russian forces attacked settlements in the region 37 times over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, two people were injured as Russian forces attacked 10 settlements using a missile, Molniya and FPV drones, and dozens of other UAVs, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, one person was injured in an attack on the city of Zaporizhzhia, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 957 strikes against 52 settlements across the oblast over the past day.

articles.title: Trump Suggests Renaming Strait of Hormuz the 'Trump Strait' Amid Renewed Iran Hostilities
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz the “Trump Strait” amid renewed hostilities with Iran following a brief period of respite.
“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to Trump Strait? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” the President said Wednesday.
Trump floated the idea a day after the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) launched a new wave of strikes against Iranian military targets.
The U.S. military said it struck air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Iran’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday released a statement insisting the U.S. had attacked civilian areas and service infrastructure in the provinces of Khuzestan, Sistan and Baluchestan, Hormozgan, and Kerman. It said a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak, Sirik County, had been struck, resulting in fatalities and injuries.
In a statement to TIME, CENTCOM spokesperson Navy Captain Tim Hawkins said: “We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC.”
The IRGC said it had launched retaliatory strikes on U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain, alongside an additional U.S. facility in Iraq, overnight Tuesday.
The renewed hostilities and threats come after a roughly month-long pause in active hostilities between the two countries. On Sunday, the U.S. military struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island it said were preparing to fire rockets carrying naval mines into the Strait.
Trump’s attempt to rename the Strait underscores how both Iran and the U.S. have continued to vie for control of the vital waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil transited before the war.
The President has previously turned to name changes as a show of power and a way to undermine his perceived adversaries, most recently renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” during the U.S. trade war with Canada.
Meanwhile, although Trump has claimed the U.S. has near total control of the Strait, the tussle over the body of water—which reignited after both countries adopted different interpretations of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)—rages on.
With no clear path to a negotiated truce, Washington has doubled down on its “economic D-Day” threats against Tehran, increasing the pressure by tightening sanctions in addition to military action.
Traffic falls once more amid renewed instability for the Strait of Hormuz
The latest round of strikes between the U.S. and Iran has further disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, shared data with TIME that shows only six ships crossed the Strait on Tuesday—a drop from 19 vessels on Friday last week.
Before the Iran war began on Feb. 28, 138 vessels typically passed through the vital trade waterway during a 24-hour period.
On Wednesday, U.K. Maritime Operations (UKMTO) reported an attack on a tanker transiting the Strait that resulted in two casualties.
Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry reported that Iran had targeted a Saudi tanker in the waterway, with UKMTO later stating that two crew members had been killed.
Iran's Gulf neighbors condemn Tehran's “heinous” retaliatory attacks
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) described Iran’s overnight retaliatory strikes against U.S. bases in the region as a “heinous” act. Secretary General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi said "these Iranian attacks represent a blatant violation of state sovereignty and a direct threat to their security and stability."
He stated that the GCC stands “firmly alongside” these countries “in all measures and actions taken to preserve their sovereignty, protect their security and stability, and ensure the safety of their peoples and residents.”
The council is made up of six countries on the Arabian Peninsula: Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
The UAE, which suspended trade with Iran in August amid missile strikes, released its own statement condemning Iran’s strikes across the wider Gulf region.
“These hostile attacks constitute a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the brotherly nations and a threat to their security and stability,” said the UAE’S Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Wednesday.

articles.title: Deputy commander of Russian Volunteer Corps describes detention in secret prison, where he was threatened with "disappearing forever"
articles.body:
Deputy commander of Russian Volunteer Corps describes detention in secret prison, where he was threatened with "disappearing forever"
Stepan Kaplunov, Deputy Commander for Combat Operations of the Russian Volunteer Corps The Russian Volunteer Corps is a military and political organisation established in 2022 that consists of Russian volunteers who have been fighting for Ukraine since 2014. , has described details of his abduction by Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) officers and explained why, under pressure and threats in a secret prison, he was forced to admit to having links with the Russian FSB.
Source: Kaplunov in an interview with Radio NV
Details: According to Kaplunov, he was abducted on 23 August near his house. He was handcuffed, had his eyes taped shut and was taken to a secret prison.
"For the first two days, I was interrogated more intensively. On the third day, they hardly spoke to me at all. As far as I understand, most likely the aim was to discredit the Tymur Special Unit [special-purpose unit within Defence Intelligence of Ukraine – ed.], including our commander directly – Tymur. I was accused of having links with representatives of the FSB. I later attributed this connection to my immediate superior, Dmytro – Commander Dmytro Ivanov. So this was not about WhiteRex [Russian Volunteer Corps commander Denis Kapustin – ed.]. Accordingly, I was not subjected to physical violence, apart from the abduction itself at the beginning. Nevertheless, there were remarks that I could disappear forever. In other words, there was talk of digging holes. We all understand what that means," he said.
Kaplunov said that, while in that difficult situation, he fully agreed with the version that he "had a connection with the FSB and subsequently attributed this contact to my immediate commander, Dmytro".
"Although in reality nothing of the sort had happened. I went along with it because of my situation and under psychological pressure," he stressed.
Kaplunov added that during his detention he was held at two different locations, but was released after nine days.
"I cannot tell you about events in the outside world, interaction between the services, communications and so on. After nine days, I was simply told: 'Get out.' I was also transferred – either to one vehicle or two. After that, I was taken to the place where, roughly speaking, I had been abducted, but I was not warned in advance that my flat would also be searched," he said.
Asked whether Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President, had contacted Kaplunov during that period, he replied: "Not at all."
"I know that Kyrylo Oleksiiovych is following this situation closely and keeping his finger on the pulse, but directly – no," Kaplunov said.
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that Kaplunov had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of the building where he was living.
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) and the SSU in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi District, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance. As of 10:00 on the same day, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the standoff was still ongoing.
- Later, officers from the State Bureau of Investigation and the head of the SSU's Special Operations Centre Alpha arrived at the scene. According to Ukrainska Pravda sources, three DIU officers were injured in the confrontation.
- Meanwhile, the SSU said that together with DIU, it had foiled a terrorist attack against a leader of a Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine.

articles.title: Hey EU, your new rules for ChatGPT don’t cover chat
articles.body:
Hey EU, your new rules for ChatGPT don’t cover chat
The world’s most popular chatbot is now under Europe’s stringent regulatory purview. But classifying it as a search engine leaves many of its core functionalities uncovered.
The EU's decision to regulate ChatGPT as a search engine will make sense to those who use it as one. But what if you use it as a friend? Or a therapist? Or to have a chat about the upcoming election?
Those are among the multitude of new questions that the advent of generative AI poses for European regulators — who, experts say, have yet to find sufficient answers.
The EU executive on Monday designated ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Search Engine under the Digital Services Act, imposing a range of transparency and risk-mitigation obligations similar to those faced by traditional search leaders like Google and Microsoft’s Bing, which exceed 45 million monthly users. ChatGPT’s parent company, OpenAI, risks fines of up to 6% of its annual global revenue if it fails to meet these requirements.
Advertisement
Still, the designation is narrow and applies only to the parts of the tool that act as a search engine, meaning conversations in which the chatbot adds its own input don't appear to be covered. Under the DSA, the Commission could instead have opted to categorize ChatGPT as a Very Large Online Platform, a designation that usually applies to social media and e-commerce and imposes different obligations.
Yet neither category corresponds to the range of uses that chatbots offer.
“ChatGPT is much more than a search engine and there are also risks connected to the chatbot itself which fall outside the (regulation’s) strongest obligations” Danish socialist MEP Christel Schaldemose who was among the key negotiators for the law, said.
MEP Christel Schaldemose pointed out the risks to children. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
She pointed to risks to children, "such as emotional dependency and manipulative or addictive design,” urging the Commission to clarify how they are covered by existing rules.
ChatGPT and its peers have been the subject of global controversy for allegedly contributing to the tragic suicides of teenagers, including 16-year-old Adam Raine of California, whose parents have sued the company.
Therapy and companionship are hardly fringe use cases for AI chatbots; as many as 60 percent of adults globally use them for therapy, one recent insurance industry study found.
Advertisement
Hybrid space
The current digital services law, finalized in 2022, did not foresee the boom in chatbots. João Pedro Quintais, associate law professor at the University of Amsterdam, describes ChatGPT as "a hybrid” technology that has the functions of both a search engine and online platforms, as well as others closer to those of a publisher of its own content.
The “search engine” designation may limit the Commission's ability to supervise how ChatGPT handles risks not only to teens' mental health, but also to election integrity or illegal content.
Asking ChatGPT to name the candidates in a local election should now be covered under the DSA. Instead, a conversation between a user and a chatbot about who to vote for, where misinformation could come out, may not be.
The chatbot’s designation took just under a year for the Commission to conclude, with questions around which bucket to put it in stumping the bureaucrats. Experts say that without seeing the full text of this week's designation, it is hard to know exactly what OpenAI's obligations will be.
While a platform designation would have imposed additional obligations on OpenAI for content moderation under the Digital Services Act, it would have let the company off the hook in a significant way. The DSA and other platform laws globally are built around the concept of 'safe harbor,' under which companies are not liable for content on their platforms because it is uploaded by users. But the advent of chatbots poses the question of whether a two-way chat between a person and machine counts as “user-generated content.”
Models and risks
While the regulatory focus on ChatGPT as a consumer-facing application is new, the Commission has been keeping a close eye on the artificial intelligence models that power it through the AI Act.
Advertisement
ChatGPT’s parent company OpenAI, along with the likes of Anthropic and Google’s Gemini, are builders of what are known as general-purpose AI models, which can perform a wide variety of tasks that can pose “possible systemic risks.”
Since last August, under the bloc’s flagship AI law, these companies have the obligation to “assess and mitigate” the risks those models pose. The Commission started enforcing it at the end of August, when it grilled a series of AI companies on their security procedures.
Previously, a group of experts had singled out four risks: enabling nuclear weapons or the development of bioweapons, losing control over the models, rogue AI models starting to hack, or models performing large-scale manipulation.
Photo illustration of a virtual friend on the screen of an iPhone. | Olivier DoulieryAFP via Getty Images
But as scary as they are, these systemic risks leave out a whole series of potential problems for both users and society as a whole.
“[That guidance] is more focused on so-called existential risks than risks to fundamental rights,” said Daniel Leufer, emerging technologies policy lead at AccessNow.
He argued that with the DSA designation of ChatGPT, there’s a chance “to get into the weeds of design decisions and treat ChatGPT more like what it really is, which is a product.”
Advertisement
Since AI has had such a rapid and far-reaching impact, regulation around it is still taking shape. Italian Social-Democrat lawmaker Brando Benifei, the Parliament’s lead on artificial intelligence, defended the European response that divides oversight between applications and the AI models, saying the two rulebooks can “powerfully complement” one another.
Still, Benifei acknowledged that oversight through the DSA is “urgently needed” to protect the people actually using AI tools, citing “dangerous mental health dependencies” that people develop through companion chatbots as a specific example.
“Scrutiny now expands from the underlying model to how these services are actually designed and deployed.”

articles.title: Ukraine gets first Skyranger 35 systems on Leopard 1 tanks
articles.body:
- Ukraine's 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment has reportedly received the first Rheinmetall Skyranger 35 air defense systems mounted on Leopard 1 chassis.
- The contract, signed in the second half of 2025, is financed by an EU country using proceeds from frozen Russian assets.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces have shown footage of what appears to be one of the first Skyranger 35 short-range air defense systems mounted on a Leopard 1 tank chassis to reach Ukrainian units.
GAU, an account that tracks German military assistance to Ukraine, identified the unit in the footage as Ukraine’s 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment, part of the Ground Forces. The account said the regiment appears to have taken delivery of the first Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 systems built by Rheinmetall.
Rheinmetall announced the contract for the systems in October 2025, saying an unnamed European Union country would finance the deal using proceeds from frozen Russian assets under the EU’s Windfall Profit Mechanism. The company put the order’s value in the hundreds of millions of euros and said production and integration would take place at Rheinmetall Italia’s headquarters in Rome. Ukraine had already fielded earlier Skyranger 35 systems mounted on truck chassis; the Leopard 1 version is a separate, tracked variant.
The Skyranger 35 is built around a KDG 35/1000 revolver cannon firing 35x228mm ammunition at a rate of 1,000 rounds per minute, with an effective range up to 4,000 meters (2.5 miles). The system fires airburst rounds that detonate near a target and scatter tungsten sub-projectiles, a design intended to improve hit probability against small, fast-moving threats such as Shahed-type drones and FPVs. Rheinmetall has said the turret shares a high degree of commonality with the company’s Oerlikon Revolver Gun Mk 3 and could eventually be fitted with guided missiles.
Rheinmetall first showed the Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 publicly in September 2024, at a demonstration event at the Erprobungszentrum Ochsenboden test site in Switzerland. That demonstrator used a Leopard 1A5BE hull with an unmanned turret carrying 252 rounds, with the two-person crew, a commander and a gunner, seated in the front of the hull. Representatives from defense ministries and industry in 26 countries attended.
Germany’s own military has ordered 19 Skyranger systems and has discussed acquiring several hundred more, following reports of unidentified drones appearing in European airspace. Ukraine’s version reaching the field ahead of Germany’s own fielding was noted at the time the October contract was announced.
Rheinmetall has previously delivered Skyranger 35 units to Ukraine mounted on wheeled truck platforms. The Leopard 1 chassis gives the new variant tracked mobility and armor protection not available on the truck-based version, allowing it to operate closer to the front line. Ukraine has received roughly 170 Leopard 1 tanks from Germany and other partners since 2023, with about 25 confirmed damaged or destroyed, according to the open-source tracking project Oryx.

articles.title: Ukrainian brigade trials Serval Cube EW dome in combat-like conditions, suppresses every drone launched at it
articles.body:
Ukraine's 58th Separate Motorized Infantry Brigade has tested a domestic dome-type electronic-warfare system, Serval Cube, against drones simulating a Russian attack. The brigade's electronic-warfare unit staged the trial under conditions close to real combat, the brigade said.
Serval Cube jams the control, navigation, and video-transmission channels a drone depends on rather than destroying it outright, Armyinform said. That kind of interference does not bring down the aircraft. It strips it of the ability to complete a mission or return to its operator.
Ukraine's counter-drone field is crowded
Ukrainian defense firms have been racing to field more of this kind of gear this year: in July, Contra Drone unveiled a 20-system counter-drone architecture combining electronic warfare, radar, and autonomous interceptors.
Another firm, Rebel Group, said this week its stationary jamming and signals intelligence system, Brama, has cleared range and lab testing and is now seeking official codification. Brama works by detecting a drone's analog video frequency, decoding it, and jamming both the video and control channels at once.
EW now shields nearly everything at the front
Electronic warfare has become one of the key elements of front-line defense, the brigade said, covering troops, positions, logistics routes, transport, shelters, and the launch sites of Ukraine's own drones against Russian FPV drones and reconnaissance UAVs.
FPV drones — small, camera-equipped quadcopters flown by a remote pilot wearing video goggles — have become a primary strike weapon for both sides along the front this year. That is why soldiers constantly test and refine the equipment they carry, the brigade said.
A scripted attack, and nothing got through
The brigade's electronic-warfare company ran the test, building a scenario meant to mirror combat as closely as possible: at one position, operators launched Mavic quadcopters, widely used for reconnaissance, alongside FPV strike drones. At another, the unit deployed the Serval Cube complex.
Serval Cube suppressed every drone launched against it during the trial — none reached its designated target, the brigade said.

articles.title: Doubling of F-15EX Fleet Comes with Risks for USAF to Manage: New Pentagon Report
articles.body:
The Air Force’s decision to more than double its purchase of F-15EX Eagle II jets may bolster the service’s fighter fleet, but it also comes with risks and questions officials will have to manage in the years ahead, a new Pentagon report warns.
Earlier this year, Air Force officials announced plans to expand its planned F-15EX fleet from 129 to 267 jets, as they move recapitalize the older F-15E Strike Eagle. When the change was announced as part of the fiscal 2027 budget rollout, the Air Force said it needed to buy more F-15EXs alongside F-35As because both jets bring different capabilities that will be needed in in a future war.
Yet in the F-15EX’s selected acquisition report released in August, program officials noted “new cost and schedule uncertainties” that come with the increase they’re trying to mitigate.
Boeing declined to comment on the concerns raised in the acquisition report. The Air Force did not immediately respond to a query.
One concern is how the expanded procurement plan will play out over time. The previous F-15EX acquisition strategy called for eight lots of the jet; the new one calls for 12. This will likely require Boeing to conduct “a major technical refresh” to overcome diminishing manufacturing sources and material shortages, the report states.
Eventually, key systems such as the F-15EX’s radar, mission computer, electronic warfare suite, and engines could become obsolete and need to be replaced. This “constitutes a significant redesign effort,” the report states.
The program’s method for managing this risk involves testing and integrating those upgraded subsystems as part of future operational flight program releases now scheduled for between 2031 and 2035.
“This provides a structured, risk-reduced pathway for flight testing and fielding these new capabilities without causing a gap in the production line,” the report said.
Another concern is uncertainty around the costs of extending production. Program officials say they have not yet fully estimated those costs, though they has begun a rapid cost estimation process to inform the fiscal 2028 budget request. Until then, the EX program is using government estimates for its initial budget sizing, while “commissioning formal studies to obtain preliminary cost and schedule estimates from the contractors,” the report said.
The report also highlighted schedule issues that will need to be worked through in the short and long term. Parts and material shortages risk slowing the production of F-15EX jets in Lot 2 and beyond, officials wrote, noting that some of the most acute shortages including the jet’s Elbit-made large area displays and low-profile heads-up displays, General Electric F110 engines, and Collins-made cartridges for ejection systems.
Those shortages were mitigated for Lot 1B largely by stocking up on supplies during the production halt caused by a factory strike from August to November 2025—but the risks remain for future lots, the report said. The Pentagon is taking actions to keep the F-15EX’s production schedule on track, such as by putting borrowing and payback agreements in place with foreign military sales customers to maintain the supply of crucial parts.
But the strike at Boeing’s St. Louis, Mo., plant that makes the F-15EX has permanently set the jet behind schedule, the report said. Boeing’s F-15EX contract requires it to deliver all 12 Lot 3 jets in early calendar 2026, but due to the strike, the report said the company will only be able to deliver six of those jets by the end of 2026.
These “unrecoverable delays” are having cascading effects on the Air Force’s plans to field the Eagle II. The acquisition report notes the 142nd Wing of the Oregon Air National Guard will not receive all of its F-15EXs from Lot 2 until at least mid-2026, and the first Lot 3 F-15EXs, meant to be stationed overseas, will not be fielded until at least the first quarter of fiscal 2027, the report said.
These oversea jets will be stationed at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan. Kadena previously had F-15C and D Eagle fighters, but the Air Force started retiring those aging fighters in November 2022. Since then, a steady stream of other fighters have rotated through Kadena. The planned permanent force of F-15EXs, which were originally supposed to start arriving in spring 2026, have been delayed into 2027.
The F-15EX program management office is working with the Defense Department’s Business Operators for National Defense, or BOND, team to figure out how to optimize the F-15EX production schedule and prioritize the Lot 3 jets planned for overseas assignments as they go through the final assembly process, the report said.
The program office is also working with Air Combat Command and the National Guard Bureau to create a coordinated bridging strategy, that makes sure older jets or alternate force structures are available to cover the Air Force’s operational requirements, until the F-15EXs arrive.
The fourth lot of F-15EXs is also already behind schedule, according to the report. Boeing should have started delivering those jets in 2026, the report said, but they are now not expected to start arriving until calendar 2028. Boeing has to increase its F-15EX production rate to two per month to meet its delivery requirements, the report said.

articles.title: Danish intelligence says Russia preparing sabotage attacks against defense industry
articles.body:
Seyma Erkul Dayanc
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Russian intelligence services are actively preparing sabotage operations against companies in Denmark's defense industry, public broadcaster DR reported Wednesday, citing the Danish intelligence service.
"We see that Danish companies are also targets for concrete Russian sabotage planning, and that Russian intelligence services are actively preparing sabotage operations aimed at the defense industry in Denmark," said Emil Graesholm, head of counterintelligence at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET).
Graesholm also told Danish newspaper Berlingske that authorities had uncovered specific Russian plans for sabotage operations against companies in Denmark.
"Therefore, this is not just a warning that it might come to Denmark one day. We are already seeing the planning now. Very concretely," he said.
The companies that could be targeted include firms in the defense industry linked to military aid to Ukraine, according to PET.
The intelligence service said it has identified "concrete examples" of Russia attempting to recruit ordinary Danes through social media and other online platforms.
Such individuals could be asked to perform tasks including photographing companies or installations for use in planning sabotage operations, PET said.
"It is extremely serious if ordinary Danes help Russian intelligence services – either intentionally or unknowingly," Graesholm said.
PET said it works closely with Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service and the Danish Agency for Social Security and Preparedness, and regularly updates police districts on the threat assessment.
"We have continuously briefed selected companies and industry organizations on the threat picture, and together with other authorities we have advised on specific security measures," Graesholm said.
He added that the defense industry broadly needed to take the “necessary security measures" to protect itself.
Graesholm said PET considered the threat sufficiently concrete to publicly warn about it.
"It is such a concrete identification and preparation that we find it necessary to go out with the message that it is a threat that must be taken seriously," he said.
The Confederation of Danish Industry said it was taking PET's assessment seriously and was in close contact with relevant authorities.
"The changed threat picture calls for increased attention from companies, but also for calm and proportionality," said Rasmus Anderskouv, head of security and preparedness at the organization.
Anderskouv said companies should assess their specific exposure and ensure their security and emergency preparedness measures were functioning properly.
Flemming Splidsboel, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, described PET's announcement as serious and said the threat was "new," "concrete" and "advanced."
Former Defense Intelligence Service chief analyst Jakob Kaarsbo said PET's decision to speak publicly could be intended to signal to Russia that Danish authorities were aware of its activities.

articles.title: Rubio explained the CIA director’s unexpected visit to Moscow
articles.body:
Rubio explained the CIA director’s unexpected visit to Moscow
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described John Ratcliffe’s trip to Moscow as an attempt to preserve intelligence communication channels. The visit took place amid the Russia–Ukraine war.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio downplayed CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s unexpected trip to Moscow last week, calling it an attempt to keep channels of communication with Russia open. Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
His visit there was largely routine in the sense that it was aimed only at establishing and further developing these channels of communication between intelligence services. Such things may prove useful during a period of crisis or conflict
Context
During a secret visit to Moscow, CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed holding a trilateral meeting involving U.S. President Donald Trump, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
In response, Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov called reports about the proposed trilateral summit “information hoaxes.”
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin himself refused to meet with the head of the United States Central Intelligence Agency, John Ratcliffe, after it became clear for what purpose he had come to Moscow.
Reminder
U.S. President Donald Trump said that Ukraine and Russia should end the war. He also recalled that he had previously stopped eight other wars.

articles.title: Zelensky warns airlines Russian skies not safe due to Ukraine drones
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Tuesday that his country's drones would make Russia's airspace "completely unsafe" for the duration of the war, drawing accusations of "state terrorism" from Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Mark Owen, Former British Military Intelligence Officer Philip Ingram explains that Zelensky's warning is addressed to "those international airlines from the Middle East, from South East Asia, China included that are still operating into Moscow" adding that "it's all part of the information war and bringing the overall conflict to the Russian people".

articles.title: Ukraine Requests EU Funding for PAC-3 Missiles for Patriot Systems
articles.body:
Ukraine has submitted a new request to the European Union for funding to purchase PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made the statement during a joint appearance with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels, Ukrinform news agency reported.
According to von der Leyen, the request is worth several billion euros and would cover expenses related to strengthening Ukraine’s air defense capabilities.
“We have received a new payment request. It is worth several billion euros and would cover Ukraine’s air defences, including the highly advanced PAC-3 Patriot air defence systems,” Ursula von der Leyen said.
The European Commission president said EU member states are currently reviewing the request, but the process is already “moving in the right direction.”
Ukraine recently received AIM missiles and additional missiles for Patriot air defense systems, as well as confirmation that several Crotale systems and ammunition for them would be transferred.
Ukraine’s MIM-104 Patriot air defense systems use PAC-2 missiles to engage aerodynamic targets at long ranges and PAC-3 interceptors designed to destroy ballistic missiles through direct kinetic interception.
